entries.literal: Returning, he reported affairs and was transferred to be assistant to the Chamberlain for Ceremonials.

entries.zh: 御史大夫張湯劾偃矯制大害，法至死。
entries.en: Imperial Counselor Zhang Tang impeached him for counterfeiting orders with grave consequences—a capital crime.
entries.literal: Imperial Counselor Zhang Tang impeached Yan for forging an edict with great harm; by law it reached death.

entries.zh: 偃以為春秋之義，大夫出疆，有可以安社稷，存萬民，顓之可也。
entries.en: Xu Yan cited the Spring and Autumn principle that a minister abroad may act on his own authority if the altars and the lives of the people hang in the balance.
entries.literal: Yan thought that according to the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals, when a grandee goes beyond the border, if there is something by which he can secure the altars of soil and grain and preserve the myriad people, to assume authority is permissible.

entries.zh: 湯以致其法，不能詘其義。
entries.en: Zhang Tang could press the statute but could not overturn the moral argument.
entries.literal: Tang by this applied the law but could not refute his meaning.

entries.zh: 有詔下軍問狀，軍詰偃曰：「古者諸侯國異俗分，百里不通，時有聘會之事，安危之勢，呼吸成變，故有不受辭造命顓己之宜；
entries.en: An edict ordered Zhong Jun to examine the case. He questioned Xu Yan: 'In ancient times each feudal state kept its own ways; a hundred li might as well have been a world apart. Envoys hurried between courts because fortune could turn in a breath, so a minister might rightly assume emergency powers without waiting for a written order.
entries.literal: There was an edict sent down to Jun to ask the circumstances; Jun interrogated Yan, saying: 'In antiquity the feudal states differed in custom and were divided; within a hundred li they did not communicate; from time to time there were matters of visiting and meeting; the posture of safety and danger could change in a breath; therefore there was propriety in not receiving orders and making commands, assuming authority for oneself.

entries.zh: 今天下為一，萬里同風，故春秋『王者無外』。
entries.en: Today the empire is one house under a single wind for ten thousand li, and the Annals teach that the king knows no "outside."
entries.literal: Now the realm is one, ten thousand li share one wind; therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals say "the king has nothing outside."

entries.zh: 偃巡封域之中，稱以出疆何也？
entries.en: You never left the emperor's domain—how can you call that "crossing the border"?
entries.literal: Yan toured within the sealed domain—calling it going beyond the border, how is that?

entries.zh: 且鹽鐵，郡有餘臧，正二國廢，國家不足以為利害，而以安社稷存萬民為辭，何也？」
entries.en: Besides, every commandery stockpiles salt and iron; ending the two kingdoms' local monopolies would barely touch the central treasury. What sense is there in pleading the fate of the altars and the people?'
entries.literal: Moreover as for salt and iron, the commanderies have surplus in store; whether or not the two kingdoms' monopolies were suspended would not materially help or harm the central government—so to cite securing the altars and preserving the myriad people as your excuse, how is that?'

entries.zh: 又詰偃：「膠東南近琅邪，北接北海，魯國西枕泰山，東有東海，受其鹽鐵。
entries.en: Zhong Jun pressed further: 'Jiaodong borders Langye to the south and Beihai to the north; Lu lies against Mount Tai in the west and the Eastern Sea in the east—both regions already draw salt and iron from their own ground.
entries.literal: He again interrogated Yan: 'Jiaodong on the south nears Langye, on the north joins Beihai; the state of Lu on the west pillows Mount Tai, on the east has the Eastern Sea—they draw on their own salt and iron.

entries.zh: 偃度四郡口數田地，率其用器食鹽，不足以并給二郡邪？
entries.en: If you reckoned the population and acreage of the four neighboring commanderies, could their usual tools and salt rations not have supplied both kingdoms?
entries.literal: Yan estimated the four commanderies' population numbers and fields and lands; generally their tools and eating salt—was it not enough to supply together the two states?

entries.zh: 將勢宜有餘，而吏不能也？
entries.en: Or was there plenty of capacity while the local officials simply failed to manage it?
entries.literal: Or was the situation fitting to have surplus, yet the clerks could not?

entries.zh: 何以言之？
entries.en: What proves that?
entries.literal: By what is this said?

entries.zh: 偃矯制而鼓鑄者，欲及春耕種贍民器也。
entries.en: You forged orders to cast tools, you say, so peasants would have iron for the spring planting.
entries.literal: Yan forged an edict and smelted and cast because he wished to catch up with spring plowing and planting to supply the people's tools.

entries.zh: 今魯國之鼓，當先具其備，至秋乃能舉火。
entries.en: If Lu were really to fire its forges, the works would need to be readied first; the furnaces could not even be lit until autumn.
entries.literal: Now as for Lu's smelting, one must first complete its preparations; only by autumn can fires be raised.

entries.zh: 此言與實反者非？
entries.en: Does that not flatly contradict what you claim?
entries.literal: Is this not words and facts being opposite?

entries.zh: 偃已前三奏，無詔，不惟所為不許，而直矯作威福，以從民望，干名采譽，此明聖所必加誅也。
entries.en: You had already memorialized three times and received no imperial reply. Not only were you never authorized to act, you forged orders, threw your weight about, pandered to popular opinion, and traded on moral prestige for personal fame—conduct that any enlightened ruler would punish with death.
entries.literal: Yan had already thrice submitted memorials earlier, without edict; not only were his actions not permitted, but he directly forged authority, making awe and blessings, in order to follow the people's hopes, seeking name and harvesting reputation—this is what a clear sage must add execution to.

entries.zh: 『枉尺直尋』，孟子稱其不可；
entries.en: Mencius rejected the notion of bending a cubit to gain eight cubits;
entries.literal: 'Bending a foot to straighten eight feet'—Mencius called it unacceptable;

entries.zh: 今所犯罪重，所就者小，偃自予必死而為之邪？
entries.en: Your offense is grave and your supposed public benefit slight. Did you expect execution and press ahead anyway?
entries.literal: Now the crime committed is heavy, what was accomplished is small—did you yourself grant that you would surely die and still do it?

entries.zh: 將幸誅不加，欲以采名也？」
entries.en: Or did you count on escaping the law and merely wanted the glory?'
entries.literal: Or did you hope punishment would not be applied and wished to harvest reputation?'

entries.zh: 偃窮詘，服罪當死。
entries.en: Xu Yan had no answer left; he confessed and accepted that he deserved death.
entries.literal: Yan was exhausted and refuted; he admitted guilt fitting death.

entries.zh: 軍奏「偃矯制顓行，非奉使體，請下御史徵偃即罪。」
entries.en: Zhong Jun memorialized: 'Xu Yan falsely invoked imperial authority and acted on his own. This is not the proper conduct of an envoy. I request that the matter be sent down to the Imperial Clerk, and that Xu Yan be summoned to answer for his crime.'
entries.literal: Jun memorialized: 'Yan forged edicts and acted on his own authority; it is not in the form of one who bears a mission; request to send down to the Imperial Clerk to summon Yan to answer for his crime.'

entries.zh: 奏可。
entries.en: The throne approved the memorial.
entries.literal: The memorial was approved.

entries.zh: 上善其詰，有詔示御史大夫。
entries.en: The emperor commended Zhong Jun's cross-examination and issued an edict laying out the case for the Imperial Counselor.
entries.literal: The emperor praised his examination; there was an edict shown to the Imperial Counselor.

entries.zh: 王褒字子淵，蜀人也。
entries.en: Wang Bao, courtesy name Ziyuan, was a native of Shu.
entries.literal: Wang Bao, courtesy name Ziyuan, was a man of Shu.

entries.zh: 宣帝時修武帝故事，講論六藝群書，博盡奇異之好，徵能為楚辭九江被公，召見誦讀，益召高材劉向、張子僑、華龍、柳褒等待詔金馬門。
entries.en: Under Emperor Xuan the court revived Emperor Wu's cultural program: debate on the Six Classics and the wider corpus, a restless taste for the rare and marvelous. It summoned Bei Gong of Jiujiang, famed for his Chu-style verse, heard him recite, and then added brilliant men such as Liu Xiang, Zhang Ziqiao, Hua Long, and Liu Bao to the roster of scholars awaiting summons at the Golden Horse Gate.
entries.literal: In Emperor Xuan's time they restored Emperor Wu's precedents, lectured and discussed the six arts and collected books, broadly exhausting the fondness for strange things; they summoned one who could compose Chu Ci—Bei Gong of Jiujiang—summoned and saw him recite; further summoned talented men Liu Xiang, Zhang Ziqiao, Hua Long, Liu Bao, and others to await edict at the Golden Horse Gate.

entries.zh: 神爵、五鳳之間，天下殷當，數有嘉應。
entries.en: Between the Shenjue and Wufeng reign titles the empire prospered, and auspicious omens arrived again and again.
entries.literal: Between the Shenjue and Wufeng periods, the realm was abundant and appropriate; repeatedly there were auspicious responses.

entries.zh: 上頗作歌詩，欲興協律之事，丞相魏相奏言知音善鼓雅琴者渤海趙定、梁國龔德，皆召見待詔。
entries.en: The emperor himself began writing lyrics and wished to revive the office for tuning pitch standards. Chancellor Wei Xiang recommended Zhao Ding of Bohai and Gong De of Liang, both masters of the classical zither, and they too were summoned to the waiting roster.
entries.literal: The emperor somewhat composed songs and poems, wishing to raise the business of harmonizing pitch; Chancellor Wei Xiang memorialized saying those who knew tones and were good at strumming the ya zither—Zhao Ding of Bohai and Gong De of Liang—were all summoned and awaited edict.

entries.zh: 於是益州刺史王襄欲宣風化於眾庶，聞王褒有俊材，請與相見，使褒作中和、樂職、宣布詩，選好事者令依鹿鳴之聲習而歌之。
entries.en: The governor of Yizhou, Wang Xiang, hoped to bring moral suasion to the common people. Learning of Wang Bao's gifts, he invited him in and commissioned the poems 'Central Harmony,' 'Joy in Duty,' and 'The Proclamation,' then picked enthusiasts to set them to the tune of the 'Deer Call' ode and teach them by singing.
entries.literal: Thereupon the Governor of Yizhou, Wang Xiang, wished to spread transformation by custom among the multitude; hearing that Wang Bao had outstanding talent, he requested to meet him, had Bao compose the poems 'Central Harmony,' 'Joy in Office,' and 'Proclamation,' selected those fond of affairs and ordered them to practice and sing according to the sound of 'Deer Call.'

entries.zh: 時氾鄉侯何武為僮子，選在歌中。
entries.en: Among the choristers was the future Marquis of Fanxiang, He Wu, still a schoolboy.
entries.literal: At that time Marquis of Fanxiang He Wu was a boy; he was selected to be in the songs.

entries.zh: 久之，武等學長安，歌太學下，轉而上聞。
entries.en: Years later, when He Wu and his companions were students in Chang'an, they sang the pieces below the walls of the Imperial Academy until word of them reached the throne.
entries.literal: After a long time, Wu and others studied in Chang'an, sang beneath the Imperial Academy, and in turn it was heard above.

entries.zh: 宣帝召見武等觀之，皆賜帛，謂曰：「此盛德之事，吾何足以當之！」
entries.en: Emperor Xuan called He Wu and his fellows in to perform, rewarded each with silk, and said, 'Such music belongs to a reign of supreme virtue; how can I deserve it?'
entries.literal: Emperor Xuan summoned Wu and others to observe them; all were granted silk; he said to them: 'This is a matter of abundant virtue—how am I sufficient to match it!'

entries.zh: 初，軍從濟南當詣博士，步入關，關吏予軍繻。
entries.en: Long ago, when Zhong Jun left Jinan to enroll as a student of the imperial academy, he entered the frontier pass on foot, and the gate officer handed him the return-token of split silk.
entries.literal: At first, when Jun was going from Jinan to attend the erudites, he walked into the pass; the pass clerk gave Jun a silk tally.

entries.zh: 軍問：「以此何為？」
entries.en: Zhong Jun asked, 'What is this for?'
entries.literal: Jun asked: 'By this, what is to be done?'

entries.zh: 吏曰；
entries.en: The gate officer replied:
entries.literal: The clerk said:

entries.zh: 「為復傳，還當以合符。」
entries.en: 'It is your return chit; when you come back you must present the matching half.'
entries.literal: 'It is for the return pass; when returning you must match the tally.'

entries.zh: 軍曰：「大丈夫西游，終不復傳還。」
entries.en: Zhong Jun said, 'A man of spirit who sets out for the west does not plan to slink home on a return pass.'
entries.literal: Jun said: 'A great man travels west—will never use the return pass to come back.'

entries.zh: 棄繻而去。
entries.en: He threw away the token and walked on.
entries.literal: He discarded the silk and departed.

entries.zh: 軍為謁者，使行郡國，建節東出關，關吏識之，曰：「此使者乃前棄繻生也。」
entries.en: Later, as court herald on an inspection tour of the commanderies, Zhong Jun rode east through the same pass with the imperial credentia staff. The gate officer recognized him and exclaimed, 'This is the young scholar who threw away his chit!'
entries.literal: When Jun became Herald, sent to tour commanderies and kingdoms, bearing the scepter he went east out of the pass; the pass clerk recognized him and said: 'This envoy is that former youth who discarded the silk.'

entries.zh: 軍行郡國，所見便宜以聞。
entries.en: Wherever he went, he reported every useful measure or abuse he observed.
entries.literal: When Jun toured commanderies and kingdoms, whatever he saw that was advantageous he reported.

entries.zh: 還奏事，上甚說。
entries.en: When he returned to give account, the emperor was delighted.
entries.literal: Returning, he reported affairs; the emperor was very pleased.

entries.zh: 當發使使匈奴，軍自請曰：「軍無橫草之功，得列宿衛，食祿五年。
entries.en: When envoys were to be sent to the Xiongnu, Zhong Jun volunteered: 'I have never so much as thrown a blade of grass across the battlefield for the dynasty, yet I have stood in the palace guard and drawn a stipend for five years.
entries.literal: When it was time to dispatch envoys to the Xiongnu, Jun volunteered, saying: 'Jun has no merit of laying grass across (the path), yet was able to be ranked among the palace guard, receiving salary five years.

entries.zh: 邊境時有風塵之警，臣宜被堅執銳，當矢石，啟前行。
entries.en: Whenever the frontier flares with war, a subject ought to buckle on armor, take up arms, face arrow and stone, and lead the van.
entries.literal: The border from time to time has alarms of wind and dust; your servant ought to don hard armor and grasp sharp weapons, stand against arrows and stones, open the forward march.

entries.zh: 駑下不習金革之事，今聞將遣匈奴使者，臣願盡精厲氣，奉佐明使，畫吉凶於單于之前。
entries.en: I am a poor hand at war. Now that the court will send an embassy to the Chanyu, I beg to marshal all my wit and zeal as aide to the chief envoy and to lay out before the Chanyu himself where fortune and peril lie.
entries.literal: Your servant is lowly and does not practice metal-and-leather affairs; now hearing that envoys will be sent to the Xiongnu, your servant wishes to exhaust essence and sharpen spirit, to assist the enlightened envoy, and paint good and ill before the Chanyu.

entries.zh: 臣年少材下，孤於外官，不足以亢一方之任，竊不勝憤懣。」
entries.en: I am young, my talents slight, and I have languished in minor posts without a frontier command worthy of the trust you place in me—the thought leaves me choked with frustration.'
entries.literal: Your servant is young and talent is low, isolated in outer offices, not sufficient to bear one region's responsibility—privately cannot overcome frustration.'

entries.zh: 詔問畫吉凶之狀，上奇軍對，擢為諫大夫。
entries.en: An edict asked him to spell out what he meant by laying out good and ill fortune. The emperor was so struck by his answer that he promoted him to Grandee Remonstrant.
entries.literal: An edict asked about the situation of painting good and ill; the emperor marveled at Jun's reply and promoted him to Grandee Remonstrant.

entries.zh: 南越與漢和親，乃遣軍使南越，說其王，欲令入朝，比內諸侯。
entries.en: After Southern Yue sealed a marriage alliance with Han, the court dispatched Zhong Jun to persuade its king to come to audience and accept the status of an internal feudatory.
entries.literal: Southern Yue made peace and kinship with Han; then they sent Jun as envoy to Southern Yue, persuading its king, wishing to make him enter court, comparable to inner feudal lords.

entries.zh: 軍自請：「願受長纓，必羈南越王而致之闕下。」
entries.en: Zhong Jun volunteered: 'Give me a long cord and I will bind the King of Southern Yue and haul him to the palace steps.'
entries.literal: Jun himself requested: 'I wish to receive a long cord—I will surely tie the King of Southern Yue and bring him beneath the palace gate.'

entries.zh: 軍遂往說越王，越王聽許，請舉國內屬。
entries.en: Zhong Jun went south and won the king's ear; the king agreed to place his entire realm under Han.
entries.literal: Jun then went to persuade the Yue king; the Yue king listened and assented, requesting to offer the whole state in internal submission.

entries.zh: 天子大說，賜南越大臣印綬，壹用漢法，以新改其俗，令使者留填撫之。
entries.en: The emperor was overjoyed. He issued Han seals and ribbons to Yue ministers, extended Han law uniformly to refashion local custom, and ordered the envoys to stay behind to stabilize the new order.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven was greatly pleased, granted Southern Yue great ministers seals and ribbons, uniformly applied Han law, in order to renew and change their customs, ordered envoys to remain to fill and pacify.

entries.zh: 越相呂嘉不欲內屬，發兵攻殺其王，及漢使者皆死。
entries.en: The Yue prime minister Lü Jia refused submission, rose in arms, murdered his king, and killed the Han envoys as well.
entries.literal: The Yue chancellor Lü Jia did not wish internal submission; he raised troops, attacked and killed the king, and the Han envoys all died.

entries.zh: 語在南越傳。
entries.en: The full story is told in the biography of Southern Yue.
entries.literal: The words are in the Biography of Southern Yue.

entries.zh: 軍死時年二十餘，故世謂之「終童」。
entries.en: He was barely past twenty when he died, and posterity remembers him as 'Zhong the lad'—the boy who never grew old.
entries.literal: When Jun died he was over twenty; therefore the world calls him 'Zhong the Boy.'

entries.zh: 褒既為刺史作頌，又作其傳，益州刺史因奏褒有軼材。
entries.en: Wang Bao had not only written the governor's celebratory verse but drafted his biography as well, and on that basis the governor reported Wang Bao's exceptional gifts to the capital.
entries.literal: Bao, having composed a eulogy for the governor, also composed his biography; the Governor of Yizhou thereupon memorialized that Bao had outstanding talent.

entries.zh: 上乃徵褒。
entries.en: The emperor thereupon summoned Wang Bao to court.
entries.literal: The emperor then summoned Bao.

entries.zh: 既至，詔褎為聖主得賢臣頌其意。
entries.en: Once he arrived, an edict instructed him to compose a rhapsody expounding the theme 'How a sage ruler wins worthy ministers.'
entries.literal: When he had arrived, an edict ordered Bao to eulogize the meaning of 'The Enlightened Lord Obtains Worthy Ministers.'

entries.zh: 褒對曰：
entries.en: Wang Bao replied:
entries.literal: Bao replied, saying:

entries.zh: 後方士言益州有金馬碧雞之寶，可祭祀致也，宣帝使褒往祀焉。
entries.en: Later a wizard reported that Yizhou held the spirits of the Golden Horse and Green Cock, which might be summoned by sacrifice. Emperor Xuan dispatched Wang Bao to conduct the rites.
entries.literal: Afterward a fangshi said Yizhou had the treasures of the golden horse and green fowl; they could be brought by sacrifice; Emperor Xuan sent Bao to go sacrifice there.

entries.zh: 褒於道病死，上閔惜之。
entries.en: Wang Bao died of illness en route, and the emperor mourned his loss.
entries.literal: Bao died of illness on the road; the emperor pitied and regretted him.

entries.zh: 是時，上頗好神僊，故褒對及之。
entries.en: The emperor was much taken with spirits and immortals at the time, so Wang Bao touched the theme in his answer.
entries.literal: At this time the emperor somewhat favored divine immortals; therefore Bao's reply reached to it.

entries.zh: 上令褒與張子僑等並待詔，數從褒等放獵，所幸宮館，輒為歌頌，第其高下，以差賜帛。
entries.en: The emperor kept Wang Bao and Zhang Ziqiao on the waiting roster and often took them along on the hunt. Wherever the royal party lodged, Wang Bao would compose a celebratory piece; the emperor ranked the poems and handed out silk according to merit.
entries.literal: The emperor ordered Bao and Zhang Ziqiao and others together to await edict; repeatedly took Bao and others along on hunts; at favored palaces and lodges, then composed songs and eulogies, ranked their high and low, and by gradation granted silk.

entries.zh: 議者多以為淫靡不急，上曰：「『不有博弈者乎，為之猶賢乎已！』
entries.en: Critics dismissed such verse as frivolous and irrelevant, but the emperor replied with a line from the Analects: 'Are there not board games? Playing them is still better than doing nothing.'
entries.literal: Most critics considered them dissolute and inessential. The emperor said, 'Is it not written, "Are there not board games? Playing them is still better than doing nothing?"

entries.zh: 辭賦大者與古詩同義，小者辯麗可喜。
entries.en: The greater rhapsodies pursue the same ends as the ancient odes; the lighter pieces charm with wit and color.
entries.literal: Ci and fu, large ones share meaning with ancient poems; small ones are eloquent and lovely and pleasing.

entries.zh: 辟如女工有綺縠，音樂有鄭衛，今世俗猶皆以此虞說耳目，辭賦比之，尚有仁義風諭，鳥獸草木多聞之觀，賢於倡優博弈遠矣。」
entries.en: Think of figured damask among weavers or the airs of Zheng and Wei among tunes: the world already delights its eyes and ears with such things. Beside them, rhapsody still carries moral allegory in birds, beasts, plants, and trees—it is infinitely superior to buffoonery or a game of weiqi.'
entries.literal: It is like women workers having patterned silk, music having Zheng and Wei; now the vulgar custom still all by this pleases and delights ear and eye; compared to this, ci and fu still have benevolence and rightness wind instruction, birds, beasts, plants, and trees much-heard observation—better than entertainers and chess by far.'

entries.zh: 頃之，擢褒為諫大夫。
entries.en: Soon afterward Wang Bao was promoted to Grandee Remonstrant.
entries.literal: Before long, Bao was promoted to Grandee Remonstrant.

entries.zh: 初，武帝征南越，元封元年立儋耳、珠崖郡，皆在南方海中洲居，廣袤可千里，合十六縣，戶二萬三千餘。
entries.en: When Emperor Wu conquered Southern Yue, he founded the commanderies of Dan'er and Zhuya in the first year of Yuanfeng. They lay on islands in the southern sea, stretched perhaps a thousand li from end to end, comprised sixteen counties, and counted a little over twenty-three thousand households.
entries.literal: At first, Emperor Wu campaigned against Southern Yue; in the first year of Yuanfeng he established Dan'er and Zhuya commanderies; both dwelt on islets in the sea to the south, breadth and length perhaps a thousand li, together sixteen counties, households a little over twenty-three thousand.

entries.zh: 其民暴惡，自以阻絕，數犯吏禁，吏亦酷之，率數年壹反，殺吏，漢輒發兵擊定之。
entries.en: The inhabitants were fierce and lawless, confident that distance shielded them. They broke official regulations again and again, and the magistrates repaid them with cruelty. Every few years they would rise, murder Han officials, and prompt a punitive expedition from the mainland.
entries.literal: Their people were violent and wicked; relying on barrier isolation, they repeatedly violated clerical prohibitions; the clerks also were cruel to them; on average every several years once they rebelled, killed clerks, and Han always raised troops to strike and pacify them.

entries.zh: 自初為郡至昭帝始元元年，二十餘年間，凡六反叛。
entries.en: Between the founding of the commanderies and Emperor Zhao's first Shiyuan year—barely twenty years—there were six full-scale revolts.
entries.literal: From first becoming commanderies to Emperor Zhao's first year of Shiyuan, in more than twenty years, there were six rebellions in all.

entries.zh: 至其五年，罷儋耳郡并屬珠崖。
entries.en: In the fifth year of that reign Dan'er was abolished and its territory folded into Zhuya.
entries.literal: By its fifth year, Dan'er commandery was abolished and merged to belong to Zhuya.

entries.zh: 至宣帝神爵三年，珠崖三縣復反。
entries.en: Under Emperor Xuan, in the third Shenjue year, three Zhuya counties rose again.
entries.literal: By Emperor Xuan's third year of Shenjue, three counties of Zhuya again rebelled.

entries.zh: 反後七年，甘露元年，九縣反，輒發兵擊定之。
entries.en: Seven years later, in the first Ganlu year, nine counties mutinied and were again beaten down by Han arms.
entries.literal: Seven years after the rebellion, in the first year of Ganlu, nine counties rebelled; troops were immediately raised to strike and pacify them.

entries.zh: 元帝初元元年，珠崖又反，發兵擊之。
entries.en: In Emperor Yuan's first Chuyuan year Zhuya rebelled once more, and the court sent troops against it.
entries.literal: Emperor Yuan's first year of Chuyuan, Zhuya again rebelled; troops were raised to strike them.

entries.zh: 諸縣更叛，連年不定。
entries.en: County after county changed sides; the turmoil dragged on without end.
entries.literal: The various counties rebelled in turn; year after year it was not settled.

entries.zh: 上與有司議大發軍，捐之建議，以為不當擊。
entries.en: The emperor and his ministers debated a major mobilization, but Jia Juanzhi argued that conquest was the wrong course.
entries.literal: The emperor with the responsible officials discussed greatly raising troops; Juanzhi proposed a plan, thinking one ought not strike.

entries.zh: 上使侍中駙馬都尉樂昌侯王商詰問捐之曰：「珠崖內屬為郡久矣，今背畔逆節，而云不當擊，長蠻夷之亂，虧先帝功德，經義何以處之？」
entries.en: The emperor ordered Wang Shang, the marquis of Yuechang, who served as palace attendant and commandant of household cavalry, to confront Jia Juanzhi. 'Zhuya has been an internal commandery for ages,' he said. 'Now it breaks faith. To refuse a campaign is to encourage barbarian revolt and blot the achievement of the late emperor. What do the classics say to that?'
entries.literal: The emperor sent Palace Attendant, Commandant of Household Cavalry, Marquis of Yuechang Wang Shang to examine and question Juanzhi, saying: 'Zhuya has long been internally submissive as a commandery; now it turns its back and violates norm; yet you say one ought not strike—lengthening the barbarian Yi's disorder, diminishing the former emperor's merit and virtue—how does the meaning of the classics dispose of this?'

entries.zh: 捐之對曰：
entries.en: Jia Juanzhi replied:
entries.literal: Juanzhi replied, saying:

entries.zh: 賴聖漢初興，為百姓請命，平定天下。
entries.en: Our sacred Han rose in mercy, pleaded Heaven for the people's lives, and brought peace to the world.
entries.literal: Relying on sage Han's first rise, it pleaded life for the hundred surnames and pacified the realm.

entries.zh: 至孝文皇帝，閔中國未安，偃武行文，則斷獄數百，民賦四十，丁男三年而一事。
entries.en: Emperor Wen, grieving that the heartland was still unsettled, sheathed the sword and promoted civil rule until court dockets numbered only in the hundreds, the poll tax fell to forty cash, and each able-bodied man owed the state only one month's labor every three years.
entries.literal: Reaching Emperor Xiaowen, he pitied that the central states were not yet secure; laid down arms and raised culture; then cases judged were in the hundreds, people's tax forty, adult males once in three years one affair.

entries.zh: 時有獻千里馬者，詔曰：「鸞旗在前，屬車在後，吉行日五十里，師行二十里，朕乘千里之馬，獨先安之？」
entries.en: When someone offered a horse said to cover a thousand li a day, the emperor replied with an edict: 'The imperial pennons lead and the train follows; on a peaceful journey I cover fifty li a day, on campaign twenty. Where under Heaven could I gallop alone on such a beast?'
entries.literal: At that time there was one who presented a thousand-li horse; an edict said: 'The phoenix banner is in front, the attendant carriages behind; auspicious travel is fifty li a day, army travel twenty li—if I ride a thousand-li horse, alone where would I go first?'

entries.zh: 於是還馬，與道里費，而下詔曰：「朕不受獻也，其令四方毋求來獻。」
entries.en: He sent the horse back with money for the donor's journey and proclaimed, 'I accept no gifts. Let no region send tribute of this kind again.'
entries.literal: Thereupon he returned the horse, gave travel expenses, and issued an edict saying: 'We do not accept offerings; order the four directions not to seek to come offering.'

entries.zh: 當此之時，逸游之樂絕，奇麗之賂塞，鄭衛之倡微矣。
entries.en: At that moment wasteful pastimes died away, lavish bribes dried up, and the lewd music of Zheng and Wei faded from court.
entries.literal: At this time, wandering pleasure was cut off, strange and lovely bribes were blocked, Zheng and Wei entertainers became slight.

entries.zh: 夫後官盛色則賢者隱處，佞人用事則諍臣杜口，而文帝不行，故諡為孝文，廟稱太宗。
entries.en: A harem crowded with beauties drives the good into hiding; when sycophants hold power, honest advisers fall silent. Emperor Wen would have none of it, which is why posterity calls him 'the Filial and Cultured' and honors his shrine as Taizong.
entries.literal: When the rear palace abounds in beauty, then worthies hide; when fawning men handle affairs, then remonstrating ministers shut their mouths; yet Emperor Wen did not practice these; therefore his posthumous name was Xiaowen, his temple was called Taizong.

entries.zh: 至孝武皇帝元狩六年，太倉之粟紅腐而不可食，都內之錢貫朽而不可挍。
entries.en: By the sixth Yuanshou year of Emperor Wu the imperial granaries held grain that had rotted to pink dust, and the strings of cash in the capital vaults had decayed so that the coins could not be tallied.
entries.literal: Reaching Emperor Xiaowu's sixth year of Yuanshou, the Grand Granary's grain was red-rotten and could not be eaten; the capital's inner cash strings were rotten and could not be counted.

entries.zh: 乃探平城之事，錄冒頓以來數為邊害，籍兵厲馬，因富民以攘服之。
entries.en: He brooded on the humiliation of Pingcheng, reviewed how Modu and his heirs had ravaged the frontier, mobilized armies and bred horses, and drew on the wealthy to fund conquest until the steppe submitted.
entries.literal: Then he investigated the affair of Pingcheng, recorded since Modu repeatedly being border harm, registered troops and sharpened horses, relying on rich people in order to seize and subdue them.

entries.zh: 西連諸國至于安息，東過碣石以玄菟、樂浪為郡，比卻匈奴萬里，更起營塞，制南海以為八郡，則天下斷獄萬數，民賦數百，造鹽鐵酒榷之利以佐用度，猶不能足。
entries.en: He linked the western states as far as Parthia, pushed east beyond Jieshi to found Xuantu and Lelang, drove the Xiongnu back ten thousand li, threw up a chain of fortresses, and carved eight commanderies from the southern sea. Court cases mounted into the tens of thousands, the poll tax into the hundreds of cash, and even the monopolies on salt, iron, and wine could not fill the treasury.
entries.literal: West he linked the various states reaching to Anxi; east he passed Jieshi and made Xuantu and Lelang commanderies; pressing back the Xiongnu ten thousand li, repeatedly raising camps and barriers, controlling the South Sea to make eight commanderies—then cases judged in the realm were in the ten thousands, people's taxes in the hundreds; he created salt, iron, and wine monopoly profits to assist expenditures, yet still could not suffice.

entries.zh: 當此之時，寇賊並起，軍旅數發，父戰死於前，子鬥傷於後，女子乘亭鄣，孤兒號於道，老母寡婦飲泣巷哭，遙設虛祭，想魂乎萬里之外。
entries.en: Banditry flared everywhere. Campaign followed campaign: fathers fell in the van while sons bled in the rear, women mounted the signal towers of frontier posts, orphans screamed along the highways, and gray-haired widows wept in the alleys, offering ghost feasts to souls lost ten thousand li away.
entries.literal: At this time, bandits and thieves arose together; armies repeatedly set out; fathers died in battle in front, sons fought wounded behind; women mounted watchtowers; orphans wailed on the roads; old mothers and widows swallowed tears and wept in lanes; from afar they set empty sacrifices, imagining souls ten thousand li beyond.

entries.zh: 淮南王盜寫虎符，陰聘名士，關東公孫勇等詐為使者，是皆廓地泰大，征伐不休之故也。
entries.en: The king of Huainan forged the tiger tally and hired secret partisans; east of the passes men such as Gongsun Yong posed as imperial envoys. All of it sprang from overgrown frontiers and endless war.
entries.literal: The king of Huainan secretly copied the tiger tally, secretly hired famous knights; east of the passes Gongsun Yong and others falsely acted as envoys—these all were because territory was expanded too greatly and campaigns did not cease.

entries.zh: 卷六十四下 嚴朱吾丘主父徐嚴終王賈傳 第三十三下
entries.en: Volume 64b, Part Two: biographies of Yan Zhu, Zhu Mai Chen, Wuqiu Shouwang, Zhufu Yan, Xu Le, Yan An, Zhong Jun, Wang Bao, and Jia Juanzhi—the thirty-third set of biographies, lower scroll.
entries.literal: Volume 64b: Biographies of Yan, Zhu, Wuqiu, Zhufu, Xu, Yan, Zhong, Wang, and Jia, Part Two, Number 33b.

entries.zh: 東方朔字曼倩，平原厭次人也。
entries.en: Dongfang Shuo, whose courtesy name was Manqian, came from Yanci in Pingyuan commandery.
entries.literal: Dongfang Shuo, courtesy name Manqian, was a man of Yanci in Pingyuan.

entries.zh: 武帝初即位，征天下舉方正賢良文學材力之士，待以不次之位，四方士多上書言得失，自衒鬻者以千數，其不足采者輒報聞罷。
entries.en: Early in Emperor Wu's reign the court summoned men of integrity, literary talent, and practical ability, promising posts outside the normal ladder of promotion. Memorials poured in from every quarter—thousands of men peddling their wares—and those without merit received a polite note of receipt and heard no more.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu had first ascended the throne, he summoned from the realm those recommended for square integrity, worthy excellence, literary learning, and strength of talent, treating them with appointments outside the usual sequence; knights from the four quarters largely submitted memorials discussing gain and loss; those who displayed and hawked themselves numbered in the thousands; those not worth gathering were always answered with heard and dismissed.

entries.zh: 朔初來，上書曰：「臣朔少失父母，長養兄嫂。
entries.en: In his first memorial Dongfang Shuo wrote, "I lost my parents while young and was raised by my brother and his wife.
entries.literal: When Shuo first arrived, he submitted a memorial, saying, "Your servant Shuo in youth lost father and mother and was brought up by my elder brother and sister-in-law.

entries.zh: 年十三學書，三冬文史足用。
entries.en: By thirteen he had mastered literacy; three winters of study gave him all the documentary learning he needed.
entries.literal: At age thirteen he studied writing; in three winters his command of documents and histories sufficed for use.

entries.zh: 十五學擊劍。
entries.en: At fifteen he took up fencing.
entries.literal: At fifteen he studied swordsmanship.

entries.zh: 十六學《詩》、《書》，誦二十二萬言。
entries.en: At sixteen he studied the Odes and Documents until he could recite two hundred twenty thousand characters.
entries.literal: At sixteen he studied the Odes and the Documents, memorizing two hundred twenty thousand graphs.

entries.zh: 十九學孫、吳兵法，戰陣之具，鉦鼓之教，亦誦二十二萬言。
entries.en: At nineteen he mastered Sunzi and Wuzi on war—formations, gongs, and drums—and committed another two hundred twenty thousand characters to memory.
entries.literal: At nineteen he studied the military methods of Sun and Wu—the gear of battle lines, the signals of gongs and drums—and likewise memorized two hundred twenty thousand graphs.

entries.zh: 凡臣朔固已誦四十四萬言。
entries.en: In sum I have four hundred forty thousand characters by heart.
entries.literal: In all your servant Shuo has thus memorized four hundred forty thousand graphs.

entries.zh: 又常服子路之言。
entries.en: I try always to live by what Zilu taught.
entries.literal: I also constantly take to heart the words of Zilu.

entries.zh: 臣朔年二十二，長九尺三寸，目若懸珠，齒若編貝，勇若孟賁，捷若慶忌，廉若鮑叔，信若尾生。
entries.en: I am twenty-two, stand nine feet three inches, my eyes shine like pearls and my teeth line up like shells; in courage I match Meng Ben, in agility Qingji, in integrity Bao Shu, in good faith Weisheng.
entries.literal: Your servant Shuo is twenty-two years old, nine feet three inches tall, with eyes like suspended pearls and teeth like strung shells, brave as Meng Ben, swift as Qingji, incorrupt as Bao Shu, trustworthy as Weisheng.

entries.zh: 若此，可以為天子大臣矣。
entries.en: A man of such parts may stand as a minister to the Son of Heaven.
entries.literal: If thus, I may serve as a great minister to the Son of Heaven.

entries.zh: 臣朔昧死再拜以聞。」
entries.en: I risk execution to lay this before you twice over."
entries.literal: Your servant Shuo, risking death, twice bows to report."

entries.zh: 武帝既招英俊，程其器能，用之如不及。
entries.en: Emperor Wu had called the best minds to court, weighed what each could do, and put them to work as if he feared he might never hire fast enough.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu, having summoned outstanding men, measured their capacities and abilities, and employed them as if he could not catch up.

entries.zh: 時方外事胡、越，內興制度，國家多事，自公孫弘以下至司馬遷，皆奉使方外，或為郡國守相至公卿，而朔嘗至太中大夫，後常為郎，與枚皋、郭舍人俱在左右，詼啁而已。
entries.en: While the empire was busy with the Xiongnu and the Yue on the frontier and with new institutions at home, everyone from Gongsun Hong down to Sima Qian was dispatched abroad or made a regional governor or rose to the highest offices. Shuo had briefly reached grand counselor of the palace, but he usually held only the modest rank of gentleman-attendant and, with Mei Gao and Guo Sheren, hovered at the ruler's elbow cracking jokes.
entries.literal: At the time they were just then conducting external affairs with the Hu and Yue, and internally raising up institutions; the state had many tasks. From Gongsun Hong down to Sima Qian, all were sent on missions beyond the borders, or served as shepherds and chancellors of commanderies and kingdoms up to duke and minister rank, whereas Shuo had once reached grand counselor of the palace, but afterward was normally a gentleman-attendant; together with Mei Gao and Guo Sheren he was only at the left and right, jesting and bantering, that is all.

entries.zh: 久之，朔上書陳農戰強國之計，因自訟獨不得大官，欲求試用。
entries.en: In time he memorialized with schemes for agriculture, war, and national strength, lamenting that he alone had never been given a weighty post and asking to be tried in a serious role.
entries.literal: After a long while, Shuo submitted a memorial setting forth plans for farming, warfare, and strengthening the state, and on that occasion sued himself, saying that he alone had not obtained high office, and wished to seek a trial appointment.

entries.zh: 其言專商鞅、韓非之語也，指意放蕩，頗復詼諧，辭數萬言，終不見用。
entries.en: The piece was pure Shang Yang and Han Fei in tone, loose in structure and laced with humor; it ran to many thousands of characters and was never adopted.
entries.literal: His words were exclusively the language of Shang Yang and Han Fei; his intent was unrestrained, and again rather humorous; the phrasing ran to several tens of thousands of characters, yet in the end he was not employed.

entries.zh: 朔因著論，設客難己，用位卑以自慰諭。
entries.en: So he wrote a philosophical dialogue, inventing a guest who rebuked him, to console himself for his low rank.
entries.literal: Thereupon Shuo composed a treatise, setting up a guest who rebuked himself, using low position to console and instruct himself.

entries.zh: 其辭曰：
entries.en: The text begins:
entries.literal: Its words say:

entries.zh: 時，有幸倡郭舍人，滑稽不窮，常侍左右，曰：「朔狂，幸中耳，非至數也。
entries.en: At that time there was a favored entertainer, Guo Sheren, inexhaustibly witty, who constantly attended left and right, saying: "Shuo is mad—he hit by luck, not by ultimate reckoning.
entries.literal: At that time there was a favored entertainer, Guo Sheren, inexhaustibly witty, who constantly attended left and right, saying: Shuo is mad—he hit by luck, not by ultimate reckoning.

entries.zh: 臣願令朔復射，朔中之，臣榜百，不能中，臣賜帛。」
entries.en: Let him guess again: if he succeeds I take a hundred lashes; if he fails I claim the silk."
entries.literal: Your servant wishes to have Shuo shoot again; if Shuo hits, your servant takes a hundred strokes; if he cannot hit, your servant is granted silk."

entries.zh: 乃覆樹上寄生，令朔射之。
entries.en: They hid a mistletoe sprig from a tree and challenged him to name it.
entries.literal: Thereupon they covered a tree parasite and ordered Shuo to shoot it.

entries.zh: 朔曰：「是寠藪也。」
entries.en: Shuo said: "It is a nest-thicket (wordplay)."
entries.literal: Shuo said: It is a nest-thicket (wordplay).

entries.zh: 舍人曰：「果知朔不能中也。」
entries.en: Sheren said: "As expected, I knew Shuo could not hit."
entries.literal: Sheren said: As expected, I knew Shuo could not hit.

entries.zh: 朔曰：「生肉為膾，乾肉為脯；
entries.en: Shuo said: "Raw meat is mince; dried meat is jerky;
entries.literal: Shuo said: Raw meat is mince; dried meat is jerky;

entries.zh: 著樹為寄生，盆下為寠藪。」
entries.en: on a tree that growth is mistletoe; under a bowl the same thing is called nest-thicket."
entries.literal: on a tree it is mistletoe; under a bowl it is a nest-thicket."

entries.zh: 上令倡監榜舍人，舍人不勝痛，呼□。
entries.en: The emperor told the master of jesters to flog Guo Sheren until he howled with pain.
entries.literal: The emperor ordered the jester-supervisor to flog Sheren; Sheren could not bear the pain and cried out (text damaged).

entries.zh: 朔笑之曰：「咄！
entries.en: Shuo laughed at him and said: "Tut!
entries.literal: Shuo laughed at him and said: Tut!

entries.zh: 口無毛，聲謷謷，尻益高。」
entries.en: No beard about the mouth, piping shrill as a nestling, haunches reared like a crane."
entries.literal: No hair about the mouth, sound áo áo, rump rising higher."

entries.zh: 舍人恚曰：「朔擅詆欺天子從官，當棄市。」
entries.en: Sheren angrily said: "Shuo presumptuously slanders and deceives the Son of Heaven's attendants—he should be executed in the market."
entries.literal: Sheren angrily said: Shuo presumptuously slanders and deceives the Son of Heaven's attendants—he should be executed in the market.

entries.zh: 上問朔：「何故詆之？」
entries.en: The emperor asked Shuo: "Why did you slander him?"
entries.literal: The emperor asked Shuo: Why did you slander him?

entries.zh: 對曰：「臣非敢詆之，乃與為隱耳。」
entries.en: He replied: "Your servant did not dare slander him; he was playing a riddle with him."
entries.literal: He replied: Your servant did not dare slander him; he was playing a riddle with him.

entries.zh: 上曰：「隱云何？」
entries.en: The emperor said: "What did the riddle mean?"
entries.literal: The emperor said: What did the riddle mean?

entries.zh: 朔曰：「夫口無毛者，狗竇也；
entries.en: Dongfang Shuo said, "No hair around the mouth is a dog's burrow;
entries.literal: Shuo said, "As for no hair about the mouth—it is a dog hole;

entries.zh: 聲謷謷者，鳥哺鷇也；
entries.en: A piping cry is fledglings begging in the nest;
entries.literal: As for sound áo áo—it is birds feeding nestlings;

entries.zh: 尻益高者，鶴俛啄也。」
entries.en: Haunches lifted high is a crane stooping to strike."
entries.literal: As for the rump rising higher—it is a crane bending forward to peck."

entries.zh: 舍人不服，因曰：「臣願復問朔隱語，不知，亦當榜。」
entries.en: Sheren was not convinced and therefore said: "Your servant wishes again to question Shuo with a riddle; if he does not know, he too should be flogged."
entries.literal: Sheren was not convinced and therefore said: Your servant wishes again to question Shuo with a riddle; if he does not know, he too should be flogged.

entries.zh: 即妄為諧語曰：「令壺齟，老柏塗，伊優亞，狋吽牙。
entries.en: He spouted nonsense: "Order—jar—crooked teeth; old—cypress—muddy path; yi-you-ya; mingled growls.
entries.literal: He thereupon recklessly made a jesting phrase: Order pot crooked, old cypress smear, yi-you-ya, dog snarls.

entries.zh: 何謂也？」
entries.en: What does that mean?"
entries.literal: What does it mean?"

entries.zh: 朔曰：「令者，命也。
entries.en: Shuo said: "Order means mandate.
entries.literal: Shuo said: Order means mandate.

entries.zh: 壺者，所以盛也。
entries.en: A jar is a vessel.
entries.literal: Pot means that by which one contains.

entries.zh: 齟者，齒不正也。
entries.en: Crooked teeth are snaggleteeth.
entries.literal: Crooked means teeth not straight.

entries.zh: 老者，人所敬也。
entries.en: Age is venerable.
entries.literal: Old means what people revere.

entries.zh: 柏者，鬼之廷也。
entries.en: A cypress is the courtyard of ghosts—dark and forbidding.
entries.literal: Cypress means the court of ghosts.

entries.zh: 塗者，漸洳徑也。
entries.en: Mire is a boggy track.
entries.literal: Smear means a soggy path.

entries.zh: 伊優亞者，辭未定也。
entries.en: Yi-you-ya is the babble of someone who cannot make up his mind.
entries.literal: Yi-you-ya means words not yet settled.

entries.zh: 狋吽牙者，兩犬爭也。」
entries.en: The snarls are two dogs snapping at each other."
entries.literal: Dog snarls means two dogs quarreling."

entries.zh: 舍人所問，朔應聲輒對，變詐鋒出，莫能窮者，左右大驚。
entries.en: Whatever Guo Sheren threw at him, Dongfang Shuo answered in the same breath with wit that never flagged; the whole court stared.
entries.literal: To whatever Sheren asked, Shuo answered on the instant; shifts and tricks poured sharp as a blade—none could exhaust him; those left and right were greatly amazed.

entries.zh: 上以朔為常侍郎，遂得愛幸。
entries.en: The emperor named him a regular palace gentleman, and from then on he basked in imperial favor.
entries.literal: The emperor made Shuo a regular attendant gentleman, and he thereupon obtained favor.

entries.zh: 臣聞謙遜靜愨，天表之應，應之以福；
entries.en: I have heard that humility and quiet reverence draw Heaven's favor and bring good fortune;
entries.literal: Your servant has heard that modesty, yielding, quietness, and sincerity are Heaven's outward signs; responding to them brings blessing;

entries.zh: 驕溢靡麗，天表之應，應之以異。
entries.en: while arrogance and wanton luxury draw Heaven's warning in strange portents.
entries.literal: arrogance, overflow, dissipation, and splendor are Heaven's outward signs; responding to them brings prodigies.

entries.zh: 今陛下累郎台，恐其不高也；
entries.en: You raise tower upon tower, as though none were high enough;
entries.literal: Now Your Majesty piles terrace on terrace, fearing they are not high enough;

entries.zh: 弋獵之處，恐其不廣也。
entries.en: and you widen the hunting grounds as though no park were ever broad enough.
entries.literal: and at the places of archery and hunting, fearing they are not broad enough.

entries.zh: 如天不為變，則三輔之地盡可以為苑，何必盩厔、鄠、杜乎！
entries.en: If Heaven raised no omens against it, you could turn the entire capital region into a hunting park—why stop at Zhouzhi, Hu, and Du?
entries.literal: If Heaven did not make prodigies for it, then the lands of the three assistants could all be made into parks—why must it be Zhouzhi, Hu, and Du!

entries.zh: 奢侈越制，天為之變，上林雖小，臣尚以為大也。
entries.en: Extravagance beyond the rites draws Heaven's rebuke; even the existing Shanglin seems to me already too vast.
entries.literal: Extravagance exceeding regulation—Heaven makes prodigies for it; though Shanglin is small, your servant still thinks it large.

entries.zh: 久之，隆慮公主子昭平君尚帝女夷安公主，隆慮主病困，以金千斤、錢千萬為昭平君豫贖死罪，上許之。
entries.en: Zhao Pingjun, son of the Princess of Longlü, married Princess Yi'an. On her deathbed his mother deposited a thousand pounds of gold and ten million cash to ransom any capital crime he might commit, and the emperor agreed.
entries.literal: After a long time, the Princess of Longlü's son Zhao Pingjun married the emperor's daughter Princess Yi'an; when the Princess of Longlü was gravely ill, with a thousand jin of gold and ten million cash she prepaid a ransom for Zhao Pingjun's death crime; the emperor assented.

entries.zh: 隆慮主卒，昭平君日驕，醉殺主傅，獄繫內官。
entries.en: After her death Zhao Pingjun grew insolent, slew his tutor in a drunken rage, and was jailed under the inner officials.
entries.literal: When the Princess of Longlü died, Zhao Pingjun daily grew arrogant; drunk, he killed the princess's tutor and was imprisoned under the Inner Officials.

entries.zh: 以公主子，廷尉上請請論。
entries.en: As a princess's son the case went to the commandant of justice for sentence.
entries.literal: Because he was a princess's son, the commandant of justice submitted a request asking for judgment.

entries.zh: 左右人人為言：「前又入贖，陛下許之。」
entries.en: Every attendant pleaded, saying, "His mother paid the ransom in advance, and you granted it."
entries.literal: Those left and right all spoke for him, saying, "Before, she also paid ransom in advance; Your Majesty permitted it."

entries.zh: 上曰：「吾弟老有是一子，死以屬我。」
entries.en: The emperor said: "My younger sister in old age had this one son; dying she entrusted him to me."
entries.literal: The emperor said: My younger sister in old age had this one son; dying she entrusted him to me.

entries.zh: 於是為之垂涕歎息良久，曰：「法令者，先帝所造也，用弟故而誣先帝之法，吾何面目入高廟乎！
entries.en: Thereupon for him he shed tears and sighed long, saying: "Laws and orders are what the former emperor established; because of a younger sibling's sake to violate the former emperor's laws—what face have I to enter the High Temple!
entries.literal: Thereupon for him he shed tears and sighed long, saying: Laws and orders are what the former emperor established; because of a younger sibling's sake to violate the former emperor's laws—what face have I to enter the High Temple!

entries.zh: 又下負萬民。」
entries.en: How could I face the people below?"
entries.literal: Again below I would betray the myriad people."

entries.zh: 乃可其奏，哀不能自止，左右盡悲。
entries.en: He approved the death sentence, wept uncontrollably, and the whole court wept with him.
entries.literal: Thereupon he approved the memorial; grief could not stop itself; those left and right were all sorrowful.

entries.zh: 朔前上壽，曰：「臣聞聖王為政，賞不避仇讎，誅不擇骨肉。
entries.en: Dongfang Shuo stepped up with a toast: "The sage king rewards even his foes and punishes even his kin.
entries.literal: Shuo stepped forward with a longevity toast, saying: Your servant has heard that when a sage king conducts government, rewards do not avoid enemies, punishments do not pick kin.

entries.zh: 《書》曰：『不偏不黨，王道蕩蕩。』
entries.en: The Documents say, Without favor, without clique, the royal way runs straight and wide.
entries.literal: The Documents say: "Without partiality, without faction—the kingly way is vast."

entries.zh: 此二者，五帝所重，三王所難也。
entries.en: Both precepts were honored by the Five Emperors and strained even the Three Kings.
entries.literal: These two things are what the Five Emperors esteemed and what the Three Kings found hard.

entries.zh: 陛下行之，是以四海之內元元之民各得其所，天下幸甚！
entries.en: Your Majesty has done this: every commoner in the realm finds justice, and the empire is the better for it.
entries.literal: Your Majesty practices them—therefore within the four seas the black-haired people each obtain their place; the realm is greatly fortunate!

entries.zh: 臣朔奉觴，昧死再拜上萬歲壽。」
entries.en: I raise my cup and wish Your Majesty ten thousand years of life."
entries.literal: Your servant Shuo raises the cup, in darkness of death twice bows and offers the myriad-years longevity."

entries.zh: 上乃起，入省中，夕時召讓朔，曰：「傳曰『時然後言，人不厭其言』。
entries.en: The emperor then rose and entered the private chambers. That evening he summoned Dongfang Shuo and rebuked him, saying, "The tradition says, 'Speak only when the time is right, and people will not weary of your words.'
entries.literal: The emperor thereupon rose, entered the private chambers; at evening he summoned and rebuked Shuo, saying: The tradition says, "When it is timely then speak—people do not tire of his words.

entries.zh: 今先生上壽，時乎？」
entries.en: Now, sir, your longevity toast—was it timely?"
entries.literal: Now, sir, your longevity toast—was it timely?"

entries.zh: 朔免冠頓首曰：「臣聞樂太盛則陽溢，哀太盛則陰損，陰陽變則心氣動，心氣動則精神散，精神散而邪氣及。
entries.en: Dongfang Shuo kowtowed bareheaded and said, "Your servant has heard that extreme joy floods the yang ether; extreme grief drains the yin. When yin and yang reel, the heart loses its anchor, the spirit frays, and evil humors invade the body.
entries.literal: Shuo removed his cap and knocked his head, saying, "Your servant has heard that when joy is too great yang overflows; when grief is too great yin is harmed; when yin and yang shift, heart qi moves; when heart qi moves, spirit scatters; when spirit scatters, evil qi arrives.

entries.zh: 銷憂者莫若酒，臣朔所以上壽者，明陛下正而不阿，因以止哀也。
entries.en: Wine best drives care away. I raised a cup to show that Your Majesty holds straight to justice without favoritism, and to help you set grief aside.
entries.literal: Nothing dispels worry like wine; the reason your servant offered the longevity toast was to show Your Majesty is upright and not partial, and thereby to stop grief.

entries.zh: 愚不知忌諱，當死。」
entries.en: I spoke bluntly and deserve death."
entries.literal: Stupidly not knowing taboo, I deserve death."

entries.zh: 先是，朔嘗醉入殿中，小遺殿上，劾不敬。
entries.en: Earlier, drunk in the palace, he had relieved himself on the hall floor and was charged with lèse-majesté.
entries.literal: Before this, Shuo had once entered the hall drunk and urinated a little on the hall; he was impeached for irreverence.

entries.zh: 有詔免為庶人，待詔宦者署。
entries.en: An edict reduced him to commoner rank on the eunuchs' office waiting list.
entries.literal: An edict ordered him demoted to commoner status, awaiting edict at the eunuchs' office.

entries.zh: 因此對復為中郎，賜帛百匹。
entries.en: After this exchange he was restored as gentleman of the palace and given a hundred bolts of silk.
entries.literal: Because of this reply he was again made gentleman of the palace and granted a hundred bolts of silk.

entries.zh: 初，建元三年，微行始出，北至池陽，西至黃山，南獵長楊，東遊宜春。
entries.en: In the third year of Jianyuan the emperor began slipping out in disguise—north to Chiyang, west to Huangshan, south to hunt at Changyang, east to sport at Yichun.
entries.literal: At first, in the third year of Jianyuan, incognito outings began: north to Chiyang, west to Huangshan, south to hunt at Changyang, east to roam Yichun.

entries.zh: 微行常用飲酎已。
entries.en: These secret jaunts usually waited until after the ritual tasting of the new ale.
entries.literal: Incognito outings commonly used the drinking of the autumn ale as their finish.

entries.zh: 八九月中，與侍中常侍武騎及待詔隴西北地良家子能騎射者期諸殿門，故有「期門」之號自此始。
entries.en: "In the eighth or ninth month, together with palace attendants, regular attendants, military riders, and awaiting-edict good-family sons of Longxi and Beidi who could ride and shoot, he would rendezvous at the palace gates—therefore the title Gate Rendezvous began from this."
entries.literal: In the eighth or ninth month, together with palace attendants, regular attendants, military riders, and awaiting-edict good-family sons of Longxi and Beidi who could ride and shoot, he would rendezvous at the palace gates—therefore the title Gate Rendezvous began from this.

entries.zh: 微行以夜漏下十刻乃出，常稱平陽侯。
entries.en: He left only after the tenth night watch and passed himself off as the marquis of Pingyang.
entries.literal: Incognito outings waited until the clepsydra had dropped ten night marks before setting out; he always called himself Marquis of Pingyang.

entries.zh: 旦明，入山下馳射鹿豕狐兔，手格熊羆，馳騖禾稼稻粳之地。
entries.en: At daybreak he would gallop through the foothills shooting deer, boar, fox, and hare, grapple bears with his bare hands, and thunder across standing grain.
entries.literal: At dawn, entering the hills below he galloped and shot deer, boar, fox, and hare, wrestled bears with his hands, and raced through fields of grain and rice.

entries.zh: 民皆號呼罵詈，相聚會，自言鄠杜令。
entries.en: Farmers howled abuse, banded together, and claimed to be the magistrates of Hu and Du.
entries.literal: The people all shouted and cursed, gathered in meetings, and declared themselves the magistrates of Hu and Du.

entries.zh: 令往，欲謁平陽侯，諸騎欲擊鞭之。
entries.en: When a real magistrate came to call on the marquis, the escort wanted to whip him away.
entries.literal: When a magistrate went, wishing to pay court to the Marquis of Pingyang, the riders wished to strike him with whips.

entries.zh: 令大怒。
entries.en: The magistrate exploded with rage.
entries.literal: The magistrate was greatly angered.

entries.zh: 使吏呵止，獵者數騎見留，乃示以乘輿物，久之乃得去。
entries.en: He sent runners to intervene; a few of the hunting party were held until he produced tokens of the imperial equipage, and only then were they allowed to go.
entries.literal: He sent clerks to shout and stop them; several riders of the hunt party were detained until he showed them imperial carriage gear; only after a long time could they leave.

entries.zh: 時夜出夕還，後齎五日糧，會朝長信宮，上大歡樂之。
entries.en: At first the emperor slipped out at night and returned the following evening. Later he took provisions for five days, timing his return for court at Changxin Palace. He thoroughly enjoyed these excursions.
entries.literal: At that time he would go out at night and return the following evening. Later he took five days' provisions, returning for court at Changxin Palace; the emperor delighted greatly in these excursions.

entries.zh: 是後，南山下乃知微行數出也，然尚迫於太后，未敢遠出。
entries.en: Word spread south of the capital that the emperor was often abroad in disguise, but the empress dowager still kept him from roaming too far.
entries.literal: After this, south of Mount Zhong those below knew incognito outings went out repeatedly, yet still pressed by the empress dowager, he did not dare go far.

entries.zh: 丞相御史知指，乃使右輔都尉徼循長楊以東，右內史發小民共待會所。
entries.en: Reading the signs, the chancellor and censor ordered the right-flank commandant to patrol east of Changyang and the right metropolitan superintendent to draft peasants to line the emperor's routes.
entries.literal: The chancellor and Imperial Counselor grasped the intent and thereupon sent the right assistant metropolitan commandant to patrol east of Changyang, and the right metropolitan superintendent to mobilize common folk to await together at the rendezvous points.

entries.zh: 後乃私置更衣，從宣曲以南十二所，中休更衣，投宿諸宮，長楊、五柞、倍陽、宣曲尤幸。
entries.en: Later he had a dozen discreet lodges built south of Xuqu where he could change dress, rest, and sleep over at Changyang, Wuzuo, Beiyang, and Xuqu—his favorite haunts.
entries.literal: Afterward he privately set up changing rooms—twelve places from Xuqu south—resting midway to change clothes, lodging overnight in the various palaces; Changyang, Wuzuo, Beiyang, and Xuqu were especially favored.

entries.zh: 於是上以為道遠勞苦，又為百姓所患，乃使太中大夫吾丘壽王與待詔能用算者二人，舉籍阿城以南，□以東，宜春以西，提封頃畝，乃其賈直，欲除以為上林苑，屬之南山。
entries.en: Weary of the long rides and the havoc among the people, he sent Wuqiu Shouwang and two mathematicians on the waiting roster to survey every registered field from south of Acheng eastward (one toponym is missing in the text) to west of Yichun, tally acreage and price, and annex the tract as the Shanglin hunting park running to the Southern Mountains.
entries.literal: Thereupon the emperor, thinking the way was distant and toilsome and also a trouble to the common people, sent Grand Counsellor Wuqiu Shouwang together with two awaiting-edict men skilled in calculation to raise the registers from south of Acheng, east of (lacuna), west of Yichun, the sealed field acreage and their purchase values, wishing to set these aside to make the Shanglin Park, joining it to the Southern Mountains.

entries.zh: 又詔中尉、左右內史表屬縣草田，欲以償鄠杜之民。
entries.en: He ordered the capital commandant and the metropolitan superintendents to list idle public land in their counties as compensation for the farmers of Hu and Du.
entries.literal: He also issued an edict the commandant of the capital and the left and right metropolitan superintendents to list waste fields of subordinate counties, wishing to use them to compensate the people of Hu and Du.

entries.zh: 吾丘壽王奏事，上大說稱善。
entries.en: Wuqiu Shouwang's report delighted the emperor.
entries.literal: When Wuqiu Shouwang reported on the affair, the emperor was greatly pleased and praised it.

entries.zh: 時朔在傍，進諫曰：
entries.en: Dongfang Shuo, standing by, offered remonstrance:
entries.literal: At that time Shuo was at his side and advanced remonstrance, saying:

entries.zh: 朔文辭不遜，高自稱譽，上偉之，令待詔公車，奉祿薄，未得省見。
entries.en: Dongfang Shuo's memorial was immodest and his self-praise extravagant, yet the emperor was impressed and rostered him at the Public Carriage office—meager pay and no audience in the inner palace.
entries.literal: Shuo's phrasing was not deferential; he praised himself highly. The emperor marveled at him and ordered him to await edict at the Public Carriage office; his stipend was meager and he was not granted audience.

entries.zh: 久之，朔紿騶硃儒，曰：「上以若曹無益於縣官，耕田力作固不及人，臨眾處官不能治民，從軍擊虜不任兵事，無益於國用，徒索衣食，今欲盡殺若曹。」
entries.en: After long neglect Dongfang Shuo hoaxed the court dwarfs, saying, "His Majesty says you people are useless to the treasury—you cannot outwork farmers, cannot govern if given office, cannot fight if sent to the army; you only eat and wear what the state provides, so he means to execute the lot of you."
entries.literal: After a long time Shuo deceived the dwarf attendants, saying, "The emperor thinks you fellows do the exchequer no good—in farming and heavy labor you cannot match others, in facing crowds and holding office you cannot govern the people, in following the army to strike bandits you cannot bear military affairs; you benefit the state's budget not at all, only demand clothes and food—now he intends to kill you all."

entries.zh: 硃儒大恐，啼泣。
entries.en: The dwarfs were panic-stricken and sobbed.
entries.literal: The dwarfs were greatly terrified and wept.

entries.zh: 朔教曰：「上即過，叩頭請罪。」
entries.en: Dongfang Shuo told them, "When he comes by, throw yourselves on the ground and plead for mercy."
entries.literal: Shuo instructed them, "When the emperor passes, knock your heads and beg forgiveness."

entries.zh: 居有頃，聞上過，硃儒皆號泣頓首。
entries.en: Soon they heard the imperial progress approaching and set up a chorus of weeping and kowtows.
entries.literal: Presently they heard the emperor passing; the dwarfs all wailed and knocked their heads.

entries.zh: 上問：「何為？」
entries.en: The emperor asked: "What is this?"
entries.literal: The emperor asked: What is this?

entries.zh: 對曰：「東方朔言上欲盡誅臣等。」
entries.en: They said, "Dongfang Shuo told us Your Majesty planned to slaughter every dwarf."
entries.literal: They replied, "Dongfang Shuo said Your Majesty wished to execute us all."

entries.zh: 上知朔多端，召問朔：「何恐硃儒為？」
entries.en: The emperor knew Dongfang Shuo's tricks and called him in, "Why did you terrify my dwarfs?"
entries.literal: The emperor, knowing Shuo had many stratagems, summoned and asked Shuo, "Why did you frighten the dwarf attendants?"

entries.zh: 對曰：「臣朔生亦言，死亦言。
entries.en: He answered, "I speak my mind in life and in death.
entries.literal: He replied, "Your servant Shuo speaks whether I live or die.

entries.zh: 硃儒長三尺餘，奉一囊粟，錢二百四十。
entries.en: Those fellows stand a little over three feet high yet draw one full sack of grain and two hundred forty cash a month.
entries.literal: The dwarfs are a little over three feet tall; they receive one sack of grain and two hundred forty cash.

entries.zh: 臣朔長九尺餘，亦奉一囊粟，錢二百四十。
entries.en: I stand well over nine feet and am paid the same sack and the same two hundred forty cash.
entries.literal: Your servant Shuo is over nine feet tall, yet likewise receives one sack of grain and two hundred forty cash.

entries.zh: 朱儒飽欲死，臣朔飢欲死。
entries.en: They are bloated to bursting while I starve on the same ration.
entries.literal: The dwarfs are so stuffed they could die; your servant Shuo is so hungry he could die.

entries.zh: 臣言可用，幸異其禮；
entries.en: If my counsel is worth hearing, grant me a different scale of treatment;
entries.literal: If your servant's words may be used, may you graciously alter his treatment;

entries.zh: 不可用，罷之，無令但索長安米。」
entries.en: if not, dismiss me and spare the capital's grain."
entries.literal: if they may not be used, dismiss me—do not let me merely demand Chang'an's rice."

entries.zh: 上大笑，因使待詔金馬門，稍得親近。
entries.en: The emperor roared with laughter, moved him to the Golden Horse Gate waiting list, and little by little drew him nearer the throne.
entries.literal: The emperor laughed greatly and thereupon had him await edict at the Golden Horse Gate; gradually he obtained closeness.

entries.zh: 上嘗使諸數家射覆，置守宮盂下，射之，皆不能中。
entries.en: Once the emperor set the diviners a riddle: a gecko hidden under a jar. None could name it.
entries.literal: The emperor once had the various diviners play shoot the cover: he placed a gecko under a bowl and had them guess; none could hit it.

entries.zh: 朔自讚曰：「臣嘗受《易》，請射之。」
entries.en: Dongfang Shuo stepped forward and said, "I have studied the Book of Changes; let me try."
entries.literal: Shuo himself volunteered, saying, "Your servant has studied the Changes; allow me to shoot it."

entries.zh: 乃別蓍布卦而對曰：「臣以為龍又無角，謂之為蛇又有足，跂跂脈脈善緣壁，是非守宮即蜥蜴。」
entries.en: He cast the stalks and said, "It has not the dragon's horn nor the snake's limbless glide; it pads along the wall with a creeping gait—it must be a gecko or a wall lizard."
entries.literal: He then sorted the milfoil and spread the hexagrams and replied, "Your servant thinks it is a dragon yet has no horns; call it a snake yet it has feet; creeping and pulsing it climbs walls well—if not a gecko then a lizard."

entries.zh: 上曰：「善。」
entries.en: The emperor said: "Good."
entries.literal: The emperor said: Good.

entries.zh: 賜帛十匹。
entries.en: He rewarded him with ten bolts of silk.
entries.literal: He granted ten bolts of silk.

entries.zh: 復使射他物，連中，輒賜帛。
entries.en: Further riddles followed; each time Dongfang Shuo hit the mark and silk was piled into his hands.
entries.literal: Again he had him shoot other objects; he hit in succession and each time was granted silk.

entries.zh: 久之，伏日，詔賜從官肉。
entries.en: On a midsummer dog-day the emperor ordered meat distributed to his attendants.
entries.literal: After a long time, on the dog-day festival, an edict ordered meat granted to the attendants.

entries.zh: 大官丞日晏下來，朔獨拔劍割肉，謂其同官曰：「伏日當蚤歸，請受賜。」
entries.en: The grand provisioner's assistant came down late in the day; Shuo alone drew his sword and carved meat, saying to his fellow officials: "On dog-days one should return early—allow me to accept the gift."
entries.literal: The grand provisioner's assistant came down late in the day; Shuo alone drew his sword and carved meat, saying to his fellow officials: On dog-days one should return early—allow me to accept the gift.

entries.zh: 即懷肉去。
entries.en: He stuffed the meat in his robe and walked off.
entries.literal: He thereupon tucked the meat in his bosom and left.

entries.zh: 大官奏之。
entries.en: The steward reported him.
entries.literal: The grand provisioner reported him.

entries.zh: 朔入，上曰：「昨賜肉，不待詔，以劍割肉而去之，何也？」
entries.en: When Shuo entered, the emperor said: "Yesterday when meat was granted, without awaiting edict you carved meat with a sword and left—why?"
entries.literal: When Shuo entered, the emperor said: Yesterday when meat was granted, without awaiting edict you carved meat with a sword and left—why?

entries.zh: 朔免冠謝。
entries.en: Dongfang Shuo doffed his cap and apologized.
entries.literal: Shuo removed his cap and apologized.

entries.zh: 上曰：「先生起，自責也！」
entries.en: The emperor said, "Stand up, Master, and blame yourself!"
entries.literal: The emperor said, "Sir, rise—blame yourself!"

entries.zh: 朔再拜曰：「朔來！
entries.en: Dongfang Shuo bowed twice and said, "Shuo, come forward! Shuo, come forward!
entries.literal: Shuo twice bowed and said, "Shuo, come! Shuo, come!

entries.zh: 朔來！
entries.en: Shuo, come forward!
entries.literal: Shuo comes!

entries.zh: 受賜不待詔，何無禮也！
entries.en: To take a gift without the emperor's word—how rude!
entries.literal: Accepting a gift without awaiting edict—how lacking in propriety!

entries.zh: 拔劍割肉，一何壯也！
entries.en: To carve meat with your own blade—how bold!
entries.literal: Drawing a sword to carve meat—how bold!

entries.zh: 割之不多，又何廉也！
entries.en: To take so modest a slice—how temperate!
entries.literal: Carving not much—how incorrupt again!

entries.zh: 歸遺細君，又何仁也！」
entries.en: To carry it home to my wife—how tender-hearted!"
entries.literal: Taking it home to give to my wife—how humane again!"

entries.zh: 上笑曰：「使先生自責，乃反自譽！」
entries.en: The emperor laughed and said, "I asked you to blame yourself, and you have praised yourself instead!"
entries.literal: The emperor laughed and said, "Having you blame yourself, you instead praise yourself!"

entries.zh: 復賜酒一石，肉百斤，歸遺細君。
entries.en: He sent him another stone of wine and a hundred jin of meat for his wife.
entries.literal: He again granted a stone of wine and a hundred jin of meat to take home to his wife.

entries.zh: 是日因奏《泰階》之事，上乃拜朔為太中大夫給事中，賜黃金百斤。
entries.en: That day he lectured on the Grand Steps; the emperor named him Grand Counsellor with access to the inner palace and sent a hundred jin of gold.
entries.literal: That day he thereupon presented the matter of the Grand Steps; the emperor then appointed Shuo Grand Counsellor with Palace Attendance and granted a hundred jin of gold.

entries.zh: 然遂起上林苑，如壽王所奏雲。
entries.en: The Shanglin Park was built anyway, just as Wuqiu Shouwang had proposed.
entries.literal: Yet thereupon Shanglin Park was raised, as Shouwang had memorialized.

entries.zh: 初，帝姑館陶公主號竇太主，堂邑侯陳午尚之。
entries.en: The emperor's aunt, the Princess of Guantao, was known as Grand Princess Dou and had married Chen Wu, Marquis of Tangyi.
entries.literal: At first, the emperor's aunt, the Princess of Guantao, was known as Grand Princess Dou and was married to Chen Wu, Marquis of Tangyi.

entries.zh: 午死，主寡居，年五十餘矣，近幸董偃。
entries.en: When Chen Wu died she was past fifty, a widow who took Dong Yan as her lover.
entries.literal: When Wu died, the princess dwelt a widow, being over fifty years old, and drew near and favored Dong Yan.

entries.zh: 始偃與母以賣珠為事，偃年十三，隨母出入主家。
entries.en: Dong Yan and his mother had sold pearls for a living; at thirteen he began following his mother to the princess's mansion.
entries.literal: At first Yan and his mother made their living selling pearls; at thirteen Yan followed his mother in and out of the princess's house.

entries.zh: 左右言其姣好，主召見，曰；
entries.en: Her attendants praised the boy's looks; she called him in and said,
entries.literal: Those about spoke of his handsome looks; the princess summoned and saw him, saying;

entries.zh: 「吾為母養之。」
entries.en: "I will raise him for his mother."
entries.literal: I will raise him for his mother.

entries.zh: 因留第中，教書計相馬御射，頗讀傳記。
entries.en: She kept him in her household, taught him reckoning, horsemanship, and archery, and had him read histories and tales.
entries.literal: Thereupon she kept him in the mansion, teaching accounts, judging horses, riding and archery; he read somewhat of chronicles and records.

entries.zh: 至年十八而冠，出則執轡，入則侍內。
entries.en: At his capping at eighteen he led her carriage abroad and attended her within.
entries.literal: When he reached eighteen he capped; going out he held the reins, entering he attended within.

entries.zh: 為人溫柔愛人，以主故，諸公接之，名稱城中，號曰董君。
entries.en: Courteous and affable, he was received by the nobility for the princess's sake and was known through the capital as Lord Dong.
entries.literal: In person he was gentle and warm and loved people; because of the princess the great lords received him; his name was praised in the capital; he was called Lord Dong.

entries.zh: 主因推令散財交士，令中府曰：「董君所發，一日金滿百斤，錢滿百萬，帛滿千匹，乃白之。」
entries.en: The princess thereupon urged him to scatter wealth and befriend knights, ordering the inner treasury: "Whatever Lord Dong disburses—if in one day gold fills a hundred jin, cash fills a million, silk fills a thousand bolts, then report it."
entries.literal: The princess thereupon urged him to scatter wealth and befriend knights, ordering the inner treasury: Whatever Lord Dong disburses—if in one day gold fills a hundred jin, cash fills a million, silk fills a thousand bolts, then report it.

entries.zh: 安陵爰叔者，爰盎兄子也，與偃善，謂偃曰：「足下私侍漢主，挾不測之罪，將欲安處乎？」
entries.en: Yuanshu of Anling was the nephew of Yuan Ang; he was on good terms with Yan and said to Yan: "You privately serve the Han ruler, bearing immeasurable crime—where do you intend to end up?"
entries.literal: Yuanshu of Anling was the nephew of Yuan Ang; he was on good terms with Yan and said to Yan: You privately serve the Han ruler, bearing immeasurable crime—where do you intend to end up?

entries.zh: 偃懼曰：「憂之久矣，不知所以。」
entries.en: Yan fearfully said: "I have worried long; I do not know what to do."
entries.literal: Yan fearfully said: I have worried long; I do not know what to do.

entries.zh: 爰叔曰：「顧城廟遠無宿宮，又有萩竹籍田，足下何不白主獻長門園？
entries.en: Yuanshu said: "Consider that the suburban altars are far and have no lodging palace, and there is also reed bamboo and the ritual field—why do you not report to the princess to offer the Changmen garden?
entries.literal: Yuanshu said: Consider that the suburban altars are far and have no lodging palace, and there is also reed bamboo and the ritual field—why do you not report to the princess to offer the Changmen garden?

entries.zh: 此上所欲也。
entries.en: That is exactly what he wants.
entries.literal: This is what the superior desires.

entries.zh: 如是，上知計出於足下也，則安枕而臥，長無慘怛之憂。
entries.en: He will know the gift was your idea, sleep without fear, and cease to brood on silencing you.
entries.literal: If so, when the superior knows the plan came from your feet, then he will pillow peacefully and sleep, and long have no bitter grief.

entries.zh: 久之不然，上且請之，於足下何如？」
entries.en: Delay, and the emperor may take it by force—what then for you?"
entries.literal: If after long it is not so, the superior will ask for it—how will that be for your feet?"

entries.zh: 偃頓首曰：「敬奉教。」
entries.en: Yan kowtowed and said, "Respectfully I receive your teaching."
entries.literal: Yan kowtowed and said, "Respectfully I receive your teaching."

entries.zh: 入言之主，主立奏書獻之。
entries.en: He told the princess; she memorialized the offer at once.
entries.literal: He entered and spoke to the princess; she immediately submitted a memorial presenting it.

entries.zh: 上大說，更名竇大主園為長門宮。
entries.en: The emperor was delighted and renamed her estate the Changmen Palace.
entries.literal: The emperor was greatly pleased and renamed Grand Princess Dou's garden Changmen Palace.

entries.zh: 主大喜，使偃以黃金百斤為爰叔壽。
entries.en: Overjoyed, she sent Dong Yan with a hundred jin of gold to thank Yuanshu.
entries.literal: The princess was greatly pleased and sent Yan with a hundred jin of gold to toast Yuanshu's longevity.

entries.zh: 叔因是為董君畫求見上之策，令主稱疾不朝。
entries.en: Yuanshu then arranged Dong Yan's introduction: the princess was to feign illness and skip court.
entries.literal: Yuanshu thereupon for Lord Dong plotted the plan of seeking audience with the emperor, ordering the princess to claim illness and not attend court.

entries.zh: 上往臨疾，問所欲，主辭謝曰：「妾幸蒙陛下厚恩，先帝遺德，奉朝請之禮，備臣妾之儀，列為公主，賞賜邑入，隆天重地，死無以塞責。
entries.en: The emperor went to visit her illness and asked what she wished; the princess declined with thanks, saying: "Your handmaid has fortunately received Your Majesty's thick grace and the former emperor's bequeathed virtue, observed the rite of court attendance, fulfilled the deportment of subject and concubine, been ranked a princess, been granted fief income—heaven high, earth heavy—in death I have no means to repay the obligation.
entries.literal: The emperor went to visit her illness and asked what she wished; the princess declined with thanks, saying: Your handmaid has fortunately received Your Majesty's thick grace and the former emperor's bequeathed virtue, observed the rite of court attendance, fulfilled the deportment of subject and concubine, been ranked a princess, been granted fief income—heaven high, earth heavy—in death I have no means to repay the obligation.

entries.zh: 一日卒有不勝灑掃之職，先狗馬填溝壑，竊有所恨，不勝大願，願陛下時忘萬事，養精游神，從中掖庭回輿，枉路臨妾山林，得獻觴上壽，娛樂左右。
entries.en: If I should die before repaying you, one wish would remain: that you set the state aside awhile, refresh your spirit, turn your carriage from the palace, and deign to visit my poor villa so I may pour wine for you and cheer your attendants.
entries.literal: If one day I suddenly am unequal to the duty of sprinkling and sweeping, before the dogs and horses I fill ditches and gullies—privately I have a regret, unable to overcome a great wish: I wish Your Majesty from time to time to forget the myriad affairs, nurture essence and roam spirit, turn the carriage from the central palace lanes, bend the road to visit your handmaid's mountain grove, be able to raise a cup and offer longevity, and delight those left and right.

entries.zh: 如是而死，何恨之有！」
entries.en: Then I could die content."
entries.literal: If I die thus, what regret would there be!"

entries.zh: 上曰：「主何憂？
entries.en: The emperor said: "What does the princess worry about?
entries.literal: The emperor said: What does the princess worry about?

entries.zh: 幸得愈。
entries.en: You will recover.
entries.literal: Fortunately you will recover.

entries.zh: 恐群臣從官多，大為主費。」
entries.en: I only fear a full train of officials would burden you with expense."
entries.literal: I fear the many ministers and followers would greatly cost the princess."

entries.zh: 上還，有頃，主疾愈，起謁，上以錢千萬從主飲。
entries.en: Soon she recovered and attended court; the emperor brought ten million cash to drink with her.
entries.literal: The emperor returned; after a while the princess's illness improved; she rose and paid court; the emperor brought ten million cash to drink with the princess.

entries.zh: 後數日，上臨山林，主自執宰敝膝，道入登階就坐。
entries.en: Days later he visited her estate; she met him in a cook's apron like a common hostess, led him in, and seated him.
entries.literal: Several days later the emperor visited the mountain grove; the princess herself took the cook's worn apron, guided him in, ascended the steps, and took seat.

entries.zh: 坐未定，上曰：「願謁主人翁。」
entries.en: Before seating was settled, the emperor said: "I wish to greet the master of the house."
entries.literal: Before seating was settled, the emperor said: I wish to greet the master of the house.

entries.zh: 主乃下殿，去簪珥，徒跣頓首謝曰：「妾無狀，負陛下，身當伏誅。
entries.en: She slipped from the dais, stripped her ornaments, and kowtowed barefoot: "I have shamed you and deserve death.
entries.literal: The princess thereupon descended the hall, removed hairpins and earrings, went barefoot and knocked her head in apology, saying: Your handmaid has behaved disgracefully and failed Your Majesty; her person should suffer execution.

entries.zh: 陛下不致之法，頓首死罪。」
entries.en: Yet you have not held me to the law—I kowtow for my capital crime."
entries.literal: Your Majesty has not applied the law to me—I knock my head for a capital crime."

entries.zh: 有詔謝。
entries.en: An edict bade her rise.
entries.literal: There was an edict to excuse her.

entries.zh: 主簪履起，之東廂自引董君。
entries.en: She dressed again, went to the east wing, and led Dong Yan out.
entries.literal: The princess pinned hair and donned shoes, rose, went to the east wing and herself led forth Lord Dong.

entries.zh: 董君綠幘傅□，隨主前，伏殿下。
entries.en: Dong Yan wore the green turban of a servant and jeweled sleeves; he followed her forward and knelt below the steps.
entries.literal: Lord Dong in green headcloth and (lacuna) attached, followed the princess forward and prostrated below the hall.

entries.zh: 主乃讚：「館陶公主胞人臣偃昧死再拜謁。」
entries.en: The princess then announced: "The Princess of Guantao's chamberlain, your subject Yan, in darkness of death twice bows to pay court."
entries.literal: The princess then announced: The Princess of Guantao's chamberlain, your subject Yan, in darkness of death twice bows to pay court.

entries.zh: 因叩頭謝，上為之起。
entries.en: Dong Yan kowtowed; the emperor rose for him.
entries.literal: Thereupon he knocked his head in thanks; the emperor for him rose.

entries.zh: 有詔賜衣冠上。
entries.en: An edict summoned him to don proper cap and robes.
entries.literal: An edict ordered court dress granted and he ascend.

entries.zh: 偃起，走就衣冠。
entries.en: Dong Yan rose and went to change.
entries.literal: Yan rose and hastened to take the cap and robes.

entries.zh: 主自奉食進觴。
entries.en: The princess herself poured his wine and served the meal.
entries.literal: The princess herself served food and advanced cups.

entries.zh: 當是時，董君見尊不名，稱為「主人翁」，飲大歡樂。
entries.en: "At that time Lord Dong was honored without being named; he was called master of the house; drinking was greatly joyful."
entries.literal: At that time Lord Dong was honored without being named; he was called master of the house; drinking was greatly joyful.

entries.zh: 主乃請賜將軍、列侯、從官金錢雜繒各有數。
entries.en: She asked the emperor to reward every general, marquis, and attendant with gold, cash, and silk.
entries.literal: The princess then requested grants of gold, cash, and assorted silks to generals, ranked marquises, and followers, each in set amounts.

entries.zh: 於是董君貴寵，天下莫不聞。
entries.en: Dong Yan's favor became famous throughout the empire.
