entries.literal: Later Ji became market director for the chariot-and-cavalry general’s army, was promoted grand general’s chief clerk; Huo Guang greatly esteemed him, and he entered as supernumerary household grandee with palace access.

entries.zh: 昭帝崩，無嗣，大將軍光遣吉迎昌邑王賀。
entries.en: When Emperor Zhao died heirless, Huo Guang sent Bing Ji to escort Prince He of Changyi to the capital.
entries.literal: Emperor Zhao passed away without heir; Grand General Guang sent Ji to welcome King He of Changyi.

entries.zh: 賀即位，以行淫亂廢，光與車騎將軍張安世諸大臣議所立，未定。
entries.en: Prince He was enthroned but deposed for debauchery; Huo Guang and Zhang Anshi debated a replacement without reaching agreement.
entries.literal: When He assumed the throne, because of conduct of debauchery and disorder he was deposed; Guang with Chariot-and-Cavalry General Zhang Anshi and the various great ministers deliberated whom to establish, not yet settled.

entries.zh: 吉奏記光曰：「將軍事孝武皇帝，受襁褓之屬，任天下之寄，孝昭皇帝早崩亡嗣，海內憂懼，欲亟聞嗣主，發喪之日以大誼立後，所立非其人，復以大誼廢之，天下莫不服焉。
entries.en: Bing Ji wrote Huo Guang: ‘General, you served Emperor Wu, received the charge of the swaddling-clothes regency, and bear the empire’s trust; when Emperor Zhao died without heir the realm was anxious; you established a successor on the day mourning was announced, and when he proved unworthy you deposed him again by great duty—none under Heaven failed to submit.
entries.literal: Ji submitted a sealed note to Guang saying: ‘General, you served Emperor Wu, received the swaddling-clothes charge, bore the empire’s trust; Emperor Zhao passed early without heir; within the seas there was worry and fear, eager quickly to hear of a successor lord; on the day mourning was announced you by great duty established a successor; the one established was not the right man, again by great duty you deposed him—none under Heaven failed to submit.

entries.zh: 方今社稷宗廟群生之命在將軍之一舉。
entries.en: Now the fate of the altars of soil and grain, the ancestral temples, and every living being turns on your next move.
entries.literal: At present the altars of soil and grain, the ancestral temples, and the host of living beings’ fate hang on a single move of the General’s.

entries.zh: 竊伏聽於眾庶，察其所言，諸侯宗室在位列者，未有所聞於民間也。
entries.en: I have listened to common talk: none of the ranked princes or imperial kinsmen wins the people’s hope.
entries.literal: Your servant has prostrated himself to listen among the multitude and observe what they say; among the feudal lords and imperial lineage who hold rank, none has been heard of favorably among the common folk.

entries.zh: 而遺詔所養武帝曾孫名病已在掖庭外家者，吉前使居郡邸時見其幼少，至今十八九矣，通經術，有美材，行安而節和。
entries.en: The edict-nurtured great-grandson Liu Bingyi, raised outside the harem—whom Bing Ji had known as a child in the hostel—is now a young man of eighteen or nineteen, learned, talented, and even-tempered.
entries.literal: Yet the testamentary edict’s nurtured imperial great-grandson named Bingyi, dwelling with his maternal kin outside the Lateral Courts—Ji earlier, when he had him stay at the commandery hostel, saw him in childhood; to the present he is eighteen or nineteen, understands the classics and techniques, has fine talent, conduct steady and temper harmonious.

entries.zh: 願將軍詳大議，參以蓍龜，豈宜褒顯，先使入侍，令天下昭然知之，然後決定大策，天下幸甚！」
entries.en: I beg you to weigh the great deliberation and consult the tortoise and milfoil—would it not be fitting to honor and display him? First have him enter attendance so all under Heaven may plainly know it, then decide the great plan—under Heaven would be greatly fortunate!’
entries.literal: I beg the general to examine the great deliberation and consult tortoise and milfoil—would it not be fitting to honor and display him? First have him enter attendance; let all under Heaven plainly know it—then decide the great plan; under Heaven will be greatly fortunate!’

entries.zh: 光覽其議，遂尊立皇曾孫，遣宗正劉德與吉迎曾孫於掖庭。
entries.en: Huo Guang accepted the plan, elevated Liu Bingyi, and sent Liu De with Bing Ji to fetch him from the harem compound.
entries.literal: Guang read his proposal, then honored and established the imperial great-grandson, dispatching Director of Imperial Clan Liu De together with Ji to welcome the great-grandson from the Lateral Courts.

entries.zh: 宣帝初即位，賜吉爵關內侯。
entries.en: Emperor Xuan ennobled Bing Ji as a marquis-within-the-passes as soon as he took the throne.
entries.literal: When Emperor Xuan first assumed the throne, he bestowed on Ji noble rank as marquis within the passes.

entries.zh: 丙吉字少卿，魯國人也。
entries.en: Bing Ji, courtesy name Shaoqing, was a native of Lu.
entries.literal: Bing Ji, courtesy name Shaoqing, was a man of Lu.

entries.zh: 治律令，為魯獄史。
entries.en: He studied law and served as clerk of Lu’s prisons.
entries.literal: He studied statutes and ordinances and became Lu’s jail clerk.

entries.zh: 積功勞，稍遷至廷尉右監。
entries.en: Merit promotions carried him up to right superintendent under the commandant of justice.
entries.literal: Accumulating merit and toil, he gradually rose to right superintendent of the commandant of justice.

entries.zh: 坐法失官，歸為州從事。
entries.en: A legal fault cost him his post, and he went home as a provincial inspector’s aide.
entries.literal: He sat under the law and lost office, returning to serve as staff to the provincial inspector.

entries.zh: 武帝末，巫蠱事起，吉以故廷尉監征，詔治巫蠱郡邸獄。
entries.en: Late in Emperor Wu’s reign, when the witchcraft trials began, Bing Ji—once a justice superintendent—was recalled to oversee the witchcraft jail in the imperial hostel.
entries.literal: At the end of Emperor Wu, when the witchcraft affair arose, Ji because he had formerly been superintendent of the commandant of justice was summoned, issued an edict to try the witchcraft case in the commandery hostel prison.

entries.zh: 時，宣帝生數月，以皇曾孫坐衛太子事系，吉見而憐之。
entries.en: The future Emperor Xuan was only months old when, as the imperial great-grandson, he was imprisoned in the Crown Prince Wei affair; Bing Ji saw the infant and pitied him.
entries.literal: At the time the future Emperor Xuan was several months old; as the imperial great-grandson he was implicated in Crown Prince Wei’s affair and imprisoned; Ji saw him and pitied him.

entries.zh: 又心知太子無事實，重哀曾孫無辜，吉擇謹厚女徒，令保養曾孫，置閒燥處。
entries.en: Knowing the crown prince was innocent and the child blameless, he chose a trustworthy woman convict to nurse the boy and lodged him in a warm, quiet cell.
entries.literal: Also in his heart he knew the heir apparent had no factual guilt; doubly he pitied the great-grandson’s innocence; Ji selected a careful and honest female convict, ordered her to nurture the great-grandson, and placed him in a quiet, dry place.

entries.zh: 吉治巫蠱事，連歲不決。
entries.en: Bing Ji oversaw the witchcraft trials, which dragged on unresolved year after year.
entries.literal: Ji handled the witchcraft affair; year after year it was not decided.

entries.zh: 後元二年，武帝疾，往來長楊、五柞宮，望氣者言長安獄中有天子氣，於是上遣使者分條中都官詔獄系者，亡輕重一切皆殺之。
entries.en: In 87 BCE, while Emperor Wu shuttled between hunting palaces, a diviner claimed Son-of-Heaven omens over the Chang’an jails; the emperor then sent agents to enumerate every prisoner in the capital’s edict jails and execute them all, whatever their offense.
entries.literal: In the second year of Houyuan, Emperor Wu was ill, going back and forth between Changyang and Wuzuo palaces; a qi-watcher said there was Son of Heaven qi in the Chang’an prisons; thereupon the sovereign dispatched envoys to itemize those bound in the capital offices’ edict prisons, without regard to light or heavy guilt, all to be killed.

entries.zh: 內謁者令郭穰夜到郡邸獄，吉閉門拒使者不納，曰：「皇曾孫在。
entries.en: When Guo Rang, director of palace ushers, reached the hostel prison at night, Bing Ji barred the gate and said, ‘The imperial great-grandson is inside.
entries.literal: Palace usher director Guo Rang came by night to the commandery hostel prison; Ji closed the gate and refused the envoy, not admitting him, saying: ‘The imperial great-grandson is here.

entries.zh: 他人亡辜死者猶不可，況親曾孫乎！」
entries.en: You cannot slaughter the innocent—least of all the emperor’s own great-grandson!’
entries.literal: For others to die without guilt is still not permissible—how much more the close great-grandson!’

entries.zh: 相守至天明不得入，穰還以聞，因劾奏吉。
entries.en: They stood off until dawn; Guo Rang reported back and memorialized against Bing Ji.
entries.literal: They held each other off until dawn and could not enter; Rang returned and reported it, then impeached and memorialized Ji.

entries.zh: 武帝亦寤，曰：「天使之也。」
entries.en: Emperor Wu came to his senses and said, ‘Heaven meant to spare him.’
entries.literal: Emperor Wu also awoke to it, saying: ‘Heaven made it so.’

entries.zh: 因赦天下。
entries.en: He then proclaimed a general amnesty.
entries.literal: Thereupon he amnestied all under Heaven.

entries.zh: 郡邸獄系者獨賴吉得生，恩及四海矣。
entries.en: Only the inmates of that hostel prison lived because of Bing Ji—a kindness that spread across the realm.
entries.literal: Those bound in the commandery hostel prison alone relied on Ji to obtain life—grace reached the four seas.

entries.zh: 曾孫病，幾不全者數焉，吉數敕保養乳母加致醫藥，視遇甚有恩惠，以私財物給其衣食。
entries.en: The boy nearly died several times; Bing Ji ordered better care, summoned doctors, and paid for food and clothes from his own purse.
entries.literal: The great-grandson fell ill; several times he nearly did not survive; Ji repeatedly ordered the nurse to add physicians and medicines, treated him with very much kindness and grace, and supplied his clothing and food from private property.

entries.zh: 元帝時，長安士伍尊上書言：「臣少時為郡邸小吏，竊見孝宣皇帝以皇曾孫在郡邸獄。
entries.en: In Emperor Yuan’s time, Chang’an commoner Zun submitted a memorial saying, ‘When your servant was young, I served as a petty clerk in the commandery residence and privately saw Emperor Xuan, then the imperial great-grandson, in the prison there.
entries.literal: In Emperor Yuan’s time, Chang’an commoner Zun submitted a memorial saying: ‘Your servant in youth was a petty clerk in the commandery hostel and secretly saw Emperor Xuan as imperial great-grandson in the commandery hostel prison.

entries.zh: 是時，治獄使者丙吉見皇曾孫遭離無辜，吉仁心感動，涕泣淒惻，選擇復作胡組養視皇孫，吉常從。
entries.en: Envoy Bing Ji, moved by the child’s innocence, wept and assigned Hu Zu, a woman on labor rotation, to nurse him while he stayed at hand.
entries.literal: At that time, trial-prison envoy Bing Ji saw the imperial great-grandson suffer separation and innocence; Ji’s humane heart was moved, weeping in bitter sorrow; he selected a female convict on revolving labor, Hu Zu, to nurture and watch the imperial grandson; Ji constantly accompanied.

entries.zh: 臣尊日再侍臥庭上。
entries.en: I, Zun, slept twice daily in the courtyard beside him.
entries.literal: Your servant Zun twice daily attended, lying in the courtyard.

entries.zh: 後遭條獄之召，吉扞拒大難，不避嚴刑峻法。
entries.en: When the mass execution order came, Bing Ji defied it at risk to himself.
entries.literal: Later he encountered the summons of the itemized prisons; Ji resisted the great difficulty, not avoiding harsh law.

entries.zh: 既遭大赦，吉謂守丞誰知，皇孫不當在官，使誰如移書京兆尹，遣與胡組俱送京兆尹，不受，復還。
entries.en: After the general amnesty Bing Ji told assistant warden She Zhi that the imperial grandson could not stay in jail; he sent She Ru with transfer papers to the Governor of the Capital and had Hu Zu accompany them, but the governor refused to take the child and they had to return.
entries.literal: After encountering the great amnesty, Ji told assistant warden She Zhi that the imperial grandson ought not remain in official custody; he ordered She Ru to forward documents to the Governor of the Capital and sent him together with Hu Zu to deliver the boy to the Governor of the Capital; the Governor of the Capital would not accept him, and they returned.

entries.zh: 及組日滿當去，皇孫思慕，吉以私錢顧組，令留與郭徽卿並養數月，乃遣組去。
entries.en: When Hu Zu’s term ended, Bing Ji paid her from his own pocket to stay on with Guo Zhengqing a few months longer.
entries.literal: When Zu’s term was full and she ought to depart, the imperial grandson longed for her; Ji with private cash hired Zu, ordering her to remain and together with Guo Zhengqing jointly nurture several months, then sent Zu off.

entries.zh: 後少內嗇夫白吉曰：『食皇孫亡詔令』。
entries.en: The inner granary clerk then said there was no edict to feed the boy.
entries.literal: Later the minor inner granary scribe reported to Ji saying: ‘Feeding the imperial grandson—there is no edict order.

entries.zh: 時，吉得食米肉，月月以給皇孫。
entries.en: Bing Ji supplied rice and meat each month from his own rations.
entries.literal: At the time Ji obtained food, rice, and meat, month by month to supply the imperial grandson.

entries.zh: 吉即時病，輒使臣尊朝夕請問皇孫，視省席蓐燥濕。
entries.en: When Bing Ji fell ill he sent me morning and night to check on the child’s bedding.
entries.literal: Ji immediately fell ill; then he ordered your servant Zun morning and evening to inquire after the imperial grandson, inspect matting for dry and damp.

entries.zh: 候伺組、徽卿，不得令晨夜去皇孫敖蕩，數奏甘毳食物。
entries.en: He watched the nurses so they would not neglect the boy and sent delicate food.
entries.literal: He watched Hu Zu and Guo Zhengqing, not letting them leave the imperial grandson to roam wild morning and night, repeatedly presenting sweet and soft foods.

entries.zh: 所以擁全神靈，成育聖躬，功德已無量矣。
entries.en: Thus he preserved the child’s life and raised a sage—merit beyond reckoning.
entries.literal: By these means he embraced and completed the numinous spirits, accomplished and nurtured the sagely person—merit and virtue were already beyond measure.

entries.zh: 時豈豫知天下之福，而徼其報哉！
entries.en: He could not have foreseen the throne as his reward.
entries.literal: At the time how could he have foreknown the empire’s blessing and angle for its reward!

entries.zh: 誠其仁恩內結於心也。
entries.en: His kindness came from the heart alone.
entries.literal: Truly his humane grace knotted within the heart.

entries.zh: 雖介之推割肌以存君，不足以比。
entries.en: Even Jie Zitui’s flesh-offering would not match it.
entries.literal: Though Jie Zitui sliced his flesh to preserve his lord, it is not enough to compare.

entries.zh: 教宣皇帝時，臣上書言狀，幸得下吉，吉謙讓不敢自伐，刪去臣辭，專歸美於組、徽卿。
entries.en: When Emperor Xuan came to the throne I, Zun, reported the story; Bing Ji struck out my lines and gave the credit to Hu Zu and Guo Zhengqing.
entries.literal: When it came to Emperor Xuan’s time, your servant submitted a memorial stating the facts and fortunately obtained audience below Ji; Ji modestly declined and dared not boast of himself, deleting your servant’s wording and solely attributing the praise to Zu and Zhengqing.

entries.zh: 組、徽卿皆以受田宅賜錢，吉封為博陽侯，臣尊不得比組、徽卿。
entries.en: Hu Zu and Guo Zhengqing received land and cash while Bing Ji was ennobled; I, Zun, cannot rank with them.
entries.literal: Zu and Zhengqing both thereby received fields, houses, and gifted cash; Ji was enfeoffed marquis of Boyang—your servant Zun cannot compare with Zu and Zhengqing.

entries.zh: 臣年老居貧，死在旦暮，欲終不言，恐使有功不著。
entries.en: I am old and poor and near death; I would have stayed silent but feared true merit would stay hidden.
entries.literal: Your servant is old and dwells in poverty, death at dawn or dusk; wishing finally not to speak, yet fearing to make meritorious deeds not manifest.

entries.zh: 吉子顯坐微文奪爵為關內侯，臣愚以為宜復其爵邑，以報先入功德。」
entries.en: Bing Ji’s son Xian lost his marquisate on a petty charge; I ask that his title be restored to reward his father’s virtue.’
entries.literal: Ji’s son Xian sat because of minute wording losing noble rank to marquis within the passes; your servant foolishly considers it fitting to restore his noble rank and fief, to repay the prior men’s merit and virtue.’

entries.zh: 先是，顯為太僕十餘年，與官屬大為奸利，臧千餘萬，司隸校尉昌案劾，罪至不道，奏請逮捕。
entries.en: Earlier Bing Xian, as grand coachman for over a decade, had embezzled tens of millions until Commandant Chang impeached him for inhuman crimes and sought his arrest.
entries.literal: Earlier, Xian had been grand coachman more than ten years, with office subordinates greatly practicing wicked profit, embezzling more than a thousand myriad; metropolitan commandant Chang investigated and impeached, guilt reaching lack of the Way, memorializing to request arrest.

entries.zh: 上曰：「故丞相吉有舊恩，朕不忍絕。」
entries.en: The emperor said, ‘The late Chancellor Bing Ji served me; I cannot destroy his line.’
entries.literal: The sovereign said: ‘The former chancellor Ji had old grace toward Us; We cannot bear to cut him off.’

entries.zh: 免顯官，奪邑四百戶。
entries.en: He removed Bing Xian from office and cut four hundred households from his fief.
entries.literal: He dismissed Xian from office and stripped four hundred households of the fief.

entries.zh: 後復以為城門校尉。
entries.en: Later he reappointed him colonel of the gates.
entries.literal: Later again he made him colonel of the gates.

entries.zh: 顯卒，子昌嗣爵關內侯。
entries.en: Bing Xian died; his son Chang inherited marquis-within-the-passes rank.
entries.literal: Xian died; his son Chang inherited noble rank as marquis within the passes.

entries.zh: 吉為人深厚，不伐善。
entries.en: Bing Ji was reserved and deep, never boasting of his kindness.
entries.literal: Ji as a man was deep and thick, not boasting of good deeds.

entries.zh: 自曾孫遭遇，吉絕口不道前恩，故朝廷莫能明其功也。
entries.en: After the boy became emperor, Bing Ji never mentioned his old service, so the court never knew his full merit.
entries.literal: From the great-grandson’s good fortune, Ji sealed his lips and did not speak of prior grace; therefore the court could not clarify his merit.

entries.zh: 地節三年，立皇太子，吉為太子太傅，數月，遷御史大夫。
entries.en: In 67 BCE he was made grand tutor to the new crown prince and within months promoted to imperial censor.
entries.literal: In the third year of Dijie, the imperial heir was established; Ji became grand tutor to the heir; after several months he was promoted imperial clerk.

entries.zh: 及霍氏誅，上躬親政，省尚書事。
entries.en: After the Huo family purge the emperor took personal charge and trimmed the inner court’s paperwork.
entries.literal: When the Huo clan was executed, the sovereign personally handled government and reduced the Secretariat’s business.

entries.zh: 是時，掖庭宮婢則令民夫上書，自陳嘗有阿保之功。
entries.en: Then a harem woman named Ze had her husband petition, claiming she had nursed the emperor as an infant.
entries.literal: At this time a Lateral Courts palace maid named Ze had a commoner husband submit a memorial, declaring she had once had wet-nurse merit.

entries.zh: 章下掖庭令考問，則辭引使者丙吉知狀。
entries.en: The case went to the harem director; Ze named Bing Ji as witness.
entries.literal: The document was sent down to the Lateral Courts director for examination; Ze’s testimony cited envoy Bing Ji as knowing the facts.

entries.zh: 掖庭令將則詣御史府以視吉。
entries.en: The director brought Ze to the censor’s office to confront Bing Ji.
entries.literal: The Lateral Courts director led Ze to the censor’s bureau to show Ji.

entries.zh: 吉識，謂則曰：「汝嘗坐養皇曾孫不謹督笞，汝安得有功？
entries.en: Bing Ji recognized her: ‘You were flogged for negligent nursing—what merit is that?
entries.literal: Ji recognized her and said to Ze: ‘You once sat for nursing the imperial great-grandson negligently and were whipped—how could you have merit?

entries.zh: 獨渭城胡組、淮陽郭徵卿有恩耳。」
entries.en: Only Hu Zu of Weicheng and Guo Zhengqing of Huaiyang truly helped.’
entries.literal: Only Weicheng’s Hu Zu and Huaiyang’s Guo Zhengqing had grace.’

entries.zh: 分別奏組等共養勞苦狀。
entries.en: He filed a separate memorial on Hu Zu and Guo Zhengqing’s care.
entries.literal: He separately memorialized the form of Zu and others’ joint nurturing and toil.

entries.zh: 詔吉求組、征卿，已死，有子孫，皆受厚賞。
entries.en: The court sought Hu Zu and Guo Zhengqing; both were dead, but their descendants were richly rewarded.
entries.literal: An edict ordered Ji to seek Zu and Zhengqing; they were already dead; where there were sons and grandsons, all received thick rewards.

entries.zh: 詔免則為庶人，賜錢十萬。
entries.en: Ze was stripped to commoner rank but given a hundred thousand cash.
entries.literal: An edict pardoned Ze to commoner status and bestowed one hundred thousand cash.

entries.zh: 上親見問，然後知吉有舊恩，而終不言。
entries.en: The emperor questioned her himself and learned of Bing Ji’s silence about his old debt.
entries.literal: The sovereign personally saw and questioned him, then knew Ji had old grace yet to the end did not speak.

entries.zh: 上大賢之，制詔丞相：「朕微眇時，御史大夫吉與朕有舊恩，厥德茂焉。
entries.en: Deeply moved, the emperor told the chancellor: "When I was helpless, Censor Bing Ji saved me; his virtue is profound.
entries.literal: The sovereign greatly deemed him worthy and issued an edict the chancellor: "In Our mean and slight time, Imperial Clerk Ji had old grace toward Us; his virtue is luxuriant.

entries.zh: 《詩》不雲乎？
entries.en: Does not the Odes say?
entries.literal: Does not the Odes say?

entries.zh: 『亡德不報』。
entries.en: 'No good deed goes unrewarded.'
entries.literal: 'No virtue goes unrequited.'

entries.zh: 其封吉為博陽侯，邑千三百戶。」
entries.en: Enfeoff him as Marquis of Boyang with thirteen hundred households."
entries.literal: Enfeoff Ji as marquis of Boyang, with a fief of one thousand three hundred households."

entries.zh: 臨當封，吉疾病，上將使人加紳而封之，及其生存也。
entries.en: When the patent was ready, Bing Ji fell ill; the emperor meant to invest him in person while he still lived.
entries.literal: As the enfeoffment was about to occur, Ji fell ill; the sovereign was about to send someone to add the sash and enfeoff him while he still lived.

entries.zh: 上憂吉疾不起，太子太傅夏侯勝曰：「此未死也。
entries.en: Fearing Bing Ji might die, the emperor heard Grand Tutor Xiahou Sheng say, ‘He is not dying yet.
entries.literal: The sovereign worried Ji’s illness would not rise; Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent Xiahou Sheng said: ‘This is not yet death.

entries.zh: 臣聞有陰德者，必饗其樂以及子孫。
entries.en: Men of hidden virtue enjoy blessings down to their descendants.
entries.literal: Your servant has heard that those with hidden virtue are sure to enjoy their blessing reaching sons and grandsons.

entries.zh: 今吉未獲報而疾甚，非其死疾也。」
entries.en: Bing Ji has not yet been repaid; this illness will not kill him.’
entries.literal: Now Ji has not yet received recompense while his illness is severe—this is not the illness of his death.’

entries.zh: 後病果愈。
entries.en: Bing Ji indeed recovered.
entries.literal: Afterward his illness indeed recovered.

entries.zh: 吉上書固辭，自陳不宜以空名受賞。
entries.en: He memorialized to decline, saying he deserved no empty honor.
entries.literal: Ji submitted a memorial firmly declining, declaring himself unsuited to receive reward on an empty name.

entries.zh: 上報曰：「朕之封君，非空名也，而君上書歸侯印，是顯朕不德也。
entries.en: The emperor answered: ‘This title is no empty gesture; returning the seal would only shame me.
entries.literal: The sovereign replied: ‘Our enfeoffing you, lord, is not an empty name; yet you, lord, submit a memorial returning the marquis seal—this displays Our lack of virtue.

entries.zh: 方今天下少事，君其專精神，省思慮，近醫藥，以自持。」
entries.en: Times are quiet; gather your strength, ease your mind, and follow the doctors’ care.’
entries.literal: At present under Heaven there are few affairs; you, lord, should concentrate your spirit, reduce anxious thought, draw near to physicians and medicine, thereby to sustain yourself.’

entries.zh: 後五歲，代魏相為丞相。
entries.en: Five years later he succeeded Wei Xiang as chancellor.
entries.literal: After five years he replaced Wei Xiang as chancellor.

entries.zh: 贊曰：古之制名，必繇象類，遠取諸物，近取諸身。
entries.en: The historian’s appraisal: the ancients coined titles by analogy—drawing images from nature and from the human body.
entries.literal: The appraisal says: In antiquity in instituting names, they necessarily followed images and categories, taking distantly from things, taking near at hand from the person.

entries.zh: 故經謂君為元首，臣為股肱，明其一體，相待而成也。
entries.en: The classics call the ruler the head and ministers the arms and legs, showing that ruler and minister form one body and complete each other.
entries.literal: Therefore the classics call the ruler the head’s origin, ministers thigh and forearm, clarifying they are one body, relying on each other to complete.

entries.zh: 是故君臣相配，古今常道，自然之勢也。
entries.en: Their partnership is the enduring law of government, as natural as the pairing of head and limbs.
entries.literal: Therefore ruler and minister match one another—ancient and modern constant way, the tendency of nature.

entries.zh: 近觀漢相，高祖開基，蕭、曹為冠，孝宣中興，丙、魏有聲。
entries.en: Among Han chancellors, Xiao He and Cao Shen stood first at the founding; under Emperor Xuan’s restoration Bing Ji and Wei Xiang won lasting fame.
entries.literal: Looking near at Han’s chancellors: Gaozu opened the foundation, Xiao and Cao were the cap; Emperor Xiaoxuan’s mid-restoration, Bing and Wei had reputation.

entries.zh: 是時，黜陟有序，眾職修理，公卿多稱其位，海內興於禮讓。
entries.en: In that age promotions and dismissals followed rule, every office functioned, high ministers fitted their posts, and the realm turned to courtesy and deference.
entries.literal: At that time, demotions and promotions had order; the host of duties were put in good repair; dukes and ministers mostly matched their posts; within the seas yielding courtesy arose.

entries.zh: 覽其行事，豈虛乎哉！
entries.en: Their deeds prove that reputation was no empty praise.
entries.literal: Viewing their deeds and conduct—how could they be empty!

entries.zh: 臣相幸得備員，奉職不修，不能宣廣教化。
entries.en: I fill an office I have not truly earned and have failed to extend your transforming influence.
entries.literal: Your servant Xiang has fortunately filled a place; in performing duty he has not cultivated it; he cannot spread and broaden transformation through instruction.

entries.zh: 陰陽未和，災害未息，咎在臣等。
entries.en: Yin and yang remain out of tune and omens continue—the fault is mine and my colleagues’.
entries.literal: Yin and yang are not yet harmonious; disasters and prodigies have not ceased; the fault lies with your servants and others.

entries.zh: 臣聞《易》曰：「天地以順動，故日月不過，四時不忒；
entries.en: The Book of Changes says: ‘When Heaven and earth move in harmony, sun and moon keep their courses and the seasons never falter.
entries.literal: Your servant has heard the Changes says: ‘Heaven and earth move in accord, therefore sun and moon do not err and the four seasons are not wrong;

entries.zh: 聖王以順動，故刑罰清而民服。」
entries.en: When the sage-king moves in harmony, punishments are just and the people obey.’
entries.literal: the sage king moves in accord, therefore punishments are clear and the people submit.’

entries.zh: 天地變化，必繇陰陽，陰陽之分，以日為紀。
entries.en: Heaven and earth turn on yin and yang, and yin and yang are measured by the sun’s journey.
entries.literal: Heaven and earth’s transformations must follow yin and yang; yin and yang’s divisions take the sun as their reckoning.

entries.zh: 日冬夏至，則八風之序立，萬物之性成，各有常職，不得相干。
entries.en: At the solstices the eight winds fall into order, every creature finds its nature, and each season keeps its office without trespass.
entries.literal: When the sun reaches winter and summer solstices, then the order of the eight winds is established, the natures of the myriad things are completed, each has its constant duty, and none may encroach on another.

entries.zh: 東方之神太昊，乘『震』執規司春；
entries.en: Taihao, god of the east, rides the Zhen trigram, holds the jade compass, and rules spring.
entries.literal: The god of the east, Taihao, rides Zhen, holds the compass, and oversees spring;

entries.zh: 南方之神炎帝，乘『離』執衡司夏；
entries.en: Yan Di of the south rides Li, holds the leveling cord, and rules summer.
entries.literal: the god of the south, Yan Di, rides Li, holds the leveling beam, and oversees summer;

entries.zh: 西方之神少昊，乘『兌』，執矩司秋；
entries.en: Shao Hao of the west rides Dui, holds the square, and rules autumn.
entries.literal: the god of the west, Shao Hao, rides Dui, holds the square, and oversees autumn;

entries.zh: 北方之神顓頊，乘『坎』執權司冬；
entries.en: Zhuanxu of the north rides Kan, holds the weight, and rules winter.
entries.literal: the god of the north, Zhuanxu, rides Kan, holds the weight, and oversees winter;

entries.zh: 中央之神黃帝，乘『坤』、『艮』執繩司下土。
entries.en: The Yellow Thearch at the center rides Kun and Gen, holds the plumb cord, and rules the central plain.
entries.literal: the god of the center, the Yellow Thearch, rides Kun and Gen, holds the cord, and oversees the lower earth.

entries.zh: 茲五帝所司，各有時也。
entries.en: Each of the Five Thearchs governs his season.
entries.literal: These are what the Five Thearchs oversee; each has its season.

entries.zh: 東方之卦不可以治西方，南方之卦不可以治北方。
entries.en: Eastern signs must not rule western affairs, nor southern ones northern.
entries.literal: The eastern trigram may not govern the west; the southern trigram may not govern the north.

entries.zh: 春興『兌』治則饑，秋興『震』治則華，冬興『離』治則洩，夏興『坎』治則雹。
entries.en: Invoke the wrong trigram and spring Dui brings famine, autumn Zhen brings flowers out of season, winter Li brings drought, summer Kan brings hail.
entries.literal: If in spring one raises Dui to govern, there is famine; if in autumn one raises Zhen to govern, there is unseasonable flowering; if in winter one raises Li to govern, there is drainage; if in summer one raises Kan to govern, there is hail.

entries.zh: 明王謹於尊天，慎於養人，故立羲和之官以乘四時，節授民事。
entries.en: Wise kings revere Heaven and nurture the people, setting calendar officers to harmonize the four seasons and time the agrarian commands.
entries.literal: The clear king is careful in honoring Heaven and cautious in nurturing the people; therefore he establishes Xi and He’s offices to ride the four seasons and seasonally hand down the people’s tasks.

entries.zh: 君動靜以道，奉順陰陽，則日月光明，風雨時節，寒暑調和。
entries.en: When the ruler’s every act follows the Way and yin and yang, the luminaries shine clear, rain and wind arrive on time, and cold and heat balance.
entries.literal: If the lord’s movement and stillness follow the Way, honoring and following yin and yang, then sun and moon are bright, wind and rain keep their seasons, cold and heat are tuned.

entries.zh: 三者得敘，則災害不生，五穀熟，絲麻遂，草木茂，鳥獸蕃，民不夭疾，衣食有餘。
entries.en: When those three stay ordered, omens cease, grain and silk flourish, plants and beasts thrive, and the people live out their years in plenty.
entries.literal: When these three obtain their proper order, then disasters and prodigies do not arise, the five grains ripen, silk and hemp succeed, grass and trees flourish, birds and beasts multiply, the people do not die young of sickness, and clothing and food are more than enough.

entries.zh: 若是，則君尊民說，上下亡怨，政教不違，禮讓可興。
entries.en: Then the ruler is revered, the people content, high and low free of rancor, policy untainted, and courtesy can grow.
entries.literal: If it is so, then the ruler is honored and the people pleased, high and low without resentment, government and instruction are not violated, and yielding courtesy may rise.

entries.zh: 夫風雨不時，則傷農桑；
entries.en: When wind and rain ignore the seasons, farming and silkworms suffer.
entries.literal: If wind and rain do not keep their seasons, then farming and sericulture are harmed;

entries.zh: 農桑傷，則民饑寒；
entries.en: When those fail, the people face cold and hunger.
entries.literal: when farming and sericulture are harmed, then the people are cold and hungry;

entries.zh: 饑寒在身，則亡廉恥，寇賊奸宄所繇生也。
entries.en: Want strips away shame and breeds banditry.
entries.literal: when cold and hunger are on the body, then there is no modesty and shame, and bandits, thieves, and villainy are thereby born.

entries.zh: 臣愚以為陰陽者，王事之本，群生之命，自古賢聖未有不繇者也。
entries.en: Yin and yang are the root of kingship and the breath of every creature—no sage ever ignored them.
entries.literal: Your servant foolishly considers that yin and yang are the root of kingly affairs and the mandate of the host of living beings; from antiquity worthies and sages have never not followed them.

entries.zh: 天子之義，必純取法天地，而觀於先聖。
entries.en: The Son of Heaven must model himself wholly on Heaven and earth and on the ancient sages.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven’s duty must purely take law from Heaven and earth and look to former sages.

entries.zh: 高皇帝所述書《天子所服第八》曰：「大謁者臣章受詔長樂宮，曰：『令群臣議天子所服，以安治天下。』
entries.en: Gaozu’s compiled ordinances say in Imperial Dress, Section Eight: “Grand Usher Zhang received an edict at Changle Palace, which said: ‘Have the assembled ministers deliberate on what the Son of Heaven should wear, so as to settle and govern the realm.
entries.literal: In what Gaodi set forth, the document ‘What the Son of Heaven Wears, Number Eight,’ says: ‘Grand usher your servant Zhang received edict at Changle Palace, saying: Order the host of ministers to deliberate what the Son of Heaven shall wear, thereby to pacify and order all under Heaven.’

entries.zh: 相國臣何、御史大夫臣昌謹與將軍臣陵、太子太傅臣通等議：『春夏秋冬天子所服，當法天地之數，中得人和。
entries.en: Chancellor Xiao He and Imperial Clerk Zhou Chang respectfully deliberated with General Wang Ling, Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent Shusun Tong, and others: The Son of Heaven’s clothing for spring, summer, autumn, and winter should model the numbers of Heaven and earth and attain the mean of human harmony.
entries.literal: Chancellor your servant He and Imperial Clerk your servant Chang respectfully with General your servant Ling, Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent your servant Tong, and others deliberated: ‘In spring, summer, autumn, and winter what the Son of Heaven wears should model Heaven and earth’s numbers and hit the mean of human harmony.

entries.zh: 故自天子王侯有土之君，下及兆民，能法天地，順四時，以治國家，身亡禍殃，年壽永究，是奉宗廟安天下之大禮也。
entries.en: From Son of Heaven to commoner, whoever aligns conduct with Heaven’s seasons will escape calamity, live out full years, and secure the shrines—this is the great rite of ordering the realm.
entries.literal: Therefore from the Son of Heaven, kings, and feudal lords who possess soil, down to the myriad commoners, whoever can model Heaven and earth and follow the four seasons to order the state will personally meet no misfortune or calamity, and years and life will reach their utmost—this is the great ritual of serving the ancestral temples and pacifying all under Heaven.

entries.zh: 臣請法之。
entries.en: We ask that these rules be adopted.
entries.literal: Your servants beg to take them as model.

entries.zh: 中謁者趙堯舉春，李舜舉夏，□湯舉秋，貢禹舉冬，四人各職一時。』
entries.en: Palace usher Zhao Yao was assigned spring, Li Shun summer, a certain Tang autumn, and Gong Yu winter, each man responsible for one season.’
entries.literal: Palace usher Zhao Yao presents spring, Li Shun presents summer, [text missing] Tang presents autumn, Gong Yu presents winter—the four men each take charge of one season.

entries.zh: 大謁者襄章奏，制曰：『可。』」
entries.en: Grand Usher Xiang Zhang submitted the proposal, and the edict said: ‘Approved.’”
entries.literal: Grand usher Xiang Zhang memorialized; the edict said: ‘Approved.’

entries.zh: 孝文皇帝時，以二月施恩惠於天下，賜孝弟力田及罷軍卒，祠死事者，頗非時節。
entries.en: Emperor Wen once showered favors in the second month—filial sons, diligent farmers, discharged veterans, rites for the war dead—slightly off the canonical calendar.
entries.literal: In Emperor Xiaowen’s time, in the second month he spread favor through the empire, bestowing on the filial, fraternal, and diligent farmers and on dismissed soldiers, sacrificing to those who died in service—somewhat not according to season.

entries.zh: 御史大夫朝錯時為太子家令，奏言其狀。
entries.en: Imperial Clerk Chao Cuo, then steward to the heir apparent, reported the irregularity.
entries.literal: Imperial Clerk Chao Cuo, who was then heir apparent household steward, memorialized the situation.

entries.zh: 臣相伏念陛下恩澤甚厚，然而災氣未息，竊恐詔令有未合當時者也。
entries.en: Your Majesty’s grace runs deep, yet ill omens persist—I fear some edicts still mistime seasonal policy.
entries.literal: Your servant Xiang prostrate considers that Your Majesty’s grace and moisture are very thick, yet baleful qi has not ceased; your servant secretly fears there are edicts not fitting the present season.

entries.zh: 願陛下選明經通知陰陽者四人，各主一時，時至明言所職，以和陰陽，天下幸甚！
entries.en: Choose four classicists versed in yin and yang, charge each with a season, and let them announce proper observances when their turn comes—so may Heaven and earth harmonize.
entries.literal: I beg Your Majesty select four men clear in the Classics who understand yin and yang, each to preside over one season; when the season arrives let them openly declare their duties, thereby to harmonize yin and yang—under Heaven there will be great fortune!

entries.zh: 魏相字弱翁，濟陰定陶人也，徙平陵。
entries.en: Wei Xiang, courtesy name Ruoweng, came from Dingtao in Jiyin and later relocated his household to Pingling.
entries.literal: Wei Xiang, courtesy name Ruoweng, was a man of Dingtao in Jiyin; he moved to Pingling.

entries.zh: 少學《易》，為郡卒史，舉賢良，以對策高第，為茂陵令。
entries.en: He studied the Book of Changes in youth, served as a commandery clerk, was recommended as worthy and good, ranked high on the policy examination, and was appointed magistrate of Maoling.
entries.literal: In youth he studied the Changes, became a commandery clerk, was recommended as worthy and good, by policy answers in high rank became magistrate of Maoling.

entries.zh: 頃之，御史大夫桑弘羊客詐稱御史止傳，丞不以時謁，客怒縛丞。
entries.en: Soon afterward a client of Imperial Clerk Sang Hongyang posed as an imperial clerk at a post station; when the assistant magistrate failed to appear promptly, the man flew into a rage and had him tied up.
entries.literal: Before long, a retainer of Imperial Clerk Sang Hongyang falsely claimed to be an imperial clerk and stopped at the relay station; the assistant magistrate did not in due time pay respects, and the retainer in anger bound the assistant.

entries.zh: 相疑其有奸，收捕，案致其罪，論棄客市，茂陵大治。
entries.en: Wei Xiang suspected foul play, made the arrest, tried the case, had the impostor executed in the marketplace, and brought Maoling to good order.
entries.literal: Xiang suspected he had villainy, seized and arrested him, investigated and brought his crime, sentenced and exposed the retainer in the market—Maoling was greatly well governed.

entries.zh: 寬饒初拜為司馬，未出殿門，斷其禪衣，令短離地，冠大冠，帶長劍，躬案行士卒廬室，視其飲食居處，有疾病者身自撫循臨問，加致醫藥，遇之甚有恩。
entries.en: Fresh to the colonelcy he shortened his robe, belted on a long sword, toured every barrack, tasted the gruel, nursed the sick himself, and paid doctors out of his own pocket.
entries.literal: When Kuangrao was first appointed colonel, before he had left the palace hall he cut his knee-length under-robe short so it cleared the ground, donned the great cap, girded a long sword, personally inspected the barracks and huts, examined food and quarters, and for the sick personally comforted them, supplied physicians and drugs, and treated the men with great kindness.

entries.zh: 及歲盡交代，上臨饗罷衛卒，衛卒數千人皆叩頭自請，願復留共更一年，以報寬饒厚德。
entries.en: When the year-end muster came and the emperor feasted the retiring guards, thousands begged on their knees to serve another tour under Kuangrao.
entries.literal: At year's end when duties were handed over, the emperor came in person to feast the discharged guards; several thousand guards all kowtowed and begged to stay another year on rotation together to repay Kuangrao's deep kindness.

entries.zh: 宣帝嘉之，以寬饒為太中大夫，使行風俗，多所稱舉貶黜，奉使稱意。
entries.en: Xuan made him a palace grandee and sent him circuit-riding as moral inspector; his promotions and sackings matched what the court wanted to hear.
entries.literal: Emperor Xuan praised him, appointed Kuangrao grandee of the palace, sent him to tour customs and morals, and he commended or dismissed many officials; the mission pleased the throne.

entries.zh: 擢為司隸校尉，刺舉無所迴避，小大輒舉，所劾奏眾多，廷尉處其法，半用半不用，公卿貴戚及郡國吏繇使至長安，皆恐懼莫敢犯禁，京師為清。
entries.en: As metropolitan governor he denounced wrongdoing without swerving, great and small alike; the commandant of justice applied the law to only half his memorials, yet ministers, imperial in-laws, and clerks on duty in Chang'an all feared him and dared not break the law—the capital grew clean.
entries.literal: He was promoted to metropolitan governor; in denouncing wrongdoing he never swerved, impeaching great and small alike; his memorials were so numerous that the commandant of justice applied the law to only half of them, yet high ministers, imperial in-laws, and clerks from commanderies and kingdoms on duty in Chang'an all feared him and dared not break the law—the capital grew clean.

entries.zh: 諸葛豐字少季，琅邪人也。
entries.en: Zhuge Feng, styled Shaoji, came from Langye.
entries.literal: Zhuge Feng, courtesy name Shaoji, was a man of Langye.

entries.zh: 以明經為郡文學，名特立剛直。
entries.en: He passed the classics track as literary officer and was known as a lone straight arrow.
entries.literal: On classics examination he became commandery erudite-clerk and was famed for standing alone in integrity and uprightness.

entries.zh: 貢禹為御史大夫，除豐為屬，舉侍御史。
entries.en: Gong Yu took him on staff and nominated him as palace clerk.
entries.literal: When Gong Yu was imperial counsellor, he appointed Feng as an assistant and recommended him as attendant clerk.

entries.zh: 元帝擢為司隸校尉，刺舉無所避，京師為之語曰：「間何闊，逢諸葛。」
entries.en: Emperor Yuan promoted him to Metropolitan Commandant. When exposing and impeaching wrongdoing, he avoided no one, and people in the capital made a saying of it: "Why such distance? You have met Zhuge!"
entries.literal: Emperor Yuan promoted him to metropolitan governor; in impeaching wrongdoing he never swerved, and the capital made a rhyme: "Why so wide a gap—meet Zhuge!"

entries.zh: 上嘉其節，加豐秩光祿大夫。
entries.en: The emperor praised his integrity and raised Feng's rank to Grandee of Splendid Light.
entries.literal: The emperor praised his integrity and increased Feng's rank to that of Grandee of Splendid Light.

entries.zh: 哀帝即位，徵寶為諫大夫，遷司隸。
entries.en: Ai recalled him to censor, then metropolitan governor.
entries.literal: When Emperor Ai ascended, Bao was summoned as grandee remonstrant and promoted to metropolitan governor.

entries.zh: 初，傅太后與中山孝王母馮太后俱事元帝，有隙，傅太后使有司考馮太后，令自殺，眾庶冤之。
entries.en: Fu's faction had forced Lady Feng of Zhongshan to suicide; opinion called it a frame.
entries.literal: Earlier Empress Dowager Fu and Empress Dowager Feng of Zhongshan filial king had both served Emperor Yuan and bore a rift; Empress Dowager Fu had responsible agencies investigate Empress Dowager Feng, ordering her to kill herself—the multitude thought it unjust.

entries.zh: 寶奏請覆治，傅太后大怒，曰：「帝置司隸，主使察我。
entries.en: Bao memorialized requesting reinvestigation; Empress Dowager Fu raged and said, "The emperor set up the metropolitan governor to spy on me!
entries.literal: Bao memorialized requesting reinvestigation; Empress Dowager Fu raged and said, "The emperor set up the metropolitan governor to spy on me!

entries.zh: 馮氏反事明白，故欲□觖以揚我惡。
entries.en: She said the Feng case was closed and Sun Bao only meant to smear her.
entries.literal: The Feng affair was already clear; therefore he wishes to pick at faults and broadcast my evil.

entries.zh: 我當坐之。」
entries.en: I will try him myself," she said."
entries.literal: I shall sit in judgment on him."

entries.zh: 上乃順指下寶獄。
entries.en: Ai folded and jailed Sun Bao.
entries.literal: The emperor thereupon followed her hint and sent Bao down to prison.

entries.zh: 尚書僕射唐林爭之，上以林朋黨比周，左遷敦煌魚澤障候。
entries.en: Tang Lin defended Sun Bao and was demoted to a desert outpost.
entries.literal: Vice director of the masters of writing Tang Lin disputed it; the emperor took Lin for factional clique-making and demoted him to warden of the Yuzhi barrier at Dunhuang.

entries.zh: 大司馬傅喜、光祿大夫龔勝固爭，上為言太后，出寶復官。
entries.en: Fu Xi and Gong Sheng forced a compromise through the empress dowager.
entries.literal: Grand marshal Fu Xi and grandee of the palace Gong Sheng argued firmly; the emperor spoke for Bao to the empress dowager and released Bao to resume office.

entries.zh: 劉輔，河間宗室也。
entries.en: Liu Fu belonged to the Hejian royal lineage.
entries.literal: Liu Fu was of the Hejian imperial house.

entries.zh: 舉孝廉，為襄賁令。
entries.en: A filial-incorrupt nomination made him magistrate of Xiangben.
entries.literal: Recommended as filial and incorrupt, he became magistrate of Xiangben.

entries.zh: 上書言得失，召見，上美其材，擢為諫大夫。
entries.en: A policy memorial won him an audience and a jump to grandee remonstrant.
entries.literal: He submitted a memorial on gains and losses, was summoned for audience, and the emperor praised his talent and promoted him to grandee remonstrant.

entries.zh: 會成帝欲立趙婕妤為皇后，先下詔封婕妤父臨為列侯。
entries.en: It happened that Emperor Cheng wished to establish Honorable Lady Zhao as empress and first issued an edict enfeoffing her father Lin as a full marquis.
entries.literal: It happened that Emperor Cheng wished to establish the Honorable Lady Zhao as empress and first issued an edict enfeoffing her father Lin as a full marquis.

entries.zh: 輔上書言：「臣聞天之所與，必先賜以符瑞；
entries.en: Fu submitted a memorial saying, "I have heard that what Heaven favors it first endows with talismanic omens;
entries.literal: Fu submitted a memorial saying, "I have heard that what Heaven favors it first endows with talismanic omens;

entries.zh: 天之所違，必先降以災變：此神明之徵應，自然之占驗也。
entries.en: —Heaven's anger shows first in disasters; that is how the spirits speak.
entries.literal: what Heaven rejects it first strikes with disaster and anomaly: this is the spirits' response and nature's proof.

entries.zh: 昔武王、周公承順天地，以饗魚烏之瑞，然猶君臣祗懼，動色相戒，況於季世，不蒙繼嗣之福，屢受威怒之異者虖！
entries.en: Even Wu and Zhou trembled at small omens, he argued—how much more should a childless age fear heaven's warnings.
entries.literal: Formerly King Wu and the Duke of Zhou obeyed heaven and earth and received the fish-and-crow omens, yet lord and minister still trembled in fear and warned one another with changed countenance—how much more in a declining age that does not receive heir-fortune and repeatedly suffers awesome wrath in portents!

entries.zh: 雖夙夜自責，改過易行，畏天命，念祖業，妙選有德之世，考卜窈窕之女，以承宗廟，順神祗心，塞天下望，子孫之詳猶恐晚暮，今乃觸情縱欲，傾於卑賤之女，欲以母天下，不畏於天，不愧於人，惑莫大焉。
entries.en: He begged the emperor not to make a dancing-girl empress when the altars still lacked an heir.
entries.literal: Though one reproaches oneself morning and night, reforms faults and changes conduct, fears heaven's command, remembers ancestral enterprise, finely selects a house of virtue, divines for a modest maiden to continue the ancestral temple, and obeys the spirits' hearts to stop the empire's hopes—even then good news of heirs may come too late; now you give way to passion and desire, incline toward a woman of base birth, and wish her to mother the world—without fearing heaven or shame before men—no delusion is greater.

entries.zh: 里語曰：『腐木不可以為柱，卑人不可以為主。』
entries.en: Village wisdom says rotten timber cannot be a ridgepole and a lowborn woman cannot mother the realm.
entries.literal: The village proverb says, 'Rotten wood cannot be a pillar; a base person cannot be ruler.

entries.zh: 天人之所不予，必有禍而無福，市道皆共知之，朝廷莫肯一言，臣竊傷心。
entries.en: He said every market knew the match was ill-omened while the court stayed silent.
entries.literal: What heaven and men withhold brings calamity without blessing; the marketplace knows it in common, yet the court will not speak one word—I privately grieve.

entries.zh: 自念得以同姓拔擢，尸祿不忠，污辱諫爭之官，不敢不盡死，唯陛下深察。」
entries.en: He said his clan tie obliged him to speak even at the cost of his life."
entries.literal: Reflecting that I was raised because I share the surname, I have eaten salary without loyalty and shamed the remonstrant's office—I dare not fail to exhaust death; I beg Your Majesty to examine deeply."

entries.zh: 書奏，上使侍御史收縛輔，系掖庭秘獄，群臣莫知其故。
entries.en: Chengdi jailed him in the harem's secret jail without telling the ministers why.
entries.literal: When the memorial was submitted, the emperor had an attendant clerk seize and bind Fu and confined him in the secret prison of the Rear Palace; none of the ministers knew the reason.

entries.zh: 卷七十七 蓋諸葛劉鄭孫毋將何傳第四十七
entries.en: Volume 77: Biographies of Gai, Zhuge, Liu, Zheng, Sun, Wujiang, and He—the forty-seventh series.
entries.literal: Volume 77: "Biographies of Gai, Zhuge, Liu, Zheng, Sun, Wujiang, and He," number 47.

entries.zh: 蕭望之字長倩，東海蘭陵人也，徙杜陵。
entries.en: Xiao Wangzhi, whose courtesy name was Changqian, came from Lanling in Donghai and later relocated to Duling.
entries.literal: Xiao Wangzhi, courtesy name Changqian, was a man of Lanling in Donghai; his family moved to Duling.

entries.zh: 家世以田為業，至望之，好學，治《齊詩》，事同縣後倉且十年。
entries.en: His people had long lived by the plough; Wangzhi himself loved letters, mastered the Qi recension of the Classic of Odes, and studied under Hou Cang of his county for the better part of a decade.
entries.literal: For generations his family had taken farming as their occupation; when it came to Wangzhi, he loved learning, studied the Qi version of the Odes, and served Hou Cang of the same county for nearly ten years.

entries.zh: 以令詣太常受業，復事同學博士白奇，又從夏侯勝問《論語》、《禮服》。
entries.en: On imperial summons he entered the Grand Master of Ceremonies' school, continued under the erudite Bai Qi, a classmate, and took the Analects and Mourning Dress from Xiahou Sheng.
entries.literal: By order he went to the Grand Master of Ceremonies to receive instruction, then studied again under his fellow student the erudite Bai Qi, and also questioned Xiahou Sheng on the Analects and on Mourning Dress.

entries.zh: 京師諸儒稱述焉。
entries.en: The capital's Confucians spoke of him with respect.
entries.literal: The scholars of the capital praised and recounted him.

entries.zh: 時大將軍光薨，子禹復為大司馬，兄子山領尚書，親屬皆宿衛內侍。
entries.en: At that time Grand General Huo Guang died; his son Yu again became grand marshal, his elder brother's son Shan headed the Masters of Writing, and Huo kinsmen filled palace guard and inner service.
entries.literal: At that time the great general Guang died; his son Yu again became grand marshal, his elder brother's son Shan headed the Masters of Writing, and kinsmen all stood night guard as inner attendants.

entries.zh: 地節三年夏，京師雨雹，望之因是上疏，願賜清閒之宴，口陳災異之意。
entries.en: In summer of Dijie 3 hail fell on the capital; Wangzhi memorialized, asking for a quiet audience to explain the omen in person.
entries.literal: In summer of the third year of Dijie, hail fell in the capital; Wangzhi therefore submitted a memorial, asking to be granted a leisurely banquet at which he might orally set forth the meaning of the prodigy.

entries.zh: 宣帝自在民間聞望之名，曰：「此東海蕭生邪？
entries.en: Emperor Xuan had known Wangzhi's reputation since his commoner days and said, "Is this the scholar Xiao from Donghai?
entries.literal: Emperor Xuan, since his days among the people, had heard Wangzhi's name and said: "Is this the Master Xiao of Donghai?

entries.zh: 下少府宋畸問狀，無有所諱。」
entries.en: Send Privy Treasurer Song Qi to question him and let nothing be concealed."
entries.literal: Send down to the privy treasurer Song Qi to question the facts; let there be nothing concealed."

entries.zh: 望之對，以為「春秋昭公三年大雨雹，是時季氏專權，卒逐昭公。
entries.en: Wangzhi answered that "in the third year of Duke Zhao of Lu, recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals, great hail fell while the Ji clan monopolized power and finally drove the duke into exile.
entries.literal: Wangzhi answered, holding that "in the third year of Duke Zhao in the Spring and Autumn Annals there was great hail; at that time the Ji clan monopolized power and finally drove out Duke Zhao.

entries.zh: 鄉使魯君察於天變，宜亡此害。
entries.en: Had the lord of Lu heeded heaven's warning, that disaster could have been avoided.
entries.literal: If only the lord of Lu had observed the heaven-sent change, this calamity should have been avoided.

entries.zh: 今陛下以聖德居位，思政求賢，堯舜之用心也。
entries.en: Your Majesty now rules with sage virtue, seeks good government and worthy men—the mind of Yao and Shun.
entries.literal: Now Your Majesty, with sagely virtue occupying the throne, thinks of government and seeks the worthy—the mind of Yao and Shun.

entries.zh: 然而善祥未臻，陰陽不和，是大臣任政，一姓擅勢之所致也。
entries.en: Yet good omens have not come and yin and yang remain out of harmony—because great ministers govern and one clan monopolizes power.
entries.literal: Yet good omens have not arrived and yin and yang are not in harmony—this is caused by great ministers holding government and one clan monopolizing power.

entries.zh: 附枝大者賊本心，私家盛者公室危。
entries.en: When collateral branches grow too large they wound the trunk; when private houses flourish the royal house is endangered.
entries.literal: When attached branches grow large they injure the root heart; when private houses flourish the public house is endangered.

entries.zh: 唯明主躬萬機，選同姓，舉賢材，以為腹心，與參政謀，令公卿大臣朝見奏事，明陳其職，以考功能。
entries.en: Only if the enlightened sovereign personally handles affairs, selects kinsmen and worthy talent as his inner counselors, and requires the great ministers to report at audience with clear statements of duty so that performance may be tested.
entries.literal: Only if the enlightened sovereign personally handles the myriad affairs, selects men of the same surname, raises worthy talent to be his heart and belly, deliberates with them in government, and orders dukes, ministers, and great officers to present business at audience, clearly stating their duties so that function may be examined.

entries.zh: 如是，則庶事理，公道立，姦邪塞，私權廢矣。」
entries.en: Then public business will be ordered, justice will stand, treachery will be blocked, and private power abolished."
entries.literal: If so, then the multitude of affairs will be ordered, public justice established, treachery blocked, and private power abolished."

entries.zh: 對奏，天子拜望之為謁者。
entries.en: When his answer was submitted, the emperor appointed Wangzhi usher.
entries.literal: When the answer was memorialized, the Son of Heaven appointed Wangzhi as usher.

entries.zh: 時上初即位，思進賢良，多上書言便宜，輒下望之問狀，高者請丞相御史，次者中二千石試事，滿歲以狀聞，下者報聞，或罷歸田里，所白處奏皆可。
entries.en: The newly enthroned emperor wished to advance worthy men; many memorials on practical reforms were sent to Wangzhi for review—the best he referred to the chancellor and counselor, the next he tried in middle two-thousand-shi posts and reported after a year, the least he acknowledged or sent home; his recommendations were invariably approved.
entries.literal: At that time the sovereign had just ascended the throne and wished to advance worthy men; many submitted memorials on expedient measures, and he would send them down to Wangzhi to question the facts—the highest he referred to chancellor and imperial counselor, the next he tried in posts of middle two-thousand shi, and after a full year reported on their performance; the lowest he acknowledged receipt, or dismissed to return to fields and villages; wherever Wangzhi reported, the memorials were all approved.

entries.zh: 累遷諫大夫，丞相司直，歲中三遷，官至二千石。
entries.en: He rose through remonstrance grandee and assistant for affairs to the chancellor, three promotions in one year, reaching two-thousand-shi rank.
entries.literal: He was repeatedly promoted to remonstrating grandee and assistant for affairs to the chancellor; within one year he was thrice promoted, reaching office of two-thousand shi.

entries.zh: 其後霍氏竟謀反誅，望之寖益任用。
entries.en: After the Huo clan finally rebelled and was destroyed, Wangzhi was increasingly entrusted with power.
entries.literal: Afterward the Huo clan finally plotted rebellion and was executed; Wangzhi was gradually more employed.

entries.zh: 及宣帝寢疾，選大臣可屬者，引外屬侍中樂陵侯史高、太子太傅望之、少傅周堪至禁中，拜高為大司馬車騎將軍，望之為前將軍光祿勳，堪為光祿大夫，皆受遺詔輔政，領尚書事。
entries.en: When Emperor Xuan fell gravely ill, he chose ministers to whom he could entrust the realm. He summoned his maternal kinsman Shi Gao, Palace Attendant and Marquis of Leling, together with Crown Prince Tutor Wangzhi and Junior Tutor Zhou Kan. Shi Gao was made Grand Marshal and Chariot-and-Cavalry General, Wangzhi Forward General and Minister of the Household, and Zhou Kan Grandee of Splendid Light. All three received the deathbed edict to assist the government and direct the Secretariat.
entries.literal: When Emperor Xuan fell gravely ill, he selected great ministers to whom he could entrust affairs and summoned to the inner palace his maternal kinsman Shi Gao, Palace Attendant and Marquis of Leling; Wangzhi, Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent; and Zhou Kan, Junior Tutor. He appointed Shi Gao Grand Marshal and Chariot-and-Cavalry General, Wangzhi Forward General and Minister of the Household, and Zhou Kan Grandee of Splendid Light. All received the deathbed edict to assist the government and take charge of Secretariat affairs.

entries.zh: 宣帝崩，太子襲尊號，是為孝元帝。
entries.en: When Emperor Xuan died, the crown prince succeeded as Emperor Yuan.
entries.literal: Emperor Xuan died; the heir apparent assumed the exalted title—this was Emperor Yuan of Filial Piety.

entries.zh: 望之、堪本以師傅見尊重，上即位，數宴見，言治亂，陳王事。
entries.en: Wangzhi and Zhou Kan had long been honored as tutors; once Yuan took the throne he often received them at banquets to discuss order and disorder and royal policy.
entries.literal: Wangzhi and Kan had long been respected as tutors; when the sovereign ascended the throne he often received them at banquets, spoke of order and disorder, and laid out royal affairs.

entries.zh: 望之選白宗室明經達學散騎諫大夫劉更生給事中，與侍中金敞並拾遺左右。
entries.en: Wangzhi recommended Liu Gengsheng of the imperial clan, a classicist of proven learning, as cavalier attendant and remonstrance grandee in the palace secretariat, together with Palace Attendant Jin Chang to remedy oversights at the emperor's side.
entries.literal: Wangzhi selected and reported Liu Gengsheng of the imperial clan, versed in the classics and accomplished in learning, as cavalier attendant and remonstrating grandee in the palace secretariat, together with Palace Attendant Jin Chang picking up what was neglected at the ruler's side.

entries.zh: 四人同心謀議，勸道上以古制，多所欲匡正，上甚鄉納之。
entries.en: The four counseled as one, urging the emperor toward ancient institutions and many reforms; Yuan greatly inclined to accept them.
entries.literal: The four men deliberated with one heart, urging the Way upon the sovereign through ancient institutions; many things they wished to correct, and the sovereign greatly inclined to accept them.

entries.zh: 先是，烏孫昆彌翁歸靡因長羅侯常惠上書，願以漢外孫元貴靡為嗣，得復尚少主，結婚內附，畔去匈奴。
entries.en: Earlier Wengguimi, Kunmi of Wusun, had petitioned through Chang Hui, Marquis of Changluo, asking that his son Yuanguimi, a grandson of the Han imperial house through his mother, succeed him and marry the Lesser Princess. This would renew the marriage alliance, attach Wusun to Han, and sever its ties with the Xiongnu.
entries.literal: Earlier, Wengguimi, Kunmi of Wusun, had submitted a memorial through Chang Hui, Marquis of Changluo, asking that Yuanguimi, a maternal grandson of Han, succeed him and in turn marry the Lesser Princess, renewing the marriage alliance, attaching Wusun to Han, and breaking with the Xiongnu.

entries.zh: 詔下公卿議，望之以為：烏孫絕域，信其美言，萬里結婚，非長策也。
entries.en: The edict went to council. Wangzhi said Wusun lay at impossible distance; a marriage alliance on mere fine words was no lasting policy.
entries.literal: An edict was sent down to the dukes and ministers for deliberation; Wangzhi held that Wusun was a land beyond reach; to trust their fine words and bind marriage ten thousand li away was no long-term strategy.

entries.zh: 天子不聽。
entries.en: The emperor would not hear him.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven did not listen.

entries.zh: 神爵二年，遣長羅侯惠使送公主配元貴靡。
entries.en: In Shenjue 2 he sent Chang Hui to escort the princess to Yuanguimi.
entries.literal: In the second year of Shenjue he dispatched the marquis of Changluo, Hui, as envoy to escort the princess to marry Yuanguimi.

entries.zh: 未出塞，翁歸靡死，其兄子狂王背約自立。
entries.en: Before the party crossed the frontier Wengguimi died; a nephew, the "Mad King," broke the pact and seized the throne.
entries.literal: Before they had left the passes, Wengguimi died; his elder brother's son the Mad King broke the agreement and set himself up.

entries.zh: 惠從塞下上書，願留少主敦煌郡。
entries.en: Chang Hui wrote from the border asking to hold the princess at Dunhuang.
entries.literal: Hui, from below the passes, submitted a memorial, begging to leave the young princess at Dunhuang commandery.

entries.zh: 惠至烏孫，責以負約，因立元貴靡，還迎少主。
entries.en: At Wusun he rebuked them for bad faith, enthroned Yuanguimi, and came back for the princess.
entries.literal: When Hui reached Wusun, he reproached them for breaking the agreement, thereupon set up Yuanguimi, and returned to welcome the young princess.

entries.zh: 詔下公卿議，望之復以為：「不可。
entries.en: Council was ordered again. Wangzhi memorialized again, saying, "It cannot be done.
entries.literal: An edict was sent down to the dukes and ministers for deliberation; Wangzhi again held that "it cannot be done.

entries.zh: 烏孫持兩端，亡堅約，其效可見。
entries.en: Wusun plays both sides and keeps no firm pledge—the record shows it.
entries.literal: Wusun holds two ends; it has no firm covenant; its effect can be seen.

entries.zh: 前少主在烏孫四十餘年，恩愛不親密，邊境未以安，此已事之驗也。
entries.en: The previous princess lived in Wusun for more than forty years, yet the alliance never became close and the frontier never became secure. The past already proves the point.
entries.literal: The previous princess lived in Wusun for more than forty years, yet affection between the two sides was not close and the frontier was not thereby secured. The past already proves the point.

entries.zh: 今少主以元貴靡不得立而還，信無負於四夷，此中國之大福也。
entries.en: To bring her home because Yuanguimi failed keeps good faith with the outer tribes without loss—a great boon to China.
entries.literal: Now the young princess returns because Yuanguimi could not be enthroned; in good faith there is no failing the four barbarians—this is a great blessing for the Middle Kingdom.

entries.zh: 少主不止，繇役將興，其原起此。」
entries.en: If she stays, levies and wars will follow—the trouble starts here."
entries.literal: If the young princess does not stop, corvée and campaigns will arise; the source will begin from this."

entries.zh: 天子從其議，征少主還。
entries.en: The emperor agreed and recalled the princess.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven followed his proposal and summoned the young princess back.

entries.zh: 後烏孫雖分國兩立，以元貴靡為大昆彌，漢遂不復與結婚。
entries.en: Wusun later split into two realms, with Yuanguimi as the senior Kunmi, and Han never again renewed the marriage alliance.
entries.literal: Later, although Wusun split into two realms and Yuanguimi was established as the senior Kunmi, Han never again formed a marriage alliance with Wusun.

entries.zh: 初，匈奴呼韓邪單于來朝，詔公卿議其儀，丞相霸、御史大夫定國議曰：「聖王之制，施德行禮，先京師而後諸夏，先諸夏而後夷狄。
entries.en: Earlier, when Huhanye Chanyu of the Xiongnu came to court, an edict ordered the dukes and ministers to discuss the proper ritual. Chancellor Huang Ba and Imperial Counselor Yu Dingguo proposed, "In the institutions of the sage kings, virtue is extended and ritual performed first in the capital, then among the central states; first among the central states, then among the Yi and Di peoples.
entries.literal: Earlier, when Chanyu Huhanye of the Xiongnu came to court, an edict ordered the dukes and ministers to debate his protocol; Chancellor Ba and Imperial Counselor Dingguo proposed, saying, "Under the sage kings' institutions one spreads virtue and performs ritual: first the capital, then the central domains; first the central domains, then the Yi and Di.

entries.zh: 《詩》云：『率禮不越，遂視既發；
entries.en: The Odes read, "He kept every rite within its bounds, then turned his gaze abroad;
entries.literal: The Odes says, "Observing ritual without overstepping, then looking—already issued;

entries.zh: 相土烈烈，海外有截。』
entries.en: Xiang Tu blazed with power, and even beyond the seas rivals were subdued."
entries.literal: Xiang Tu blazed with power; beyond the seas lands were cut down."

entries.zh: 陛下聖德充塞天地，光被四表，匈奴單于鄉風慕化，奉珍朝賀，自古未之有也。
entries.en: Your virtue fills heaven and earth; the chanyu has bent to the breeze of civilization with gifts and homage—unprecedented in the records.
entries.literal: Your Majesty's sagely virtue fills heaven and earth and shines to the four quarters; the Xiongnu chanyu has turned on the wind and yearned for civilization, offering tribute and congratulations at court—such a thing has never occurred since antiquity.

entries.zh: 其禮儀宜如諸侯王，位次在下。」
entries.en: He should therefore be received like a feudal king, but seated below the Han princes."
entries.literal: His ceremony should match that of the kings of the feudal domains, his place in the order below theirs."

entries.zh: 望之以為：「單于非正朔所加，故稱敵國，宜待以不臣之禮，位在諸侯王上。
entries.en: Wangzhi held, "The chanyu is not subject to our calendar and new moons; therefore he is called the ruler of a rival state. He should be received with the ritual due to one who is not a subject, and his seat should be above the kings of the domains.
entries.literal: Wangzhi held that "the chanyu is not one on whom the reigning calendar is imposed; therefore he is termed a rival power and should be received with the etiquette due one who is not made a subject—his seat above the kings of the domains.

entries.zh: 外夷稽首稱籓，中國讓而不臣，此則羈縻之誼，謙亨之福也。
entries.en: They may kowtow and call themselves vassals while China graciously withholds the language of mastery—that is the old policy of loose reins and the fortune of modest success.
entries.literal: The outer tribes kowtow and call themselves vassals; China yields and does not treat them as subjects—this is the principle of loose reins, the blessing of yielding prosperity.

entries.zh: 《書》曰『戎狄荒服』，言其來服，荒忽亡常。
entries.en: The Documents speaks of the Rong and Di in "wild service"—they attend fitfully and without fixed duty.
entries.literal: The Documents says, "Rong and Di render wild service," meaning they come to serve, fleeting and inconstant.

entries.zh: 如使匈奴後嗣卒有鳥竄鼠伏，闕如朝享，不為畔臣。
entries.en: Should their descendants someday skulk away and skip court, they still would not be treated as traitor-subjects.
entries.literal: If later Xiongnu heirs should end up scattering like birds or hiding like rats, omitting court audiences, they will not count as rebel vassals.

entries.zh: 信讓行乎蠻貉，福祚流於亡窮，萬世之長策也。」
entries.en: Patience and courtesy toward the northern tribes would spread blessing without end—the true long-term design."
entries.literal: Trust and deference extended to the Man and Mo, blessings flowing without end—this is a strategy for ten thousand generations."

entries.zh: 天子采之，下詔曰：「蓋聞五帝、三王教化所不施，不及以政。
entries.en: The emperor took his advice and proclaimed: "Where the Five Thearchs and Three Kings did not teach, law could not reach.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven adopted it and issued an edict, saying, "We have heard that where the Five Thearchs and Three Kings did not extend transformation, government did not reach.

entries.zh: 今匈奴單于稱北籓，朝正朔，朕之不逮，德不能弘覆。
entries.en: The chanyu now calls himself a northern bulwark and accepts Our calendar, yet Our virtue is too slight to embrace every people.
entries.literal: Now the Xiongnu chanyu styles himself a northern vassal and attends Our calendar; We are unequal to the task—Our virtue cannot shelter all.

entries.zh: 其以客禮待之，令單于位在諸侯王上，贊謁稱臣而不名。」
entries.en: Receive him as an honored guest, seat him above the kings, and in the levee let heralds call him 'subject' without intoning his personal name."
entries.literal: Treat him with guest ritual; order the chanyu's seat above the kings of the domains, and in audience announcements style him 'subject' without speaking his name."

entries.zh: 是時，選博士、諫大夫通政事者補郡國守、相，以望之為平原太守。
entries.en: The court was filling governorships and kingdom chancellorships with erudites and remonstrance officials who knew practical administration; Wangzhi received Pingyuan.
entries.literal: At that time those selected as erudites and grandees of remonstrance who were versed in government affairs were assigned to fill the posts of commandery governors and chancellors; Wangzhi was made governor of Pingyuan.

entries.zh: 望之雅意在本朝，遠為郡守，內不自得，乃上疏曰：「陛下哀愍百姓，恐德化之不究，悉出諫官以補郡吏，所謂憂其末而忘其本者也。
entries.en: Wangzhi had hoped to remain in the capital; distant appointment as governor sat ill with him. He memorialized: "You pity the people and fear your transforming influence may not reach the ends of the realm, so you have posted every remonstrance officer to the provinces—that is to fret over the branches and forget the root.
entries.literal: Wangzhi's true wish was to serve at court; being sent far as a commandery governor, inwardly he was discontented, and therefore he submitted a memorial, saying, "Your Majesty pities the common people, fearing that civilizing virtue may not reach everywhere, and has sent out all the remonstrance officials to supplement the commandery clerks—this is what is called worrying about the twigs and forgetting the root.

entries.zh: 朝無爭臣則不知過，國無達士則不聞善。
entries.en: Without contentious ministers at court you cannot know your errors; without worthy men in the land you will not hear what is right.
entries.literal: If at court there are no ministers who contend with you, you will not know your faults; if the state has no eminent scholars, good counsel will not be heard.

entries.zh: 願陛下選明經術，溫故知新，通於幾微謀慮之士以為內臣，與參政事。
entries.en: I ask you to choose men steeped in the classics, who renew their learning from the past, and who grasp fine points of policy, for inner posts and deliberation of state.
entries.literal: I beg Your Majesty to select men clear in the classics, able to review the old and know the new, and conversant with subtle planning, to serve as inner ministers and take part in governing affairs.

entries.zh: 諸侯聞之，則知國家納諫憂政，亡有闕遺。
entries.en: The kingdoms will then see that the court welcomes criticism and minds its business, with no duty left undone.
entries.literal: When the feudal lords hear of this, they will know that the state welcomes remonstrance and cares for government, and that nothing is neglected.

entries.zh: 若此不怠，成、康之道其庶幾乎！
entries.en: Persevere in this, and the age of Kings Cheng and Kang is not beyond reach.
entries.literal: If you do not slacken in this, the way of Cheng and Kang may perhaps be nearly achieved!

entries.zh: 外郡不治，豈足憂哉？」
entries.en: Ill-run border provinces are a lesser worry by comparison."
entries.literal: If outer commanderies are not well governed, is that worth worrying about?"

entries.zh: 書聞，征入守少府。
entries.en: The emperor read the paper and recalled him to be privy treasurer.
entries.literal: When the memorial was received, he was summoned to serve as junior privy treasurer.

entries.zh: 宣帝察望之經明持重，論議有餘，材任宰相，欲詳試其政事，復以為左馮翊。
entries.en: Emperor Xuan saw in him classical learning, gravity, and debating power fit for the chancellorship and meant to test him in government, so he named him left governor of the metropolitan area.
entries.literal: Emperor Xuan, observing that Wangzhi was clear in the classics, steady in demeanor, ample in debate, and by talent fit to be chancellor, wished to try him thoroughly in administrative affairs, and therefore appointed him left governor of Fengyi.

entries.zh: 望之從少府出為左遷，恐有不合意，即移病。
entries.en: Wangzhi regarded his transfer from acting Privy Treasurer to Left Fengyi as a demotion and, fearing he had displeased the emperor, immediately reported himself ill.
entries.literal: Wangzhi regarded leaving the acting Privy Treasurer's office for the Left Fengyi as a demotion; fearing that he had somehow displeased the emperor, he immediately pleaded illness.

entries.zh: 上聞之，使侍中、成都侯金安上諭意曰：「所用皆更治民以考功。
entries.en: The sovereign sent Attendant Jin An'shang of Chengdu to say, "I shift my men into local office to weigh their performance.
entries.literal: When the emperor heard of it, he sent the attendant-in-chamber and marquis of Chengdu Jin An'shang to convey his intent, saying, "Those whom I employ are all rotated through governing the people in order to examine merit.

entries.zh: 君前為平原太守日淺，故復試之於三輔，非有所聞也。」
entries.en: Your tenure in Pingyuan was brief; I am only giving you another tour in the capital region, not implying blame."
entries.literal: Sir, your time as governor of Pingyuan was short; therefore I am trying you again in the three adjuncts—I have heard nothing against you."

entries.zh: 望之即視事。
entries.en: Wangzhi then took his seat.
entries.literal: Wangzhi thereupon took up his duties.

entries.zh: 初，宣帝不甚從儒術，任用法律，而中書宦官用事。
entries.en: Under Emperor Xuan the court favored legal administration over Confucian learning, and eunuchs in the palace secretariat wielded real power.
entries.literal: Earlier, Emperor Xuan did not much heed Confucian learning but relied on statute, while eunuchs of the palace secretariat wielded power.

entries.zh: 中書令弘恭、石顯久典樞機，明習文法，亦與車騎將軍高為表裡，論議常獨持故事，不從望之等。
entries.en: Hong Gong and Shi Xian had long run the machinery of state, knew every clause of the code, and moved in lockstep with General Shi Gao, stonewalling Wangzhi with citations of old precedent.
entries.literal: Palace secretariat directors Hong Gong and Shi Xian long controlled the levers of government, were expert in written law, and also worked hand in glove with chariot-and-cavalry general Shi Gao; in debate they routinely insisted on precedent alone and would not follow Wangzhi and his allies.

entries.zh: 恭、顯又時傾仄見詘。
entries.en: The pair were themselves sometimes cornered and refuted in debate.
entries.literal: Gong and Xian were also at times overborne and rebuffed.

entries.zh: 望之以為中書政本，宜以賢明之選，自武帝游宴後庭，故用宦者，非國舊制，又違古不近刑人之義，白欲更置士人，由是大與高、恭、顯忤。
entries.en: Wangzhi argued that the secretariat was the heart of government and should be staffed by worthy, capable men. Eunuchs had been employed there since Emperor Wu began visiting and holding banquets in the rear palace, but this was neither an original Han institution nor consistent with the ancient principle of keeping punished men at a distance. He proposed replacing them with regular officials, bringing him into sharp conflict with Shi Gao, Hong Gong, and Shi Xian.
entries.literal: Wangzhi held that the secretariat was the root of administration and ought to be staffed with worthy, enlightened men; since Emperor Wu had roamed and feasted in the inner palace, eunuchs had been used—it was not the dynasty's original system and violated the ancient principle of not keeping mutilated men close; he proposed replacing them with literati, and for this reason deeply opposed Gao, Gong, and Xian.

entries.zh: 上初即位，謙讓重改作，議久不定，出劉更生為宗正。
entries.en: Newly enthroned, the emperor was reluctant to make sweeping changes. While the debate remained unresolved, Liu Gengsheng was transferred out to serve as Director of the Imperial Clan.
entries.literal: When the emperor had first ascended the throne, he was modest and hesitant over sweeping reform; deliberation dragged on unsettled, and Liu Gengsheng was sent out as director of the imperial clan.

entries.zh: 望之、堪數薦名儒茂才以備諫官。
entries.en: Wangzhi and Zhou Kan kept nominating distinguished scholars for remonstrance duties.
entries.literal: Wangzhi and Zhou Kan repeatedly recommended noted scholars and flourishing talents to fill remonstrance posts.

entries.zh: 會稽鄭朋陰欲附望之，上疏言車騎將軍高遣客為奸利郡國，及言許、史子弟罪過。
entries.en: Zheng Peng of Kuaiji curried favor by memorializing against General Shi Gao's clients for corruption in the provinces and against the Xu and Shi clans.
entries.literal: Zheng Peng of Kuaiji covertly wished to attach himself to Wangzhi; he submitted a memorial charging that chariot-and-cavalry general Shi Gao had sent agents to pursue illicit profit in the commanderies and kingdoms, and also detailing faults of the Xu and Shi younger kin.

entries.zh: 章視周堪，堪白令朋待詔金馬門。
entries.en: The memorial was shown to Zhou Kan, who reported it to the emperor and had Peng appointed to await imperial summons at the Golden Horse Gate.
entries.literal: He showed the draft to Zhou Kan; Kan reported it and had Peng await edicts at the Golden Horse Gate.

entries.zh: 朋奏記望之曰：「將軍體周、召之德，秉公綽之質，有卞莊之威。
entries.en: Zheng Peng submitted a note to Wangzhi, saying, "General, you embody the virtue of the Dukes of Zhou and Shao, possess the character of Meng Gongchuo, and command the awe of Bian Zhuang.
entries.literal: Peng addressed Wangzhi in a note, saying, "You, general, embody the virtue of the dukes of Zhou and Shao, bear the substance of Meng Gongchuo, and command the awe of Bian Zhuang.

entries.zh: 至乎耳順之年，履折衝之位，號至將軍，誠士之高致也。
entries.en: At sixty he held the rank that repels enemies—a pinnacle few scholars reach.
entries.literal: Having reached the 'obedient ear' years, treading the post that turns back assaults, titled up to general—truly the high mark of a gentleman.

entries.zh: 窟穴黎庶莫不歡喜，咸曰將軍其人也。
entries.en: Commoners in every lane hailed him as the man of the hour.
entries.literal: The common folk in their dens and caves all rejoice, saying the general is such a man.

entries.zh: 今將軍規模，云若管、晏而休，遂行日仄至周、召乃留乎？
entries.en: Will you, General, set your ambition like Guan Zhong and Yan Ying and then rest, or press on past sunset until the Zhou dukes themselves detain you?
entries.literal: Now does the general's scope mean that, like Guan Zhong and Yan Ying, you will then stop, or press on through the slanting sun until the dukes of Zhou and Shao detain you?

entries.zh: 若管、晏而休，則下走將歸延陵之皋，修農圃之疇，畜雞種黍，俟見二子，沒齒而已矣。
entries.en: If you rest like Guan and Yan, your humble servant will withdraw to Yanling, tend his farm plots, raise chickens and plant millet, await a meeting with the two masters, and end his days there.
entries.literal: If you rest like Guan and Yan, then your humble servant will retire to the heights of Yanling, tend the plots of his farm, raise chickens and plant millet, await a meeting with the two masters, and with that end his days.

entries.zh: 如將軍昭然度行，積思塞邪枉之險蹊，宣中庸之常政，興周、召之遺業，親日仄之兼聽，則下走其庶幾願竭區區，底厲鋒鍔，奉萬分之一。」
entries.en: If instead the general opened straight paths, sealed off crooked schemes, enacted the steady policy of the Mean, revived the Zhou dukes' work, and listened wide and late, Peng would sharpen every talent and give the thousandth part of what he could."
entries.literal: If the general clearly gauges conduct, amasses thought to block the treacherous byways of wrong, spreads the constant government of the Mean, revives the legacy of Zhou and Shao, and personally heeds comprehensive counsel at the day's end, then perhaps your humble servant might exhaust his petty strength, hone his edge, and offer one ten-thousandth."

entries.zh: 望之見納朋，接待以意。
entries.en: Wangzhi welcomed Peng and treated him with favor.
entries.literal: Wangzhi accepted Peng and received him with favor.

entries.zh: 朋數稱述望之，短車騎將軍。
entries.en: Peng kept praising Wangzhi and attacking General Shi Gao.
entries.literal: Peng repeatedly praised Wangzhi and disparaged the chariot-and-cavalry general.

entries.zh: 言許、史過失。
entries.en: He aired the faults of the Xu and Shi clans.
entries.literal: He spoke of Xu and Shi misconduct.

entries.zh: 後朋行傾邪，望之絕不與通。
entries.en: When Peng turned treacherous, Wangzhi cut him off entirely.
entries.literal: Later Peng turned crooked in conduct, and Wangzhi would have nothing to do with him.

entries.zh: 朋與大司農史李宮俱待詔，堪獨白宮為黃門郎。
entries.en: Peng and Li Gong, a clerk in the Ministry of Agriculture, were both awaiting summons; Zhou Kan alone recommended Gong for the Yellow Gate.
entries.literal: Peng and Li Gong, clerk in the grand minister of agriculture, were both awaiting summons; Kan alone reported that Gong should be made a gentleman of the yellow gates.

entries.zh: 朋，楚士，怨恨，更求入許、史，推所言許、史事曰：「皆周堪、劉更生教我，我關東人，何以知此？」
entries.en: Peng, a man of Chu, nursed a grudge, sought favor with the Xu and Shi clans, and shifted blame for his charges, saying, "Zhou Kan and Liu Gengsheng taught me all of this. I am a Guandong man—how would I know such things?"
entries.literal: Peng, a man of Chu, bore resentment, sought entry among Xu and Shi, and pushed claims about Xu and Shi affairs, saying: "All of it Zhou Kan and Liu Gengsheng taught me; I am a man of Guandong—how would I know this?"

entries.zh: 於是侍中許章白見朋。
entries.en: Palace Attendant Xu Zhang then had Peng admitted to audience.
entries.literal: Thereupon Palace Attendant Xu Zhang had Peng brought to audience.

entries.zh: 朋出揚言曰：「我見，言前將軍小過五，大罪一。
entries.en: Peng came out and declared, "I told the emperor of five minor faults and one grave crime of the former general.
