entries.en: If you lack wit to pivot, nerve to cut a loss, generosity to share the upside, and grit to hold a line, do not ask for my methods—I will not teach you."
entries.literal: Therefore if wisdom is insufficient for responding to shifts, courage insufficient for deciding and cutting, benevolence insufficient for taking and giving, strength insufficient for holding and guarding—though they wish to study my art, in the end I will not tell them."

entries.zh: 蓋天下言治生者祖白圭。
entries.en: Small wonder later ages treated Bai Gui as the patron saint of every fortune-hunter.
entries.literal: In general, all who under heaven spoke of managing livelihood took Bai Gui as their ancestor.

entries.zh: 師史既衰，至成、哀、王莽時，雒陽張長叔、薛子促訾亦十千萬。
entries.en: When Shi's house waned, Luoyang partners Zhang Changshu and Xue Zicu—through Cheng, Ai, and into Wang Mang's day—matched his nine-figure hoard.
entries.literal: After Master Shi had declined, reaching the times of Cheng, Ai, and Wang Mang, Zhang Changshu and Xue Zicu of Luoyang likewise had capital of ten thousand ten-thousands.

entries.zh: 莽皆以為納言士，欲法武帝，然不能得其利。
entries.en: Wang Mang named them court remonstrance officers and tried to copy Emperor Wu's patronage of merchants, but the treasury never saw a copper of their skill.
entries.literal: Mang appointed them all as remonstrance gentlemen, wishing to imitate Emperor Wu, yet could not obtain their profit.

entries.zh: 關中富商大賈，大氐盡諸田，田牆、田蘭。
entries.en: Guanzhong's merchant princes were almost all members of the Tian clan—Tian Qiang and Tian Lan chief among them.
entries.literal: The great merchants of Guanzhong were for the most part all the Tian—Tian Qiang, Tian Lan.

entries.zh: 韋家栗氏、安陵杜氏亦巨萬。
entries.en: The Lis of Weijia and the Dus of Anling stacked up comparable eight-figure fortunes.
entries.literal: The Li clan of Weijia and the Du clan of Anling likewise reached tens of millions.

entries.zh: 前富者既衰，自元、成訖王莽，京師富人杜陵樊嘉，茂陵摯網，平陵如氏、苴氏，長安丹王君房，豉樊少翁、王孫大卿，為天下高訾。
entries.en: Once the old houses faded, from Yuandi through Chengdi into Wang Mang's coup, Chang'an's wealthiest were Fan Jia of Duling, Zhi Gang of Maoling, the Ru and Ju families of Pingling, the cinnabar magnate Wang Junfang, the pickle king Fan Shaoweng, and Wangsun Daqing—each counted among the empire's heaviest purses.
entries.literal: After the former rich had declined, from Yuan and Cheng down to Wang Mang, the rich men of the capital—Fan Jia of Duling, Zhi Gang of Maoling, the Ru and Ju clans of Pingling, Wang Junfang the cinnabar dealer of Chang'an, Fan Shaoweng the fermented-bean paste seller, and Wangsun Daqing—were the highest capital in the realm.

entries.zh: 樊嘉五千萬，其餘皆巨萬矣。
entries.en: Fan Jia alone was worth fifty million cash; every other name on the list still cleared eight figures.
entries.literal: Fan Jia had fifty million; the rest all reached tens of millions.

entries.zh: 王孫卿以財養士，與雄桀交，王莽以為京司市師，漢司東市令也。
entries.en: Wangsun Qing bankrolled swordsmen and courted bold spirits until Wang Mang named him Capital Market Master, the old Han post of Director of the Eastern Market.
entries.literal: Wangsun Qing with wealth nurtured knights, associated with heroes and champions; Wang Mang made him metropolitan market master of the capital—the Han office of director of the eastern market.

entries.zh: 卷九十一 貨殖傳第六十一
entries.en: Volume 91: Treatise on Wealth and Trade (the sixty-first chapter).
entries.literal: Volume 91: Treatise on Enrichment and Trade, the sixty-first.

entries.zh: 自魏其、武安、淮南之後，天子切齒，衛、霍改節。
entries.en: After the Dou–Tian feud and the Huainan revolt, the emperor set his jaw, and even Wei Qing and Huo Qubing learned to keep clients at arm's length.
entries.literal: After Weiqi, Wu'an, and Huainan, the Son of Heaven gnashed his teeth, and Wei and Huo changed their conduct.

entries.zh: 然郡國豪桀處處各有，京師親戚冠蓋相望，亦古今常道，莫足言者。
entries.en: Still, every province bred its bravos, and Chang'an kinfolk still jostled in official carriages—an old story, hardly worth another line.
entries.literal: Yet in commanderies and kingdoms fierce champions existed everywhere; at the capital affinal kin and covered carriages looked upon one another—it is also the constant way of past and present, not worth speaking of.

entries.zh: 唯成帝時，外家王氏賓客為盛，而樓護為帥。
entries.en: Under Chengdi the Wang in-laws ran the richest salon of retainers, headed by Lou Hu.
entries.literal: Only in Emperor Cheng's time, the Wang affinal family's guests were at their height, and Lou Hu was their leader.

entries.zh: 及王莽時，諸公之間陳遵為雄，閭里之俠原涉為魁。
entries.en: By Wang Mang's day Chen Zun lorded it among the great ministers, while Yuan She ruled the back-alley swordsmen.
entries.literal: Reaching Wang Mang's time, among the various dukes Chen Zun was champion; among lane-knight-errants Yuan She was chief.

entries.zh: 硃家，魯人，高祖同時也。
entries.en: Zhu Jia of Lu was a man of Gaozu's generation.
entries.literal: Zhu Jia was a man of Lu, contemporary with Gaozu.

entries.zh: 魯人皆以儒教，而硃家用俠聞。
entries.en: Lu was famous for scholars, yet the Zhu family made its name with swords.
entries.literal: The people of Lu all took Confucian teaching, but the Zhu household became known by knight-errantry.

entries.zh: 所臧活豪士以百數，其餘庸人不可勝言。
entries.en: He saved hundreds of desperate fighting men and countless humbler souls besides.
entries.literal: Those he harbored and kept alive as bold knights were in the hundreds; the remaining common people cannot be fully told.

entries.zh: 然終不伐其能，飲其德，諸所嘗施，唯恐見之。
entries.en: He never bragged of his power or waited for thanks, and he hid from everyone he had helped.
entries.literal: Yet in the end he did not boast of his ability or drink in their gratitude; for all he had ever bestowed, he only feared being seen by them.

entries.zh: 振人不贍，先從貧賤始。
entries.en: When he handed out relief, the poorest got served first.
entries.literal: In raising those who lacked sufficiency, he began first from the poor and base.

entries.zh: 家亡余財，衣不兼采，食不重味，乘不過軥牛。
entries.en: His house stayed bare: plain single-color robes, one dish to a meal, and travel no grander than an ox cart.
entries.literal: The household had no surplus wealth; his clothes did not combine two colors; his food did not double flavors; his riding did not exceed a yoked ox.

entries.zh: 專趨人之急，甚於己私。
entries.en: He chased other people's crises harder than his own comfort.
entries.literal: He devoted himself solely to rushing to others' emergencies, more than to his private concerns.

entries.zh: 既陰脫季布之厄，及布尊貴，終身不見。
entries.en: After smuggling Ji Bu out of danger, he never showed his face again—not even when Ji Bu rose to high office.
entries.literal: Having secretly delivered Ji Bu from peril, when Ji Bu became honored and noble, to the end of his life he did not see him.

entries.zh: 自關以東，莫不延頸願交。
entries.en: East of Hangu every bravo strained to claim his friendship.
entries.literal: From east of the pass, none did not crane their necks wishing to associate with him.

entries.zh: 及至漢興，禁網疏闊，未之匡改也。
entries.en: When the Han rose, the law stayed slack, and no one tightened it in time.
entries.literal: Reaching to when Han arose, the prohibitory net was loose and wide, and it was not thereby corrected and reformed.

entries.zh: 是故代相陳豨從車千乘，而吳濞、淮南皆招賓客以千數。
entries.en: Hence Chen Xi, chancellor of Dai, rolled with a thousand chariots in his train, while Liu Pi in Wu and the king of Huainan each kept client armies counted in thousands.
entries.literal: Therefore Chancellor Chen Xi of Dai had a thousand chariots following his carriage, while Liu Pi of Wu and the Prince of Huainan each recruited guests by the thousands.

entries.zh: 外戚大臣魏其、武安之屬競逐於京師，布衣遊俠劇孟、郭解之徒馳騖於閭閻，權行州域，力折公侯。
entries.en: Inside Chang'an the Dou and Tian factions jostled for power, while in the alleys bare-chested swordsmen like Ju Meng and Guo Xie built reputations that cowed nobles and bent whole commanderies.
entries.literal: Affinal ministers such as Marquis Weiqi and Marquis Wu'an vied in pursuit at the capital; common-cloth wandering knights such as Ju Meng and Guo Xie raced in the lanes—their authority ran through provinces, their force bent marquises and dukes.

entries.zh: 眾庶榮其名跡，覬而慕之。
entries.en: Commoners gloried in their legends and ached to imitate them.
entries.literal: The multitude honored their names and tracks, looked up to and admired them.

entries.zh: 雖其陷於刑辟，自與殺身成名，若季路、仇牧，死而不悔也。
entries.en: Even when the law caught them, they styled themselves martyrs like Zilu or Qiu Mu—ready to die unrepentant for a famous end.
entries.literal: Although they fell into punishments and executions, they themselves aligned with killing the body to complete the name, like Jilu and Qiu Mu—dying without regret.

entries.zh: 故曾子曰：「上失其道，民散久矣。」
entries.en: Master Zeng warned, "When rulers stray from the Way, the people lose their moorings."
entries.literal: Therefore Master Zeng said: "When those above lose the Way, the people have long been scattered."

entries.zh: 非明王在上，視之以好惡，齊之以禮法，民曷由知禁而反正乎！
entries.en: Without a clear-sighted sovereign to show what he honors and detests, and ritual and statute to snap them back into line, how will folk learn where the boundary lies?
entries.literal: Unless an enlightened king is above, surveying them with likes and dislikes, aligning them with ritual and law, how can the people know prohibition and return to rectitude!

entries.zh: 劇孟者，洛陽人也。
entries.en: Ju Meng came from Luoyang.
entries.literal: Ju Meng was a man of Luoyang.

entries.zh: 周人以商賈為資，劇孟以俠顯。
entries.en: Where Zhou folk prided themselves on trade, Ju Meng made his name with a sword.
entries.literal: The Zhou people took merchants and peddlers as their capital; Ju Meng displayed himself by knight-errantry.

entries.zh: 吳、楚反時，條侯為太尉，乘傳東，將至河南，得劇孟，喜曰：「吳、楚舉大事而不求劇孟，吾知其無能為已。」
entries.en: During the Rebellion of Seven States, Zhou Yafu rode east as Grand Commandant, picked up Ju Meng in Henan, and laughed with relief: "If Wu and Chu forgot to recruit Ju Meng, they have already lost."
entries.literal: When Wu and Chu rebelled, Marquis Tiao was Grand Commandant; riding post east, about to reach Henan, he obtained Ju Meng and joyfully said: "Wu and Chu are undertaking a great affair yet do not seek Ju Meng—I know they can accomplish nothing."

entries.zh: 天下騷動，大將軍得之若一敵國雲。
entries.en: Amid the empire's turmoil, the Grand General's gaining Ju Meng was reckoned equivalent to securing the allegiance of an entire rival state.
entries.literal: All under heaven was in turmoil; for the Grand General to obtain him was like gaining an enemy state.

entries.zh: 劇孟行大類硃家，而好博，多少年之戲。
entries.en: Ju Meng lived like Zhu Jia but loved dice and the games of the young.
entries.literal: Ju Meng's conduct was greatly similar to Zhu Jia's, but he liked gambling—much youthful sport.

entries.zh: 然孟母死，自遠方送喪蓋千乘。
entries.en: When his mother died, a thousand chariots followed her bier from every corner of the realm.
entries.literal: Yet when Ju Meng's mother died, those who came from afar to join the funeral numbered roughly a thousand chariot teams.

entries.zh: 及孟死，家無十金之財。
entries.en: When he died, his heirs could not scrape together ten catties of gold.
entries.literal: When Meng died, the household had not the wealth of ten in gold.

entries.zh: 而符離王孟，亦以俠稱江、淮之間。
entries.en: Wang Meng of Fuli was another blade between the Yangzi and the Huai.
entries.literal: Moreover Wang Meng of Fuli was also called a knight-errant between the Yangzi and Huai.

entries.zh: 是時，濟南瞷氏、陳周膚亦以豪聞。
entries.en: Around then the Jians of Jinan and Zhou Fu of Chen were feared as local tyrants.
entries.literal: At this time the Jian clan of Jinan and Zhou Fu of Chen were also heard of as champions.

entries.zh: 景帝聞之，使使盡誅此屬。
entries.en: Emperor Jing sent agents to wipe out every one of those clans.
entries.literal: When Emperor Jing heard of it, he sent envoys to execute all this sort to the last.

entries.zh: 其後，代諸白、梁韓毋辟、陽翟薛況、陝寒孺，紛紛復出焉。
entries.en: Soon enough new names surfaced—the Bai families of Dai, Han Wubi in Liang, Xue Kuang in Yangdi, Han Ru in Shan—each as bold as the last.
entries.literal: Afterward the various Bai of Dai, Han Wubi of Liang, Xue Kuang of Yangdi, Han Ru of Shan—one after another reappeared.

entries.zh: 及徙豪茂陵也，解貧，不中訾。
entries.en: When the court ordered rich families moved to Maoling, Guo Xie was too poor on paper to qualify.
entries.literal: When the time came to relocate champions to Maoling, Xie was poor and did not meet the property assessment.

entries.zh: 吏恐，不敢不徙。
entries.en: The local clerks dared not exempt him for fear of higher wrath.
entries.literal: The clerks feared and did not dare not relocate him.

entries.zh: 衛將軍為言：「郭解家貧，不中徙。」
entries.en: General Wei Qing pleaded, "Guo Xie is too poor to be on the removal list."
entries.literal: General Wei spoke for him: "Guo Xie's household is poor; he does not meet relocation."

entries.zh: 上曰：「解布衣，權至使將軍，此其家不貧！」
entries.en: The emperor snapped, "A commoner who can move my general is not poor!"
entries.literal: The sovereign said: "Xie is common cloth—his power reaches to making a general speak; this means his household is not poor!"

entries.zh: 解徙，諸公送者出千餘萬。
entries.en: When he was forced west, well-wishers showered him with more than ten million cash in parting gifts.
entries.literal: Xie was relocated; those gentlemen who sent him off contributed over ten million.

entries.zh: 軹人楊季主子為縣掾，隔之，解兄子斷楊掾頭。
entries.en: Yang Jizhu's son, a county clerk, blocked the convoy, so Guo Xie's elder brother's son took the man's head.
entries.literal: A son of Yang Jizhu of Zhi was a county clerk and blocked him; Xie's elder brother's son cut off Clerk Yang's head.

entries.zh: 解入關，關中賢豪知與不知，聞聲爭交歡。
entries.en: Once inside the pass every Guanzhong notable, stranger or friend, rushed to win his smile at the mere mention of his name.
entries.literal: Xie entered the pass; within the pass worthy champions, whether they knew him or not, at hearing his name vied to associate in friendship.

entries.zh: 邑人又殺楊季主，季主家上書人又殺闕下。
entries.en: Locals murdered Yang Jizhu; when his kin sent a petitioner to the throne, someone cut the petitioner down on the palace steps.
entries.literal: Townsmen again killed Yang Jizhu; Jizhu's family sent up a memorialist, and the memorialist was again killed below the palace gate.

entries.zh: 上聞，乃下吏捕解。
entries.en: The emperor heard and ordered Guo Xie's arrest.
entries.literal: When the sovereign heard of it, thereupon he sent down clerks to arrest Xie.

entries.zh: 解亡，置其母家室夏陽，身至臨晉。
entries.en: Guo Xie ran, stashed his mother and kin in Xiayang, and slipped on alone to Linjin.
entries.literal: Xie fled, placing his mother, family, and household at Xiayang; in person he reached Linjin.

entries.zh: 臨晉籍少翁素不知解，因出關。
entries.en: Ji Shao'weng of Linjin, a stranger to Guo Xie, smuggled him through the barrier.
entries.literal: Ji Shao'weng of Linjin had never known Xie, yet thereby got him out of the pass.

entries.zh: 籍少翁已出解，解傳太原，所過輒告主人處。
entries.en: Once Ji Shao'weng had passed him through the barrier, Guo Xie sent word ahead through Taiyuan, telling every host where he would lodge.
entries.literal: After Ji Shao'weng had gotten Xie out, Xie relayed through Taiyuan; wherever he passed he always informed his hosts of his whereabouts.

entries.zh: 吏逐跡至籍少翁，少翁自殺，口絕。
entries.en: The trail led the police to Ji Shao'weng, who killed himself to seal his lips.
entries.literal: Clerks followed the trail to Ji Shao'weng; Shao'weng killed himself, cutting off the mouth.

entries.zh: 久之得解，窮治所犯為，而解所殺，皆在赦前。
entries.en: Eventually they took Guo Xie and combed his record—yet every homicide dated to before a general amnesty.
entries.literal: After a long time they obtained Xie, exhaustively investigated what he had done wrong, but Xie's killings had all been before amnesties.

entries.zh: 陳遵字孟公，杜陵人也。
entries.en: Chen Zun, styled Menggong, came from Duling.
entries.literal: Chen Zun, courtesy Menggong, was a man of Duling.

entries.zh: 祖父遂，字長子，宣帝微時與有故，相隨博弈，數負進。
entries.en: His grandfather Sui, styled Zhangzi, had known the future Emperor Xuan in his obscure days; they gambled together, and Sui often lost.
entries.literal: His grandfather Sui, courtesy Zhangzi, had old ties with the future Emperor Xuan when he was still obscure; they gambled together, and Sui often lost.

entries.zh: 及宣帝即位，用遂，稍遷至太原太守，乃賜遂璽書曰：「制詔太原太守：官尊祿厚，可以償博進矣。
entries.en: When Xuan took the throne he employed Sui, who rose to Grand Administrator of Taiyuan. The emperor sent him a sealed edict: "To the Grand Administrator of Taiyuan: your rank is high and your pay ample—you can repay your gambling losses.
entries.literal: When Emperor Xuan took the throne, he employed Sui, who gradually rose to Grand Administrator of Taiyuan. The emperor then bestowed on Sui an imperial edict saying, "By decree to the Grand Administrator of Taiyuan: your office is high and your salary ample—you can repay your gambling losses.

entries.zh: 妻君寧時在旁，知狀。」
entries.en: Your wife Jun Ning was there and knows the whole story."
entries.literal: Your wife Jun Ning was present at the time and knows the circumstances."

entries.zh: 遂於是辭謝，因曰：「事在元平元年赦令前。」
entries.en: Sui thanked him and replied, "That happened before the Yuanping amnesty of the first year."
entries.literal: Sui then declined with thanks and added, "The matter fell before the Yuanping first-year amnesty."

entries.zh: 其見厚如此。
entries.en: That was how highly he was favored.
entries.literal: Such was the favor shown him.

entries.zh: 元帝時，徵遂為京兆尹，至廷尉。
entries.en: Under Emperor Yuan, Sui was called up as Metropolitan Governor and rose to Commandant of Justice.
entries.literal: Under Emperor Yuan, Sui was summoned as Metropolitan Governor and reached the post of Commandant of Justice.

entries.zh: 原涉字巨先。
entries.en: Yuan She, styled Juxian.
entries.literal: Yuan She, courtesy name Juxian.

entries.zh: 祖父武帝時以豪桀自陽翟徙茂陵。
entries.en: His grandfather, a noted bravo, was resettled from Yangzhai to Maoling under Emperor Wu.
entries.literal: His grandfather in Emperor Wu's time, as a fierce champion, was moved from Yangzhai to Maoling.

entries.zh: 涉父哀帝時為南陽太守。
entries.en: His father governed Nanyang under Emperor Ai.
entries.literal: Yuan She's father in Emperor Ai's time was governor of Nanyang.

entries.zh: 天下殷富，大郡二千石列官，賦斂送葬皆千萬以上，妻子通共受之，以定產業。
entries.en: The empire was flush: great governors collected millions in funeral gifts, and families banked the windfall to build fortunes.
entries.literal: The realm was rich; in great commanderies two-thousand-shi officials lined out offices; levies for sending off funerals all exceeded ten million; wives and children jointly received them to settle estates.

entries.zh: 時又少行三年喪者。
entries.en: Hardly anyone still kept three years of mourning.
entries.literal: At that time there were again few who practiced the three-year mourning.

entries.zh: 及涉父死，讓還南陽賻送，行喪塚廬三年，由是顯名京師。
entries.en: When his father died he sent back the Nanyang condolence gold, mourned three years by the grave, and became famous in Chang'an.
entries.literal: When Yuan She's father died, he declined and returned the Nanyang funeral gifts, observed mourning hut and tomb for three years, whereby he displayed his name in the capital.

entries.zh: 禮畢，扶風謁請為議曹，衣冠慕之輻輳。
entries.en: After mourning Fufeng named him a deliberation clerk, and every gentleman in the capital flocked to him.
entries.literal: When the rites were finished, Fufeng invited him to serve as deliberation clerk; gentry admired him and crowded like spokes to a hub.

entries.zh: 為大司徒史丹舉能治劇，為谷口令，時年二十餘。
entries.en: Grand Minister of Education Shi Dan recommended him as capable of governing a difficult district, and Yuan She was appointed magistrate of Gukou while still in his twenties.
entries.literal: Grand Minister of Education Shi Dan recommended him as able to govern a difficult county; he became magistrate of Gukou, at the time being over twenty.

entries.zh: 谷口聞其名，不言而治。
entries.en: Gukou obeyed his reputation before he issued a single order.
entries.literal: Gukou heard his name and was governed without his speaking.

entries.zh: 涉自以為前讓南陽賻送，身得其名，而令先人墳墓儉約，非孝也。
entries.en: He decided that refusing Nanyang gold had bought him fame at the cost of shabby ancestral tombs—unfilial after all.
entries.literal: He himself thought that earlier he had declined Nanyang funeral gifts and personally gained the name, yet caused his ancestors' graves to be meager—not filial.

entries.zh: 乃大治起塚捨，周閣重門。
entries.en: So he raised a mansion-tomb with ringed galleries and doubled gates.
entries.literal: Thereupon he greatly built up tomb lodges, surrounding pavilions and double gates.

entries.zh: 初，武帝時，京兆尹曹氏葬茂陵，民謂其道為京兆仟，涉慕之，乃買地開道，立表署曰南陽仟，人不肯從，謂之原氏仟。
entries.en: Emperor Wu's Governor Cao had left a "Metropolitan Thousand" funeral avenue at Maoling; Yuan She copied the stunt, labeled his "Nanyang Thousand," but locals dubbed it the Yuan family lane.
entries.literal: At first, in Emperor Wu's time, Metropolitan Governor Cao was buried at Maoling; the people called his road Metropolitan Thousand; Yuan She admired this, bought land, opened a road, set a marker inscribed Nanyang Thousand; people would not follow and called it Yuan Clan Thousand.

entries.zh: 費用皆仰富人長者，然身衣服車馬才具，妻子內困。
entries.en: Rich friends paid the bills while he dressed plain and kept his household short.
entries.literal: Expenses all looked up to rich men and elders, yet his own clothes, carriages, and gear were modest; wife and children were inwardly pressed.

entries.zh: 專以振施貧窮赴人之急為務。
entries.en: His mission was feeding the hungry and answering every midnight plea.
entries.literal: He devoted himself solely to relieving the poor and rushing to others' emergencies as his task.

entries.zh: 人嘗置酒請涉，涉入里門，客有道涉所知母病避疾在裡宅者。
entries.en: Someone once invited Yuan She to a banquet. As he entered the ward gate, a guest told him that the mother of a family he knew was ill and had moved to a house within the ward in hopes of escaping the sickness.
entries.literal: Someone once laid out wine and invited Yuan She. As She entered the ward gate, a guest told him that the mother of a family he knew was ill and had moved to a house within the ward in hopes of escaping the sickness.

entries.zh: 涉即往候，叩門。
entries.en: He turned aside at once and knocked at her door.
entries.literal: Yuan She immediately went to wait on her and knocked at the gate.

entries.zh: 家哭，涉因入吊，問以喪事。
entries.en: He found the house in tears, stepped in to mourn, and asked what the burial needed.
entries.literal: The household was weeping; Yuan She therefore entered to condole and asked about funeral affairs.

entries.zh: 家無所有，涉曰：「但潔掃除沐浴，待涉。」
entries.en: They owned nothing; Yuan She said, "Scrub the rooms, wash the body, and wait for me."
entries.literal: The household had nothing; Yuan She said: "Only sweep clean, bathe, and wait for me."

entries.zh: 還至主人，對賓客歎息曰：「人親臥地不收，涉何心鄉此！
entries.en: Back at the party he told the crowd, "A mother lies unburied—how can I swallow your wine!
entries.literal: Returning to the host, he sighed to the guests: "With a parent lying on the ground unburied, how could I have heart for this feast!

entries.zh: 願撤去酒食。」
entries.en: Clear the table."
entries.literal: I wish to remove the wine and food."

entries.zh: 賓客爭問所當得，涉乃側席而坐，削牘為疏，具記衣被棺木，下至飯含之物，分付諸客。
entries.en: Guests pressed for tasks; he sat, cut a tally sheet, and assigned shroud, coffin, even grave goods to each man.
entries.literal: Guests vied to ask what should be obtained; Yuan She then sat sideways on the mat, shaved a slip into a list, fully noting shrouds, coffin wood, down to mouth-fill objects, assigning each to guests.

entries.zh: 諸客奔走市買，至日昳皆會。
entries.en: They scattered to the markets and reassembled by dusk with every item.
entries.literal: The guests ran to the market to buy; by late afternoon all had assembled.

entries.zh: 涉親閱視已，謂主人：「願受賜矣。」
entries.en: He checked the haul and told the host, "Now I will take your cup."
entries.literal: Yuan She personally inspected it and said to the host: "I wish to receive your gift."

entries.zh: 既共飲食，涉獨不飽，乃載棺物，從賓客往至喪家，為棺斂勞徠畢葬。
entries.en: He barely touched food, then convoyed the goods to the dead woman's house and stayed until she was sealed in the earth.
entries.literal: Having together eaten and drunk, Yuan She alone did not eat his fill; then he loaded the coffin goods and, following guests, went to the mourning house, completing encoffining, labor, and burial.

entries.zh: 其周急待人如此。
entries.en: That was how he met emergencies.
entries.literal: His relieving urgency and treating people were like this.

entries.zh: 後人有毀涉者曰「奸人之雄也」，喪家子即時刺殺言者。
entries.en: Later someone who slandered Yuan She said he was "champion of villains"; the son of the mourning house immediately stabbed and killed the speaker.
entries.literal: Later someone who slandered Yuan She said he was "champion of villains"; the son of the mourning house immediately stabbed and killed the speaker.

entries.zh: 卷九十二 遊俠傳第六十二
entries.en: Volume 92: Biographies of the Knights-Errant (the sixty-second chapter).
entries.literal: Volume 92: Biography of Wandering Knights, the sixty-second.

entries.zh: 漢興，佞幸寵臣，高祖時則有籍孺，孝惠有閎孺。
entries.en: After the Han rose, the court had its share of favorites: under Gaozu there was Ji Ru; under Emperor Hui, Hong Ru.
entries.literal: When the Han arose, among the flattering favorites who won imperial favor, in Gaozu's time there was Ji Ru, and in Xiaohui's time there was Hong Ru.

entries.zh: 此兩人非有材能，但以婉媚貴幸，與上臥起，公卿皆因關說。
entries.en: Neither had any real ability; they rose by soft flattery alone, sharing the emperor's bedchamber, and high officials routinely used them as go-betweens to reach the throne.
entries.literal: These two men had no talent or ability; they relied solely on ingratiating charm to become noble and favored, slept and rose with the sovereign, and the ministers all used them to convey pleas.

entries.zh: 故孝惠時，郎侍中皆冠鵔鸃，貝帶，傅脂粉，化閎、籍之屬也。
entries.en: So under Emperor Hui, Gentlemen of the Palace and attendants-in-chief took to zījī caps, shell-inlaid belts, and rouge—aping the style of Hong Ru and Ji Ru.
entries.literal: Therefore in Xiaohui's time the gentlemen of the palace and attendants-in-chief all wore zījī caps, shell belts, and applied face powder—transformed into the likes of Hong and Ji.

entries.zh: 兩人徙家安陵。
entries.en: Both families were resettled at Anling.
entries.literal: The two men moved their households to Anling.

entries.zh: 其後寵臣，孝文時士人則鄧通，宦者則趙談、北宮伯子；
entries.en: Later reigns had their own favorites: under Emperor Wen, the lay courtier was Deng Tong; the eunuchs were Zhao Tan and Beigong Bozi;
entries.literal: Among the later favorites: in Xiaowen's time the lay favorite was Deng Tong, the eunuchs were Zhao Tan and Beigong Bozi;

entries.zh: 孝武時士人則韓嫣，宦者則李延年；
entries.en: under Emperor Wu, the courtier was Han Yan and the eunuch Li Yannian;
entries.literal: in Xiaowu's time the lay favorite was Han Yan, the eunuch was Li Yannian;

entries.zh: 孝元時宦者則弘恭、石顯；
entries.en: under Emperor Yuan, the eunuchs Hong Gong and Shi Xian;
entries.literal: in Xiaoyuan's time the eunuchs were Hong Gong and Shi Xian;

entries.zh: 孝成時士人則張放、淳于長；
entries.en: under Emperor Cheng, Zhang Fang and Chunyu Chang;
entries.literal: in Xiaocheng's time the lay favorites were Zhang Fang and Chunyu Chang;

entries.zh: 孝哀時則有董賢。
entries.en: and under Emperor Ai, Dong Xian.
entries.literal: in Xia'ai's time there was Dong Xian.

entries.zh: 孝景、昭、宣時皆無寵臣。
entries.en: Emperors Jing, Zhao, and Xuan had no true "favorites" of this kind.
entries.literal: In Xiaojing's, Zhao's, and Xuandi's times there were none who were favorites in this sense.

entries.zh: 景帝唯有郎中令周仁。
entries.en: Jing's circle held only Zhou Ren, the palace commandant.
entries.literal: Emperor Jing had only Palace Commandant Zhou Ren.

entries.zh: 昭帝時，駙馬都尉秺侯金賞嗣父車騎將軍日磾爵為侯，二人之寵取過庸，不篤。
entries.en: Under Emperor Zhao, Jin Shang, marquis of Du and commandant of the imperial son-in-law, inherited his father Jin Midi's chariot-and-cavalry rank and marquisate; father and son were favored beyond the usual, though the affection was not deep.
entries.literal: In Zhaodi's time, Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law and Marquis of Du Jin Shang inherited his father's chariot-and-cavalry general Jin Midi's marquisate; the favor shown the two of them exceeded the ordinary, but it was not deep.

entries.zh: 宣帝時，侍中中郎將張彭祖少與帝微時同席研書，及帝即尊位，彭祖以舊恩封陽都侯，出常參乘，號為愛幸。
entries.en: Xuandi's childhood study-mate Zhang Pengzu, later a palace attendant and general of the household, was made marquis of Yangdu for past loyalty and often rode beside him as escort—people spoke of him as a favorite.
entries.literal: In Xuandi's time, Palace Attendant and General of the Household Zhang Pengzu had studied at the same mat with the emperor in humble days; when the emperor took the throne, Pengzu was enfeoffed marquis of Yangdu for old kindness, regularly rode as guard in the secondary chariot, and was called beloved and favored.

entries.zh: 其人謹敕，無所虧損，為其小妻所毒薨，國除。
entries.en: He was careful and irreproachable until a concubine poisoned him; his fief was struck from the rolls.
entries.literal: The man was cautious and restrained and did nothing improper; he died poisoned by a junior wife, and the state was abolished.

entries.zh: 鄧通，蜀郡南安人也，以濯船為黃頭郎。
entries.en: Deng Tong of Nan'an in Shu had been a Yellow-Head boatman in the imperial service.
entries.literal: Deng Tong was a man of Nan'an in Shu commandery; he served as a Yellow-Head Gentleman who worked bailing boats.

entries.zh: 文帝嘗夢欲上天，不能，有一黃頭郎推上天，顧見其衣尻帶後穿。
entries.en: Wen once dreamed he could not rise to heaven until a Yellow-Head attendant pushed him upward; glancing back, he noticed the seat of the man's trousers was split.
entries.literal: Emperor Wen once dreamed he wished to ascend to heaven but could not; there was a Yellow-Head Gentleman who pushed him up, and when he looked back he saw the seam at the back of the man's trousers was worn through.

entries.zh: 覺而之漸台，以夢中陰目求推者郎，見鄧通，其衣後穿，夢中所見也。
entries.en: He went to the Jian Terrace and quietly searched for that attendant—and found Deng Tong, whose trousers were torn exactly where the dream had shown.
entries.literal: When he awoke he went to the Jian Terrace and, with the dream still in mind, sought the gentleman who had pushed him; he saw Deng Tong, whose clothes were worn through at the back as in the dream.

entries.zh: 召問其名姓，姓鄧，名通。
entries.en: Asked his name, the man said he was Deng Tong.
entries.literal: He summoned him and asked his surname and given name: the surname was Deng, the given name Tong.

entries.zh: 鄧猶登也，文帝甚說，尊幸之，日日異。
entries.en: The emperor took "Deng" for "ascend" and was delighted; Deng Tong's favor climbed higher every day.
entries.literal: Deng is like deng ("to ascend"); the emperor was greatly pleased, honored and favored him, and day by day it grew more extraordinary.

entries.zh: 通亦願謹，不好外交，雖賜洗沐，不欲出。
entries.en: Deng Tong was obliging and discreet, avoided outside contacts, and even on bath-leave preferred not to leave the palace.
entries.literal: Tong was also willing and careful, did not like dealings with outsiders, and even when granted leave to bathe did not wish to go out.

entries.zh: 於是文帝賞賜通巨萬以十數，官至上大夫。
entries.en: Wen showered him with fortunes counted in the hundreds of thousands and promoted him to senior grandee.
entries.literal: Thereupon Emperor Wen rewarded Deng Tong with tens of counts of a hundred thousand cash, and his office rose to senior grandee.

entries.zh: 文帝嘗病癰，鄧通常為上嗽吮之。
entries.en: When Wen developed an abscess, Deng Tong habitually drew the pus with his mouth.
entries.literal: Emperor Wen once suffered from a boil, and Deng Tong often sucked the infection for the sovereign.

entries.zh: 上不樂，從容問曰：「天下誰最愛我者乎？」
entries.en: Unhappy, Wen asked casually, "Who in all the world loves me most?"
entries.literal: The sovereign was unhappy and asked at ease: "Who in the realm loves me most?"

entries.zh: 通曰：「宜莫若太子。」
entries.en: “Surely no one loves you more than the crown prince,” Deng Tong said.
entries.literal: Tong said: "None should compare to the heir apparent."

entries.zh: 太子入問疾，上使太子齰癰。
entries.en: When the crown prince visited the sickbed, Wen told him to suck the sore.
entries.literal: When the heir apparent came in to inquire after his illness, the sovereign had the heir apparent suck the boil.

entries.zh: 太子齰癰而色難之。
entries.en: The prince did it, but his face showed revulsion.
entries.literal: The heir apparent sucked the boil but his expression showed difficulty.

entries.zh: 已而聞通嘗為上齰之，太子慚，由是心恨通。
entries.en: Learning that Deng Tong had done the same for his father, the prince was mortified and nursed a grudge against him.
entries.literal: Afterward, when he heard that Tong had often sucked it for the sovereign, the heir apparent was ashamed and from this inwardly hated Tong.

entries.zh: 及文帝崩，景帝立，鄧通免，家居。
entries.en: When Wen died and Jing succeeded, Deng Tong was stripped of office and sent home.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen died and Emperor Jing took the throne, Deng Tong was dismissed and lived at home.

entries.zh: 居無何，人有告通盜出徼外鑄錢，下吏驗問，頗有，遂竟案，盡沒入之，通家尚負責數巨萬。
entries.en: Soon he was accused of illegal minting beyond the frontier; the inquiry proved true, his property was seized, and he still owed tens of millions.
entries.literal: Before long someone reported that Tong had smuggled coin-casting beyond the frontier passes; he was handed to officials for investigation, and there was quite a bit of evidence; the case was pushed to the end, everything was confiscated, and Tong's household still owed debts of several tens of millions.

entries.zh: 長公主賜鄧通，吏輒隨沒入之，一簪不得著身。
entries.en: Whenever the princess tried to help him with gifts, officials seized them before they reached him—not even a hairpin stayed his.
entries.literal: When the senior princess gave gifts to Deng Tong, the officials would follow and confiscate them, so that not a single hairpin could remain on his person.

entries.zh: 於是長公主乃令假衣食。
entries.en: At last she could only arrange meager food and clothes on loan.
entries.literal: Thereupon the senior princess ordered that he be lent food and clothing.

entries.zh: 竟不得名一錢，寄死人家。
entries.en: He died without a coin to his name, a guest in someone else's roof.
entries.literal: In the end he could not claim a single cash and died lodged in another's house.

entries.zh: 趙談者，以星氣幸，北宮伯子長者愛人，故親近，然皆不比鄧通。
entries.en: Zhao Tan rose on star-charts and portents; Beigong Bozi, a kindly elder, stayed close to the throne—but neither matched Deng Tong's hold.
entries.literal: Zhao Tan won favor through astrology; Beigong Bozi was a venerable man who loved people, and therefore was intimate with the ruler—yet neither compared to Deng Tong.

entries.zh: 文帝時間如通家遊戲，然通無他技能，不能有所薦達，獨自謹身以媚上而已。
entries.en: Wen sometimes dropped in on Deng Tong's home for sport, but Deng had no talent for recommending men—only a knack for keeping himself in the emperor's good graces.
entries.literal: From time to time Emperor Wen visited Tong's house for amusement; yet Tong had no other skills, could recommend no one for advancement, and only kept himself careful to flatter the sovereign.

entries.zh: 上使善相人者相通，曰：「當貧餓死。」
entries.en: Wen had a face-reader study Deng Tong, who said, "This man will starve in poverty."
entries.literal: The sovereign had a skilled physiognomist read Tong and he said: "He will die poor and starving."

entries.zh: 上曰：「能富通者在我，何說貧？」
entries.en: "Who makes Deng Tong rich is me," replied the emperor. "How could he end poor?"
entries.literal: The sovereign said: "Who can enrich Tong is myself—what talk of poverty?"

entries.zh: 於是賜通蜀嚴道銅山，得自鑄錢。
entries.en: So he gave Deng Tong the Yandao copper hills in Shu and let him cast his own cash.
entries.literal: Thereupon he granted Tong the copper mountains at Yandao in Shu, so that he could mint coin himself.

entries.zh: 鄧氏錢布天下，其富如此。
entries.en: Deng Tong's money circulated across the empire—such was his wealth.
entries.literal: The coin of the Deng clan spread through the realm; such was his wealth.

entries.zh: 韓嫣字王孫，弓高侯穨當之孫也。
entries.en: Han Yan, styled Wangsun, was grandson of Marquis of Gonggao Tuidang.
entries.literal: Han Yan, courtesy name Wangsun, was the grandson of Marquis of Gonggao Tuidang.

entries.zh: 武帝為膠東王時，嫣與上學書相愛。
entries.en: While Wu was still prince of Jiaodong, Han Yan studied with him and they grew inseparable.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu was Prince of Jiaodong, Yan studied writing with the sovereign and they loved each other.

entries.zh: 及上為太子，愈益親嫣。
entries.en: When Wu became heir apparent, the bond only tightened.
entries.literal: When the sovereign became heir apparent, he grew still closer to Yan.

entries.zh: 嫣善騎射，聰慧。
entries.en: Han Yan excelled at horsemanship and archery and was quick-witted.
entries.literal: Yan was skilled at riding and shooting and was clever and quick.

entries.zh: 上即位，欲事伐胡，而嫣先習兵，以故益尊貴，官至上大夫，賞賜擬鄧通。
entries.en: Once enthroned, Wu planned war on the Xiongnu; Han Yan, already versed in military matters, rose to senior grandee with largesse to rival Deng Tong's.
entries.literal: When the sovereign took the throne he wished to campaign against the Hu, and Yan had already trained in arms; for this reason he grew more honored and noble, his office rose to senior grandee, and his rewards rivaled Deng Tong's.

entries.zh: 始時，嫣常與上共臥起。
entries.en: Early on he often shared the emperor's quarters.
entries.literal: At first Yan often slept and rose with the sovereign.

entries.zh: 江都王入朝，從上獵上林中。
entries.en: The king of Jiangdu attended court and joined a hunt in Shanglin Park.
entries.literal: The king of Jiangdu came to court and accompanied the sovereign on a hunt in Shanglin Park.

entries.zh: 天子車駕蹕道未行，先使嫣乘副車，從數十百騎馳視獸。
entries.en: Before the main procession moved, Wu sent Han Yan ahead in the escort carriage with scores of horsemen to beat the cover.
entries.literal: The imperial train had not yet cleared the cordoned road when the sovereign first sent Yan in the secondary chariot, with several tens or hundreds of riders galloping ahead to scout the game.

entries.zh: 江都王望見，以為天子，辟從者，伏謁道旁。
entries.en: The king mistook the party for the emperor, sent his escort aside, and knelt by the road.
entries.literal: The king of Jiangdu saw this, thought it was the Son of Heaven, dismissed his attendants, and prostrated himself in obeisance beside the road.

entries.zh: 嫣驅不見。
entries.en: Han Yan raced past without a nod.
entries.literal: Yan drove past without acknowledging him.

entries.zh: 既過，江都王怒，為皇太后泣，請得歸國入宿衛，比韓嫣。
entries.en: Humiliated, the king wept to the empress dowager and asked to return his kingdom and enter palace guard duty, to be treated like Han Yan.
entries.literal: After he had passed, the king of Jiangdu was enraged, wept to the empress dowager, and begged to return to his state and enter palace guard duty, to be classed with Han Yan.

entries.zh: 太后由此銜嫣。
entries.en: The empress dowager never forgave Han Yan.
entries.literal: From this the empress dowager bore a grudge against Yan.

entries.zh: 嫣侍，出入永巷不禁，以奸聞皇太后。
entries.en: Han Yan moved freely through the harem lanes, and word of his misconduct reached the empress dowager.
entries.literal: When Yan attended, his comings and goings through the Eternal Lane were unrestricted, and he became known to the empress dowager for debauchery.

entries.zh: 太后怒，使使賜嫣死。
entries.en: She sent an order that he must die.
entries.literal: The empress dowager was angry and sent an envoy to grant Yan death.

entries.zh: 上為謝，終不能得，嫣遂死。
entries.en: Wu begged in vain; Han Yan was put to death.
entries.literal: The sovereign pleaded for him but in the end could not obtain it, and Yan thereupon died.

entries.zh: 初，長為侍中，奉兩宮使，親密。
entries.en: In his days as palace attendant he had run errands for both palaces and been treated as family.
entries.literal: Earlier, when Chang was palace attendant, he carried missions for both palaces and was intimate.

entries.zh: 紅陽侯立獨不得為大司馬輔政，立自疑為長毀譖，常怨毒長。
entries.en: Wang Li, marquis of Hongyang, alone had been passed over for the regency; he was convinced Chang had slandered him and nursed a murderous grudge.
entries.literal: Marquis of Hongyang Wang Li alone did not obtain appointment as grand marshal to assist government; Li suspected himself slandered by Chang and constantly bore bitter hatred.

entries.zh: 上知之。
entries.en: The emperor knew the bad blood.
entries.literal: The sovereign knew it.

entries.zh: 及長當就國也，立嗣子融從長請車騎，長以珍寶因融重遺立，立因為長言。
entries.en: When Chang prepared to leave the capital, Wang Li's heir Rong asked him for horses and carriages; Chang funneled rare gifts through Rong, and Wang Li put in a good word.
entries.literal: When Chang was to go to his state, Li's heir son Rong requested chariotry from Chang; Chang sent treasures through Rong as a heavy gift to Li, and Li then spoke for Chang.

entries.zh: 於是天子疑焉，下有司案驗。
entries.en: The arrangement struck Chengdi as wrong; he handed the matter to the judiciary.
entries.literal: Thereupon the Son of Heaven was suspicious and sent the case down to officials for investigation.

entries.zh: 史捕融，立令融自殺以滅口。
entries.en: Clerks seized Rong; Wang Li ordered his own son to commit suicide to seal his lips.
entries.literal: The clerks arrested Rong; Li ordered Rong to kill himself to silence mouths.

entries.zh: 上愈疑其有大奸，遂逮長系洛陽詔獄窮治。
entries.en: That only deepened the emperor's suspicion of a vast conspiracy; Chang was jailed under imperial warrant at Luoyang and interrogated without mercy.
entries.literal: The sovereign grew more suspicious of great villainy, thereupon arrested Chang and bound him in the Luoyang edict prison for exhaustive inquiry.

entries.zh: 長具服戲侮長定宮，謀立左皇后，罪至大逆，死獄中。
entries.en: He admitted to humiliating the Changding Palace and plotting a rival empress—capital treason—and died in custody.
entries.literal: Chang confessed fully to mocking the Palace of Lasting Settlement and plotting to establish a left empress—the crime reached great treason; he died in prison.

entries.zh: 妻子當坐者徙合浦，母若歸故郡。
entries.en: Wives and children liable under the law went to Hepu; his mother was sent home to her native commandery.
entries.literal: Wives and children who should sit for the crime were banished to Hepu; his mother was allowed to return to her old commandery.

entries.zh: 紅陽侯立就國。
entries.en: Wang Li, marquis of Hongyang, was packed off to his fief as well.
entries.literal: Marquis of Hongyang Li went to his state.

entries.zh: 將軍、卿、大夫、郡守坐長免罷者數十人。
entries.en: Several score generals, ministers, grandees, and governors fell with him.
entries.literal: Generals, ministers, grandees, and governors who sat for Chang and were dismissed numbered several tens.

entries.zh: 莽遂代根為大司馬。
entries.en: Wang Mang stepped into Wang Gen's place as grand marshal.
entries.literal: Mang thereupon replaced Gen as grand marshal.

entries.zh: 久之，還長母及子酺於長安。
entries.en: Years later his mother and son Pu were allowed back to the capital.
entries.literal: After a long time (the court) allowed Chang's mother and son Pu to return to Chang'an.

entries.zh: 後酺有罪，莽復殺之，徙其家屬歸故郡。
entries.en: When Pu offended the law, Mang had him executed and exiled the rest of the family again.
entries.literal: Later Pu committed a crime; Mang again killed him and moved his household back to their old commandery.

entries.zh: 淳于長字子鴻，魏郡元城人也。
entries.en: Chunyu Chang, styled Zihong, came from Yuancheng in Wei commandery.
entries.literal: Chunyu Chang, courtesy name Zihong, was a man of Yuancheng in Wei commandery.

entries.zh: 少以太后姊子為黃門郎，未進幸。
entries.en: Through his tie to the empress dowager's sister he entered as a yellow-gate gentleman before he had won the throne's notice.
entries.literal: In youth he became a gentleman of the yellow gate as the empress dowager's sister's son, and had not yet advanced to favor.

entries.zh: 會大將軍王鳳病，長侍病，晨夜扶丞左右，甚為甥舅之恩。
entries.en: When Wang Feng fell ill, Chang kept vigil day and night at his bedside—the bond of uncle and nephew ran deep.
entries.literal: When Grand General Wang Feng fell ill, Chang nursed him, supporting him morning and night at his side—the kindness of nephew and uncle ran very deep.

entries.zh: 鳳且終，以長屬托太后及帝。
entries.en: On his deathbed Wang Feng commended Chang to the empress dowager and the emperor.
entries.literal: When Feng was about to die, he entrusted Chang to the empress dowager and the emperor.

entries.zh: 帝嘉長義，拜為列校尉諸曹，遷水衡都尉侍中，至衛尉九卿。
entries.en: Chengdi praised his loyalty, moved him through column commandant posts to chief commandant of waters and forests and palace attendant, then to defender of the capital.
entries.literal: The emperor praised Chang's devotion, appointed him to various column commandant posts, promoted him to chief commandant of waters and forests and palace attendant, and raised him to defender of the capital among the nine ministers.

entries.zh: 元帝晚節寢疾，定陶恭王愛幸，顯擁祐太子頗有力。
entries.en: Late in Yuan's reign the emperor fell ill; King Gong of Dingtao was beloved and favored, and Shi Xian's backing of the crown prince carried real weight.
entries.literal: In Emperor Yuan's later years he took to his sickbed; King Gong of Dingtao was beloved and favored, and Xian in supporting the heir apparent was quite influential.

entries.zh: 元帝崩，成帝初即位，遷顯為長信中太僕，秩中二千石。
entries.en: After Yuan died and Chengdi took the throne, Shi Xian was transferred to Director of Palace Servants at Changxin Palace, rank fully two thousand shi.
entries.literal: When Emperor Yuan died and Emperor Cheng had just taken the throne, Xian was transferred to be Director of Palace Servants of the Changxin Palace, with a salary rank of two thousand shi.

entries.zh: 顯失倚，離權數月，丞相御史條奏顯舊惡，及其黨牢梁、陳順皆免官。
entries.en: Deprived of his patron, Shi Xian lingered out of power for months until the chancellor and censor-in-chief filed his old crimes and dismissed his allies Lao Liang and Chen Shun.
entries.literal: Xian lost his backing; removed from power for several months, the chancellor and imperial counsellor memorialized his old crimes, and his clique members Lao Liang and Chen Shun were all dismissed from office.

entries.zh: 顯與妻子徙歸故郡，憂滿不食，道病死。
entries.en: Shi Xian was sent home with his family, refused food in despair, and died on the road.
entries.literal: Xian, with wife and children, was banished to his home commandery; filled with grief he ate nothing and died on the road of illness.

entries.zh: 諸所交結，以顯為官，皆廢罷。
entries.en: Everyone who had climbed in through Shi Xian lost his post.
entries.literal: All those who had associated with him and obtained office through Xian were dismissed.

entries.zh: 少府五鹿充宗左遷玄菟太守，御史中丞伊嘉為雁門都尉。
entries.en: Wulu Chongzong was demoted from the treasury to governor of Xuantu; Yi Jia from vice censor-in-chief to commandant of Yanmen.
entries.literal: Chamberlain for the national treasury Wulu Chongzong was demoted to governor of Xuantu; vice director of the imperial counsellors Yi Jia was made commandant of Yanmen.

entries.zh: 長安謠曰：「伊徙雁，鹿徙菟，去牢與陳實無賈。」
entries.en: Chang'an gossip ran: "Yi to the goose, deer to the rabbit—good riddance to Lao and Chen, not worth a penny."
entries.literal: A Chang'an rhyme said: "When Yi moves to the goose, the deer moves to the rabbit; away with Lao and Chen—they are truly worthless."

entries.zh: 是時，成帝外家王氏衰廢，唯平阿侯譚子去疾，哀帝為太子時為庶子得幸，及即位，為侍中、騎都尉。
entries.en: The Wangs who had dominated under Chengdi were spent; only Wang Quji, son of Marquis Tan of Ping'a, who had won favor as a shuzi cadet while Ai was heir apparent, rose with him to palace attendant and commandant of cavalry.
entries.literal: At that time the Wang affines of Chengdi had declined; only Quji, son of Marquis Tan of Ping'a, had won favor as a gentleman cadet while Emperor Ai was heir apparent, and when Ai mounted the throne he became palace attendant and commandant of cavalry.

entries.zh: 上以王氏亡在位者，遂用舊恩親近去疾，復進其弟閎為中常侍，閎妻父蕭咸，前將軍望之子也，久為郡守，病免，為中郎將。
entries.en: Seeing no Wang in power, Ai favored Quji out of old affection and promoted his brother Wang Hong to regular palace attendant; Hong's father-in-law Xiao Xian—Xiao Wangzhi's son—had been a long-serving governor, left office for illness, and now served as general of the household.
entries.literal: The sovereign thought the Wangs had none left in high office, therefore drew on old kindness to draw Quji close, further advancing his younger brother Hong as regular palace attendant; Hong's father-in-law Xiao Xian, son of former general Xiao Wangzhi, had long been a governor, retired sick, and become general of the household.

entries.zh: 兄弟並列，賢父恭慕之，欲與結婚姻。
entries.en: With both brothers prominent, Dong Gong courted an alliance by marriage.
entries.literal: The brothers both held office; Xian's father Gong admired them and wished to contract marriage ties.

entries.zh: 閎為賢弟駙馬都尉寬信求咸女為婦，咸惶恐不敢當，私謂閎曰：「董公為大司馬，冊文言『允執其中』，此乃堯禪舜之文，非三公故事，長老見者，莫不心懼。
entries.en: Wang Hong asked Xiao Xian for his daughter as wife for Dong Kuanxin; Xiao Xian panicked and whispered back, "The grand marshal's patent cited 'hold the mean'—words from the Yao-Shun abdication, not a normal appointment for one of the three excellencies. Elders who read it were inwardly afraid.
entries.literal: Hong, for Xian's younger brother the commandant of the imperial son-in-law Kuanxin, sought Xiao Xian's daughter as wife; Xiao Xian was terrified and dared not accept, privately saying to Hong: "When Lord Dong became grand marshal, the rescript quoted 'sincerely hold the middle course'—that is the language of Yao yielding to Shun, not the old formula for three excellencies; every elder who saw it was inwardly afraid.

entries.zh: 此豈家人子所能堪邪！」
entries.en: How could a household like ours survive that kind of tie?"
entries.literal: How could this be something a family of our standing could bear!"

entries.zh: 閎性有知略，聞咸言，心亦悟，乃還報恭，深達咸自謙薄之意。
entries.en: Wang Hong took the point, went back to Dong Gong, and relayed Xiao Xian's polite refusal in full.
entries.literal: Hong had native shrewdness; hearing Xiao Xian's words he too understood, returned and reported to Gong, conveying in depth Xiao Xian's meaning of self-deprecation.

entries.zh: 恭歎曰：「我家何用負天下，而為人所畏如是！」
entries.en: Dong Gong sighed, "What crime have we committed against the empire to be dreaded so?"
entries.literal: Gong sighed: "What has our family done to wrong the realm, that we should be feared like this!"

entries.zh: 意不說。
entries.en: He went away sour.
entries.literal: His mood was displeased.

entries.zh: 後上置酒麒麟殿，賢父子親屬宴飲，王閎兄弟侍中、中常侍皆在側。
entries.en: Later Ai held a banquet in the Qilin Hall for the Dong clan; Wang Hong and his brothers, on duty as attendants, flanked the party.
entries.literal: Later the sovereign spread wine in the Qilin Hall; Xian and his father and kindred feasted, while Wang Hong's brothers as palace attendants and regular palace attendants were all at his side.

entries.zh: 上有酒所，從容視賢笑，曰「吾欲法堯禪舜，何如？」
entries.en: When he had drunk, Ai turned to Dong Xian and smiled. "I wish to follow Yao and yield the throne to Shun—what do you think?"
entries.literal: The sovereign, warmed with wine, at ease looked at Xian and smiled, saying: "I wish to imitate Yao yielding to Shun—how would that be?"

entries.zh: 閎進曰：「天下乃高皇帝天下，非陛下之有也。
entries.en: Wang Hong stepped in: "The empire belongs to Gaozu's line, not to Your Majesty alone to give away.
entries.literal: Hong stepped forward and said: "The realm is the realm of the High Founder; it is not something Your Majesty owns alone.

entries.zh: 陛下承宗廟，當傳子孫於亡窮。
entries.en: You hold the ancestral shrines in trust for endless generations of heirs.
entries.literal: Your Majesty inherits the temples and altars and ought to hand them to sons and grandsons without end.

entries.zh: 統業至重，天子亡戲言！」
entries.en: The succession is too grave for imperial jokes!"
entries.literal: The succession is supremely weighty; the Son of Heaven has no jesting words!"

entries.zh: 上默然不說，左右皆恐。
entries.en: Ai fell silent, clearly offended; everyone at the table froze.
entries.literal: The sovereign was silent and displeased; those at his side were all afraid.

entries.zh: 於是遣閎出，後不得復侍宴。
entries.en: He sent Wang Hong away and never again let him join the drinking parties.
entries.literal: Thereupon he sent Hong out, who afterward could no longer attend feasts.

entries.zh: 賢所厚吏沛硃詡自劾去大司馬府，買棺衣收賢屍葬之。
entries.en: Zhu Xu of Pei, an officer Dong Xian had favored, resigned from the grand marshal's staff, bought a coffin and shroud, collected Dong Xian's corpse, and buried him.
entries.literal: Zhu Xu of Pei, whom Xian had favored, impeached himself and left the grand marshal's office, bought a coffin and shroud, collected Xian's corpse, and buried it.

entries.zh: 王莽聞之而大怒，以它罪擊殺詡。
entries.en: Wang Mang, enraged, found another pretext and had Zhu Xu beaten to death.
entries.literal: When Wang Mang heard of it he was greatly furious and on another charge had Xu beaten to death.

entries.zh: 詡子浮建武中貴顯，至大司馬、司空，封侯。
entries.en: Zhu Xu’s son Zhu Fu became eminent during the Jianwu era, reaching Grand Marshal and Minister of Works and receiving a marquisate.
entries.literal: Xu's son Fu in the Jianwu era rose to eminence, reaching grand marshal and minister of works, and was enfeoffed marquis.

entries.zh: 而王閎王莽時為牧守，所居見紀，莽敗乃去官。
entries.en: Wang Hong became a provincial governor under Mang and left a good record; he quit when Mang fell.
entries.literal: Wang Hong during Mang's time served as regional governor; where he governed was recorded in praise; when Mang fell he left office.

entries.zh: 世祖下詔曰：「武王克殷，表商容之閭，閎修善謹敕，兵起，吏民獨不爭其頭首。
entries.en: Emperor Guangwu decreed: "King Wu of Zhou honored Shang Rong's lane after conquering Shang; Wang Hong lived prudently and well, so that when rebellion broke out no mob tried to kill him for sport.
entries.literal: Shizu issued an edict saying: "When King Wu conquered Yin, he marked Shang Rong's lane; Hong cultivated goodness and was restrained; when armies rose, clerks and people alone did not vie to take his head.

entries.zh: 今以閎子補吏。」
entries.en: Let his son be given an official post."
entries.literal: Now appoint Hong's son to fill a clerkship."

entries.zh: 至墨綬卒官。
entries.en: He rose to magistrate with the black ribbon and died in harness.
entries.literal: He reached black-ribbon rank and died in office.

entries.zh: 蕭咸外孫云。
entries.en: Zhu Fu was Xiao Xian's grandson on the distaff side.
entries.literal: Fu was the maternal grandson of Xiao Xian.

entries.zh: 贊曰：柔曼之傾意，非獨女德，蓋亦有男色焉。
entries.en: The summation reads: the spell of soft beauty is not only a woman's weapon; men too have turned rulers' heads with it.
entries.literal: The appraisal says: yielding softness that sways the heart is not the virtue of women alone—there is also the power of male beauty.

entries.zh: 觀籍、閎、鄧、韓之徒非一，而董賢之寵尤盛，父子並為公卿，可謂貴重人臣無二矣。
entries.en: From Ji Ru and Hong Ru through Deng Tong and Han Yan, none matched Dong Xian: father and son both sat among the highest ministers, a peak of favor without parallel.
entries.literal: Looking at Ji, Hong, Deng, Han, and their like—not a single case—Dong Xian's favor was especially great; father and son both became ministers; one may say no subject was ever more honored.

entries.zh: 然進不由道，位過其任，莫能有終，所謂愛之適足以害之者也。
entries.en: Yet they rose without moral right, outran their abilities, and none ended well—proof that doting favor can destroy what it cherishes.
entries.literal: Yet advancement did not follow the Way, rank exceeded their charge, and none could finish well—what is called loving them was just enough to harm them.

entries.zh: 漢世衰於元、成，壞於哀、平。
entries.en: Han strength ebbed under Emperors Yuan and Cheng and shattered under Ai and Ping.
entries.literal: The Han declined from Yuan and Cheng and was broken from Ai and Ping.

entries.zh: 哀、平之際，國多釁矣。
entries.en: Between those two reigns the dynasty was riven with fault lines.
entries.literal: At the turn of Ai and Ping, the state bore many cracks.

entries.zh: 主疾無嗣，弄臣為輔，鼎足不強，棟干微撓。
entries.en: The emperor ailing and heirless, kept his balance on favorites; the "three legs" of state wobbled and the roof-tree swayed.
entries.literal: The ruler was ill without heir; plaything ministers served as props; the tripod's legs were not strong; the ridgepole and rafters bent slightly.

entries.zh: 一朝帝崩，奸臣擅命，董賢縊死，丁、傅流放，辜及母后，奪位幽廢，咎在親便嬖，所任非仁賢。
entries.en: When Ai died in a night, treacherous ministers arrogated the mandate; Dong Xian died on a rope, the Ding and Fu clans were swept into exile, and even the dowager paid for misrule—the price of filling office from the pillow instead of from virtue.
entries.literal: One morning the emperor collapsed; treacherous ministers seized the mandate; Dong Xian was forced to hang himself; Ding and Fu were banished; guilt reached the empress dowager; the throne was wrested away and she was confined and deposed—the fault lay in trusting bedside favorites and employing men who were not benevolent worthies.

entries.zh: 故仲尼著「損者三友」，王者不私人以官，殆為此也。
entries.en: Confucius therefore warned of "three friendships that injure you," and the sage-kings never handed out rank for love alone—this is what he meant.
entries.literal: Therefore Zhongni recorded "the three kinds of friends who cause harm"; the true king does not hand out posts from private affection—it was roughly for this.

entries.zh: 是時，元帝被疾，不親政事，方隆好於音樂，以顯久典事，中人無外黨，精專可信任，遂委以政。
entries.en: Yuan was often ill and left state business aside while he lost himself in music. Shi Xian, long trusted in the palace, had no outside clique and seemed safe—so power passed to him.
entries.literal: At that time Emperor Yuan was afflicted with illness, did not personally handle government affairs, was then deeply fond of music; because Xian had long managed affairs, the inner attendants had no outside faction, were focused and trustworthy, and so government was entrusted to him.

entries.zh: 事無小大，因顯白決，貴幸傾朝，百僚皆敬事顯。
entries.en: Every decision, great or small, went through Shi Xian; the court leaned his way and every minister deferred to him.
entries.literal: Matters large and small were reported through Xian and decided; he was so honored and favored that he tilted the whole court, and the hundred officials all treated Xian with respect.

entries.zh: 顯為人巧慧習事，能探得人主微指，內深賊，持詭辯以中傷人，忤恨睚眥，輒被以危法。
entries.en: Shi Xian was clever, read the emperor's slightest wish, and nursed a vicious grudge: one cross word could bring a capital charge framed in legal jargon.
entries.literal: Xian was by nature clever and practiced at affairs, could probe the ruler's subtle intentions, was inwardly deep and vicious, held specious argument to wound others, and for resentment over the slightest squint he would trap them with fatal law.

entries.zh: 初元中，前將軍蕭望之及光祿大夫周堪、宗正劉更生皆給事中。
entries.en: During Chuyuan, Xiao Wangzhi, Zhou Kan, and Liu Gengsheng held joint appointments as palace attendants.
entries.literal: In the Chuyuan era, former general Xiao Wangzhi, grand counsellor of the household Zhou Kan, and director of the imperial clan Liu Gengsheng all held concurrent appointment as palace attendants.

entries.zh: 望之領尚書事，知顯專權邪辟，建白以為：「尚書百官之本，國家樞機，宜以通明公正處之。
entries.en: Xiao Wangzhi, heading the secretariat, saw Shi Xian's crooked monopoly and argued: "That office is the nerve center of government; it needs open, upright men.
entries.literal: Wangzhi headed secretariat affairs, knew Xian monopolized power in a crooked way, and submitted a memorial saying: "The secretariat is the root of the hundred offices and the pivot of the state; it should be staffed with enlightened, fair men.

entries.zh: 武帝游宴後庭，故用宦者，非古制也。
entries.en: Emperor Wu used eunuchs there because he banqueted in the inner palace—but that was never classical practice.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu roamed and feasted in the rear palace, therefore used eunuchs—this is not the ancient system.

entries.zh: 宜罷中書宦官，應古不近刑人。」
entries.en: Abolish eunuch secretaries and return to the old rule: do not keep the mutilated at the ruler's elbow."
entries.literal: The central secretariat eunuchs should be abolished, conforming to antiquity of not keeping mutilated men close."

entries.zh: 元帝不聽，由是大與顯忤。
entries.en: Yuan refused, and Xiao Wangzhi made a bitter enemy of Shi Xian.
entries.literal: Emperor Yuan did not listen, and from this he greatly opposed Xian.

entries.zh: 後皆害焉，望之自殺，堪、更生廢錮，不得復進用，語在《望之傳》。
entries.en: All were ruined: Xiao Wangzhi committed suicide; Zhou Kan and Liu Gengsheng were cashiered and blocked from office—the full story is in Wangzhi's biography.
entries.literal: Afterward they were all harmed: Wangzhi killed himself; Kan and Gengsheng were dismissed and barred from further advancement—the account is in the "Wangzhi" biography.

entries.zh: 後太中大夫張猛、魏郡太守京房、御史中丞陳咸、待詔賈捐之皆嘗奏封事，或召見，言顯短。
entries.en: Later Zhang Meng, Jing Fang, Chen Xian, and Jia Juanzhi memorialized or were called in to attack Shi Xian.
entries.literal: Later grand counsellor of the palace Zhang Meng, governor of Wei commandery Jing Fang, imperial secretary Chen Xian, and awaiting-orders Jia Juanzhi had all submitted sealed memorials or been summoned for audience to speak of Xian's faults.

entries.zh: 顯求索其罪，房、捐之棄市，猛自殺於公車，咸抵罪，髡為城旦。
entries.en: Shi Xian hunted charges: Jing Fang and Jia Juanzhi died in the market; Zhang Meng killed himself at the carriage park; Chen Xian was shorn and sentenced as corvée labor.
entries.literal: Xian sought out their crimes: Fang and Juanzhi were executed in the marketplace; Meng killed himself on the public carriage grounds; Chen Xian was convicted, shaved, and sentenced as wall dawn labor.

entries.zh: 及鄭令蘇建得顯私書奏之，後以它事論死。
entries.en: When Su Jian of Zheng presented a private letter from Shi Xian, he himself was later executed on another pretext.
entries.literal: When Magistrate of Zheng Su Jian obtained a private letter from Xian and presented it, he was later condemned to death on another charge.

entries.zh: 自是公卿以下畏顯，重足一跡。
entries.en: After that, from ministers downward, everyone feared Shi Xian and scarcely dared breathe.
entries.literal: From this the ministers down to the gentlemen were afraid of Xian, standing as if on one footprint.

entries.zh: 李延年，中山人，身及父母兄弟皆故倡也。
entries.en: Li Yannian of Zhongshan came from a family of professional performers.
entries.literal: Li Yannian was a man of Zhongshan; he and his parents and brothers had all been entertainers by profession.

entries.zh: 延年坐法腐刑，給事狗監中。
entries.en: Convicted, he was castrated and assigned to the imperial dog kennel.
entries.literal: Yannian was sentenced by law to castration and served in the dog kennel.

entries.zh: 女弟得幸於上，號李夫人，列《外戚傳》。
entries.en: His sister became Lady Li, a favorite—her story is in the "Consorts" chapter.
entries.literal: His younger sister won the sovereign's favor and was titled Lady Li; she is listed in the "Consorts" biography.

entries.zh: 延年善歌，為新變聲。
entries.en: He was a superb singer who devised new vocal styles.
entries.literal: Yannian was skilled at singing and created new, altered tones.

entries.zh: 是時，上方興天地祠，欲造樂，令司馬相如等作詩頌。
entries.en: Wu was founding state rituals to Heaven and Earth and wanted fresh ritual music; Sima Xiangru and others were told to supply hymn texts.
entries.literal: At that time the sovereign was promoting sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and wished to create music, ordering Sima Xiangru and others to compose verse for hymns.

entries.zh: 延年輒承意弦歌所造詩，為之新聲曲。
entries.en: Li Yannian set each new poem to melody and accompaniment.
entries.literal: Yannian would take the intent and set the newly composed poems to strings and song, making new musical settings for them.

entries.zh: 而李夫人產昌邑王，延年由是貴為協律都尉，佩二千石印綬，而與上臥起，其愛幸埒韓嫣。
entries.en: When Lady Li bore the king of Changyi, Yannian was made director of harmony with a two-thousand-picul seal, shared the emperor's intimacy, and matched Han Yan in favor.
entries.literal: And when Lady Li bore the king of Changyi, Yannian for this reason became noble as director of harmony, wore the seal and ribbon of two thousand piculs, slept and rose with the sovereign, and his favor rivaled Han Yan's.

entries.zh: 久之，延年弟季與中人亂，出入驕恣。
entries.en: In time his brother Ji took lovers among the eunuchs and swaggered through the palace.
entries.literal: After a long time Yannian's younger brother Ji consorted with palace attendants and came and went arrogant and unrestrained.

entries.zh: 及李夫人卒後，其愛弛，上遂誅延年兄弟宗族。
entries.en: After Lady Li's death his star faded; Wu executed Li Yannian and his whole clan.
entries.literal: When Lady Li died afterward, his favor slackened, and the sovereign executed Yannian's brothers and entire clan.

entries.zh: 石顯字君房，濟南人；
entries.en: Shi Xian, styled Junfang, was a native of Jinan;
entries.literal: Shi Xian, courtesy name Junfang, was a man of Jinan;

entries.zh: 弘恭，沛人也。
entries.en: Hong Gong came from Pei.
entries.literal: Hong Gong was a man of Pei.

entries.zh: 皆少坐法腐刑，為中黃門，以選為中尚書。
entries.en: Both were castrated for crimes in youth, entered as yellow-gate attendants, and were chosen for the central secretariat.
entries.literal: Both in youth were sentenced by law to castration and became attendants of the yellow gates, then by selection became secretaries of the central secretariat.

entries.zh: 宣帝時任中書官，恭明習法令故事，善為請奏，能稱其職。
entries.en: Under Xuandi they ran the inner chancellery; Hong Gong knew law and precedent cold and drafted petitions to perfection.
entries.literal: In Xuandi's time they held central secretariat posts; Gong was thoroughly versed in statutes and precedents, skilled at drafting memorials, and able to fill his office.

entries.zh: 恭為令，顯為僕射。
entries.en: Hong Gong was chief; Shi Xian, his deputy.
entries.literal: Gong was director; Xian was vice director.

entries.zh: 元帝即位數年，恭死，顯代為中書令。
entries.en: A few years into Yuan's reign Hong Gong died and Shi Xian became chief of the secretariat.
entries.literal: Several years after Emperor Yuan took the throne, Gong died and Xian replaced him as director of the central secretariat.

entries.zh: 卷九十三 佞幸傳第六十三
entries.en: Volume 93: "The Flatterers," the sixty-third biography.
entries.literal: Volume ninety-three: Biography of the Flatterers, the sixty-third.

entries.zh: 初，成帝性寬，進入直言，是以王音、翟方進等繩法舉過，而劉向、杜鄴、王章、朱雲之徒肆意犯上，故自帝師安昌侯，諸舅大將軍兄弟及公卿大夫、後宮外屬史許之家有貴寵者，莫不被文傷詆。
entries.en: Cheng's easy temper invited blunt speech, so ministers such as Wang Yin and Zhai Fangjin policed the law while scholars like Liu Xiang, Du Ye, Wang Zhang, and Zhu Yun flayed the throne; from the imperial tutor the marquis of Anchang through the Wang uncles and every powerful consort kin of the Shi and Xu lines, no favorite escaped their written attacks.
entries.literal: In the beginning, Emperor Cheng's nature was lenient, and those who entered remonstrated bluntly; therefore Wang Yin, Zhai Fangjin, and others applied the law and reported faults, while Liu Xiang, Du Ye, Wang Zhang, Zhu Yun, and their sort wantonly offended the throne; thus from the emperor's teacher the Marquis of Anchang down to the great uncles the grand general and his brothers, dukes, ministers, grandees, and the households of the rear-palace affines surnamed Shi and Xu who enjoyed favor and power, there was none who was not wounded by their writings and slandered.

entries.zh: 唯谷永嘗言「建始、河平之際，許、班之貴，傾動前朝，熏灼四方，賞賜無量，空虛內臧，女寵至極，不可尚矣；
entries.en: Only Gu Yong once said, "During the Jianshi and Heping eras, the eminence of the Xu and Ban houses shook the former court and blazed across the four quarters. Rewards and gifts were beyond measure; they emptied the inner treasury, and favor shown to women reached an unsurpassable extreme;
entries.literal: Only Gu Yong once said, "In the Jianshi and Heping era the eminence of the Xu and Ban houses shook the previous court, scorched the four quarters, and their gifts had no measure; they emptied the inner treasury; favor to women reached an extreme that could not be surpassed;

entries.zh: 今之後起，天所不饗，什倍於前。」
entries.en: while the new crop of favorites, heaven-rejected, would outdo them tenfold."
entries.literal: those who rise afterward, whom Heaven will not bless, are ten times what went before."

entries.zh: 永指以駮譏趙、李，亦無間云。
entries.en: He aimed the rebuke at Zhao Feiyan and Li Ping, yet commentators say no one could gainsay his point.
entries.literal: Yong pointed with this to refute and ridicule Zhao and Li, yet none could find fault with it, it is said.

entries.zh: 嗣雖修儒學，然貴老嚴之術。
entries.en: Ban Si pursued Confucian texts yet revered the Daoist teachings of Laozi and Yan Junping.
entries.literal: Although Si cultivated Confucian learning, he honored the arts of Laozi and Yan Junping.

entries.zh: 桓生欲借其書，嗣報曰：「若夫嚴子者，絕聖棄智，修生保真，清虛澹泊，歸之自然，獨師友造化，而不為世俗所役者也。
entries.en: When Huan Sheng wished to borrow his books, Ban Si replied, "As for Master Yan, he cut off sagehood and discarded cleverness, cultivated life and guarded the genuine, was clear, empty, and still, and returned to the natural; he took only creation as teacher and friend and was not enslaved by the vulgar world.
entries.literal: When Huan Sheng wished to borrow his books, Si replied, "As for Master Yan, he cut off sagehood and discarded cleverness, cultivated life and guarded the genuine, was clear, empty, and still, and returned to the natural; he took only creation as teacher and friend and was not enslaved by the vulgar world.

entries.zh: 漁釣於一壑，則萬物不奸其志；
entries.en: If he angled in one gully, then the myriad things could not corrupt his purpose;
entries.literal: If he angled in one gully, then the myriad things could not corrupt his purpose;

entries.zh: 栖遲於一丘，則天下不易其樂。
entries.en: if he rested on one hill, then all under Heaven could not alter his joy.
entries.literal: if he rested on one hill, then all under Heaven could not alter his joy.

entries.zh: 不絓聖人之罔，不齅驕君之餌，蕩然肆志，談者不得而名焉，故可貴也。
entries.en: Such a man never walked into the sages' snares or nibbled a proud king's hook; he wandered beyond labels, which is why he is worth imitating.
entries.literal: He was not caught in the nets of the sages, did not sniff at the bait of arrogant lords, roamed at will where talkers could not pin a name on him—therefore he was admirable.

entries.zh: 今吾子已貫仁誼之羈絆，繫名聲之韁鎖，伏周、孔之軌躅，馳顏、閔之極摯，既繫攣於世教矣，何用大道為自眩曜？
entries.en: Now you, sir, have already put on the fetters of benevolence and duty and tied yourself to the reins and locks of reputation. You crouch in the tracks of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius and race toward the utmost earnestness of Yan Hui and Min Ziqian; since you are already bound fast by worldly teaching, why use the great Way merely to dazzle yourself?
entries.literal: Now you, sir, have already passed through the hobbles of benevolence and duty, are tethered by the bridle of reputation, tread in the tracks of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, and gallop to the utmost earnestness of Yan and Min; you are already bound by worldly instruction—why use the great Way to dazzle yourself?

entries.zh: 昔有學步於邯鄲者。
entries.en: There was once a man who went to Handan to learn a new way of walking.
entries.literal: Formerly there was one who learned to walk in Handan.

entries.zh: 曾未得其髣彿，又復失其故步，遂匍匐而歸耳！
entries.en: Before mastering the strut he forgot his own walk and had to crawl home in shame.
entries.literal: Before he had grasped even a semblance of it, he again lost his native step, so he crawled home!

entries.zh: 恐似此類，故不進。」
entries.en: Lest your borrowing end the same way, I decline to lend the books."
entries.literal: I fear it would be like this sort of thing; therefore I do not advance them."

entries.zh: 嗣之行己持論如此。
entries.en: Such was Ban Si's conduct and the tone of his debate.
entries.literal: Thus Si conducted himself and framed his arguments.

entries.zh: 叔皮唯聖人之道然後盡心焉。
entries.en: Ban Biao reserved his full devotion for the path of the sages alone.
entries.literal: Shuipi devoted his whole heart only to the Way of the sages.

entries.zh: 年二十，遭王莽敗，世祖即位於冀州。
entries.en: At twenty he lived through Wang Mang's fall and watched Liu Xiu raise the Han banner in Ji.
entries.literal: At twenty he encountered Wang Mang's collapse, and the Founding Ancestor took the throne in Ji Province.

entries.zh: 時隗囂據壟擁眾，招輯英俊，而公孫述稱帝於蜀漢，天下雲擾，大者連州郡，小者據縣邑。
entries.en: Wei Xiao then blocked the Long road and recruited talent while Gongsun Shu styled himself emperor in Shu; the realm splintered into rival zones large and small.
entries.literal: At that time Wei Xiao held Long and gathered heroes, while Gongsun Shu declared himself emperor in Shu-Han; all under Heaven boiled like a cloud; the great linked commanderies and the small seized counties.

entries.zh: 囂問彪曰：「往者周亡，戰國並爭，天下分裂，數世然後乃定，其抑者從橫之事復起於今乎？
entries.en: Wei Xiao asked Ban Biao, "In former times when Zhou fell, the Warring States strove together and the realm split apart, and only after several generations was it settled—will the affairs of vertical and horizontal alliances rise again now,
entries.literal: Xiao asked Biao, "In former times when Zhou fell, the Warring States strove together, the realm split apart, and only after several generations was it settled—will the affairs of vertical and horizontal alliances rise again now?

entries.zh: 將承運迭興在於一人也？
entries.en: or will the received mandate pass in turn and concentrate in a single man?
entries.literal: Or will the received mandate pass in turn and concentrate in a single man?

entries.zh: 願先生論之。」
entries.en: He begged Ban Biao to give his reading."
entries.literal: I beg the master to discuss it."

entries.zh: 對曰：「周之廢興與漢異。
entries.en: He replied, "The decline and rise of Zhou differ from those of Han.
entries.literal: He replied, "The decline and rise of Zhou differ from those of Han.

entries.zh: 昔周立爵五等，諸侯從政，本根既微，枝葉強大，故其末流有從橫之事，其勢然也。
entries.en: Zhou had enfeoffed powerful barons whose branches overshadowed the crown, which is why the age of alliances followed inevitably.
entries.literal: In olden times Zhou established five ranks of nobles; the feudal lords administered government; the root was already weak while the branches grew mighty; therefore in its last currents there were vertical-and-horizontal intrigues—the tendency made it so.

entries.zh: 漢家承秦之制，並立郡縣，主有專己之威，臣無百年之柄，至於成帝，假借外家，哀、平短祚，國嗣三絕，危自上起，傷不及下。
entries.en: Han copied Qin's commandery system so the emperor kept iron control while ministers lacked hereditary leverage; down to Cheng the consort clans borrowed authority, Ai and Ping died young, the succession failed thrice, yet the rot started in the palace, not among the people.
entries.literal: The house of Han inherited Qin's system and set up commanderies and counties together; the ruler holds unchecked personal authority and ministers lack handles that last a century; down to Emperor Cheng the outer families were lent power, Ai and Ping enjoyed short reigns, the imperial succession failed three times, the danger began at the top, and harm did not reach below.

entries.zh: 故王氏之貴，傾擅朝廷，能竊號位，而不根於民。
entries.en: Thus the Wangs could bully the court and seize the throne in name, but they never sank roots in the common folk.
entries.literal: Therefore the eminence of the Wang house dominated the court and could usurp titles and the mandate, yet it struck no root among the people.

entries.zh: 是以即真之後，天下莫不引領而歎，十餘年間，外內騷擾，遠近俱發，假號雲合，咸稱劉氏，不謀而同辭。
entries.en: Once Wang Mang mounted the throne as emperor, the realm looked on with clenched throats; within a decade rebellion boiled inside the borders and out, every quarter flew false Liu banners, and men who had never conspired used the same slogan.
entries.literal: Therefore after he took the true throne, none under Heaven failed to crane their necks and sigh; within a dozen years disturbance raged within and without, near and far rose together, false titles swarmed like clouds, all called themselves Liu, and without planning they spoke with one voice.

entries.zh: 方今雄桀帶州城者，皆無七國世業之資。
entries.en: Today's strongmen who sit on walled prefectures command none of the old Warring States' hereditary depth.
entries.literal: Now those heroic men who hold commanderies and cities all lack the inherited capital of the Seven States.

entries.zh: 詩云：『皇矣上帝，臨下有赫，鑒觀四方，求民之莫。』
entries.en: As the Greater Odes put it: 'Sublime is God on high, terrible in His gaze across the realm, searching out where the people may find peace.'
entries.literal: The Odes say: 'August indeed is God on high, awesome as He looks down; He surveys the four quarters and seeks the people's rest.'

entries.zh: 今民皆謳吟思漢，鄉仰劉氏，已可知矣。」
entries.en: The folk already sing of their longing for Han and lift their eyes to the Liu name, which tells you all you need to know."
entries.literal: Now the people all chant and sigh, thinking of Han and yearning for the Liu house—this can already be known."

entries.zh: 囂曰：「先生言周、漢之勢，可也，至於但見愚民習識劉氏姓號之故，而謂漢家復興，疏矣！
entries.en: Wei Xiao said, "What you say, sir, about the tendencies of Zhou and Han is acceptable, but to infer from the mere fact that foolish commoners are habituated to the Liu surname that the house of Han will rise again is far too loose!
entries.literal: Xiao said, "What you say, sir, about the tendencies of Zhou and Han is acceptable, but to infer from the mere fact that foolish commoners are habituated to the Liu surname that the house of Han will rise again is far too loose!

entries.zh: 昔秦失其鹿，劉季逐而掎之，時民復知漢虖！」
entries.en: In olden times Qin lost the deer, and Liu Ji chased and seized it—did the people then even know there would be a Han?"
entries.literal: In olden times Qin lost the deer, and Liu Ji chased and seized it—did the people then even know there would be a Han?"

entries.zh: 既感囂言，又愍狂狡之不息，乃著王命論以救時難。
entries.en: Half persuaded by Wei Xiao yet sick of endless adventurism, Ban Biao drafted the Discourse on the King's Mandate to steady a chaotic age.
entries.literal: Having been moved by Xiao's words and also pitying that wild cunning would not cease, he thereupon composed the Discourse on the King's Mandate to rescue the troubles of the age.

entries.zh: 其辭曰：
entries.en: The text runs as follows:
entries.literal: Its words say:

entries.zh: 昔在帝堯之禪曰：「咨爾舜，天之曆數在爾躬。」
entries.en: When Emperor Yao yielded the throne he said, "Shun, the numbered seasons of Heaven now sit on you."
entries.literal: In olden times, at Yao's abdication it was said, "Ah, you Shun, Heaven's reckoned succession rests in your person."

entries.zh: 舜亦以命禹。
entries.en: Shun passed the same charge to Yu.
entries.literal: Shun also used these words to command Yu.

entries.zh: 臮于稷𢍆，咸佐唐虞，光濟四海，奕世載德，至于湯武，而有天下。
entries.en: Through ministers such as Hou Ji and Xie the virtue of Yao and Shun spread across the seas, generation on generation, until Tang of Shang and Wu of Zhou inherited the whole realm.
entries.literal: Down to Ji and Xie, all assisted Tang and Yu, their brilliance aiding the four seas; age after age they bore accumulated virtue, down to Tang and Wu, and thus possessed all under Heaven.

entries.zh: 雖其遭遇異時，禪代不同，至于應天順民，其揆一也。
entries.en: Their circumstances and transfers of power varied, yet each case matched Heaven's will and the people's heart in the same way.
entries.literal: Although their encounters differed in time and abdication differed in form, as for responding to Heaven and following the people, the measure was one.

entries.zh: 是故劉氏承堯之祚，氏族之世，著乎春秋。
entries.en: The Liu lineage thus continued Yao's mandate, a pedigree the Spring and Autumn Annals already recorded.
entries.literal: Therefore the Liu house received Yao's blessing, and the generations of the clan are set down in the Spring and Autumn Annals.

entries.zh: 唐據火德，而漢紹之，始起沛澤，則神母夜號，以章赤帝之符。
entries.en: Emperor Yao held the virtue of Fire, and Han succeeded it; when it first arose in the Pei marshes, the divine mother cried out in the night to manifest the token of the Red Emperor.
entries.literal: Tang held the virtue of Fire, and Han succeeded it; when it first arose in Pei marsh, the divine mother cried out in the night to manifest the token of the Red Emperor.

entries.zh: 由是言之，帝王之祚，必有明聖顯懿之德，豐功厚利積絫之業，然後精誠通於神明，流澤加於生民，故能為鬼神所福饗，天下所歸往，未見運世無本，功德不紀，而得屈起在此位者也。
