entries.en: Guo Tai happened to be at the academy that day; shamed by his own earlier pledge, Zuo Yuan abandoned the plot.
entries.literal: That day Linzong was at the school; Yuan felt ashamed of having betrayed his earlier words, and therefore desisted and left.

entries.zh: 後事露，衆人咸謝服焉。
entries.en: When the plot came to light, the community acknowledged Guo Tai's foresight with gratitude.
entries.literal: Later when the affair was exposed, everyone thanked him and submitted to him.

entries.zh: 郭太字林宗，
entries.en: Guo Tai, whose courtesy name was Linzong,
entries.literal: Guo Tai, style name Linzong,

entries.zh: 〈范曄父名泰，故改爲此「太」。
entries.en: 〈(Because Fan Ye's father was named Tai, the historian renders the name with this character "tai" instead.
entries.literal: 〈(Fan Ye's father was named Tai, so [the text] was changed to this character "tai".

entries.zh: 鄭公業之名亦同焉。〉
entries.en: The same substitution applies to the name of Zheng Gongye.)〉
entries.literal: Zheng Gongye's name was handled in the same way.)〉

entries.zh: 太原界休人也。
entries.en: He came from Jiexiu in Taiyuan commandery.
entries.literal: He was a man of Jiexiu in Taiyuan commandery.

entries.zh: 〈介休，今汾州縣。〉
entries.en: 〈(Present-day Jiexiu is Fenzhou county.)〉
entries.literal: 〈(Jiexiu is now Fenzhou county.)〉

entries.zh: 家世貧賤。
entries.en: His family was poor and of humble station.
entries.literal: His family background was poor and lowly.

entries.zh: 早孤，母欲使給事縣廷。
entries.en: Orphaned while still young, he was to be put to clerking in the county offices—his mother's plan.
entries.literal: He was orphaned early; his mother wished to have him serve in the county yamen.

entries.zh: 〈《蒼頡篇》曰：「廷，直也。」
entries.en: 〈(The Cangjie Pian glosses the graph: "ting means straight."
entries.literal: 〈(The Cangjie Pian says: "ting means straight."

entries.zh: 《說文》：「廷，朝中也。」
entries.en: The Shuowen defines it: "ting is the court's center."
entries.literal: The Shuowen: "ting means in the midst of court."

entries.zh: 《風俗通》：「廷，正也。
entries.en: The Fengsu Tong adds: "ting means upright.
entries.literal: The Fengsu Tong: "ting means correct.

entries.zh: 言縣廷、郡廷、朝廷，皆取平均正直也。」〉
entries.en: Thus county courts, commandery courts, and the imperial court all draw on the sense of fairness and rectitude.")〉
entries.literal: Speaking of county yamen, commandery yamen, and court—all take the sense of even, straight, and upright.")〉

entries.zh: 林宗曰：「大丈夫焉能處斗筲之役乎？」
entries.en: Linzong replied: "Would a man of stature tie himself to mean clerk's work—fit for a peck basket and dipper?"
entries.literal: Linzong said: "How can a great man occupy the service of a peck-and-dipper's measure?"

entries.zh: 遂辭。
entries.en: —and refused the post.
entries.literal: Thereupon he declined.

entries.zh: 就成皐屈伯彥學，三年業畢，博通墳籍。
entries.en: He went to Chenggao to study under Qu Boyan; three years later he had mastered the curriculum and could move fluently through the classics.
entries.literal: He then studied with Qu Boyan of Chenggao; after three years his course was finished, and he was broadly conversant with the canonical texts.

entries.zh: 善談論，美音制。
entries.en: He excelled at discourse, and his voice and bearing commanded attention.
entries.literal: He was skilled in discussion and had a fine voice and deportment.

entries.zh: 乃游於洛陽。
entries.en: He set out for Luoyang.
entries.literal: He then travelled to Luoyang.

entries.zh: 始見河南尹李膺，膺大竒之，遂相友善，於是名震京師。
entries.en: On his first meeting with Li Ying, the governor of Henan, Ying saw something remarkable in him; the two became fast friends, and Guo Tai's name soon resounded through the capital.
entries.literal: When he first met Governor of Henan Li Ying, Ying thought him extraordinary; they became close friends, and thereafter his name shook the capital.

entries.zh: 後歸鄉里，衣冠諸儒送至河上，車數千兩。
entries.en: When he went home, gowned scholars turned out in force to see him to the river—thousands of carriages lined the way.
entries.literal: Later he returned to his home district; the gentry and scholars escorted him to the river—several thousand carriages.

entries.zh: 林宗唯與李膺同舟而濟，衆賔望之，以爲神仙焉。
entries.en: Linzong alone boarded a boat with Li Ying; the crowd on the bank watched the pair cross as if they were watching immortals.
entries.literal: Linzong alone crossed in one boat with Li Ying; the assembled guests gazed after them and thought them immortals.

entries.zh: 時國政多失，內官專寵，李膺、杜密等為黨事考逮。
entries.en: The government was adrift, eunuchs held unchecked favor, and men such as Li Ying and Du Mi were rounded up in the partisan prosecutions.
entries.literal: At that time state policy had many errors, inner officials monopolized favor, and Li Ying, Du Mi, and others were examined and arrested on account of the partisan affair.

entries.zh: 永康元年，上疏諫曰：「臣聞明主不諱譏刺之言，以探幽暗之實；
entries.en: In 167 CE Dou Wu presented a memorial of remonstrance: "I have heard that a wise ruler does not shrink from pointed criticism, so as to learn what is hidden in the dark;
entries.literal: In the first year of Yongkang, he submitted a memorial remonstrating, saying: "I have heard that a bright ruler does not shun words of reproof and satire, in order to probe the truth of what is hidden and dark;

entries.zh: 忠臣不卹諫爭之患，以暢萬端之事。
entries.en: and that a loyal minister does not fear the harm that comes from remonstrance, so that every matter may be fully aired.
entries.literal: a loyal minister does not spare himself the peril of remonstrance and dispute, in order to set forth fully the myriad affairs of state.

entries.zh: 是以君臣並熙，名奮百世。
entries.en: Thus ruler and minister prosper together, and their fame endures for generations.
entries.literal: Hence ruler and minister together flourish, and their fame blazes for a hundred generations.

entries.zh: 臣幸得遭盛明之世，逢文武之化，豈敢懷祿逃罪，不竭其誠！
entries.en: I have been blessed to live in a glorious age and to meet the civilizing influence of Wen and Wu—how could I cling to office, evade blame, and withhold my utmost loyalty!
entries.literal: I have been fortunate to encounter an age of great brilliance and to meet the civilizing influence of Wen and Wu—how would I dare cling to salary and flee from blame, and not exhaust my sincerity!

entries.zh: 陛下初從藩國，爰登聖祚，天下逸豫，謂當中興。
entries.en: Your Majesty rose from a princely domain to the throne; the realm rejoiced and looked for a renewal of Han.
entries.literal: Your Majesty at first came from a feudal state and then ascended the sacred throne; the realm was at ease and delighted, and all believed there would be restoration.

entries.zh: 自即位以來，未聞善政。
entries.en: Yet since your accession I have heard of no worthy policy.
entries.literal: Since taking the throne, I have not heard of good government.

entries.zh: 梁、孫、寇、鄧雖或誅滅，而常侍黃門續為禍虐，欺罔陛下，競行譎詐，自造制度，妄爵非人，朝政日衰，姦臣日彊。
entries.en: Liang Ji, Sun Shou, Kou Rong, and Deng Wan may have been destroyed, but the eunuchs still bring ruin: they deceive Your Majesty, vie in deceit, invent their own rules, ennoble unworthy men, and day by day court government rots while wicked ministers grow stronger.
entries.literal: Liang, Sun, Kou, and Deng were perhaps executed and destroyed, yet the regular palace attendants and yellow-gate officials continue as agents of calamity and cruelty, deceiving Your Majesty, competing in treachery and fraud, inventing regulations on their own, enfeoffing unworthy men, so that court government daily declines and wicked ministers daily grow strong.

entries.zh: 伏尋西京放恣王氏，佞臣執政，終喪天下。
entries.en: I reflect on how the Wang clan ran wild in the Western Capital, how sycophants seized power, and how the dynasty was lost.
entries.literal: I bow and recall how in the Western Capital the Wang clan was indulged without restraint, flatterers held government, and in the end the realm was lost.

entries.zh: 今不慮前事之失，復循覆車之軌，臣恐二世之難，必將復及，趙高之變，不朝則夕。
entries.en: Now, heedless of past failures, the court again follows the road of the overturned cart; I fear a Second Emperor catastrophe will return, and a Zhao Gao-style coup may come overnight.
entries.literal: Now, without considering the errors of former affairs, you again follow the track of an overturned cart; I fear the calamity of the Second Emperor will surely come again, and a change like Zhao Gao's may arrive not in the morning but by evening.

entries.zh: 近者姦臣牢脩，造設黨議，遂收前司隸校尉李膺、太僕杜密、御史中丞陳翔、太尉掾范滂等逮考，連及數百人，曠年拘錄，事無效驗。
entries.en: Recently the villain Lao Xiu invented the partisan prosecutions; Li Ying, Du Mi, Chen Xiang, Fan Pang, and hundreds more were seized and held for years without a shred of proof.
entries.literal: Recently the wicked minister Lao Xiu fabricated the partisan prosecution; then the former metropolitan commandant Li Ying, grand coachman Du Mi, imperial censor Chen Xiang, and grand commandant aide Fan Pang and others were seized and examined, implicating several hundred men; for years they have been detained and recorded, yet the affair has yielded no proof.

entries.zh: 臣惟膺等建忠抗節，志經王室，此誠陛下稷、党、伊、呂之佐，而虛為姦臣賊子之所誣枉，天下寒心，海內失望。
entries.en: Li Ying and his fellows have shown loyal resolve and devotion to the royal house—they are truly ministers in the mold of Ji, Xie, Yi, and Lü—yet wicked men have falsely accused them; the realm is heartsick and the empire has lost hope.
entries.literal: I consider that Ying and the others established loyalty and upheld integrity, their will fixed on sustaining the royal house; they are truly Your Majesty's helpers like Ji, Xie, Yi, and Lü, yet they have been falsely slandered by wicked ministers and villainous sons; the realm is chilled at heart, and within the seas all are disappointed.

entries.zh: 惟陛下留神澄省，時見理出，以厭人鬼喁喁之心。
entries.en: I beg Your Majesty to attend carefully, judge clearly, and release the innocent in time, so that the murmuring hearts of men and spirits may be stilled.
entries.literal: May Your Majesty keep your mind attentive, clarify and examine, and in due time bring forth justice, so as to satisfy the murmuring hearts of men and ghosts alike.

entries.zh: 臣聞古之明君，必須賢佐，以成政道。
entries.en: I have heard that wise rulers of old always needed worthy aides to govern well.
entries.literal: I have heard that the bright rulers of antiquity necessarily required worthy assistants to complete the way of government.

entries.zh: 今臺閣近臣，尚書令陳蕃，僕射胡廣，尚書朱宇、荀緄、劉祐、魏朗、劉矩、尹勳等，皆國之貞士，朝之良佐。
entries.en: Among the ministers at court today—Director Chen Fan, Vice Director Hu Guang, and the secretaries Zhu Yu, Xun Gun, Liu You, Wei Lang, Liu Ju, and Yin Xun—are upright servants of the state and able aides of the court.
entries.literal: Now among the close ministers of the Secretariat, Director Chen Fan, Vice Director Hu Guang, and Ministers Zhu Yu, Xun Gun, Liu You, Wei Lang, Liu Ju, Yin Xun, and others are all upright men of the state and fine assistants of the court.

entries.zh: 尚書郎張陵、媯皓、苑康、楊喬、邊韶、戴恢等，文質彬彬，明達國典。
entries.en: Secretariat gentlemen such as Zhang Ling, Gui Hao, Yuan Kang, Yang Qiao, Bian Shao, and Dai Hui combine learning and integrity and know the laws of the realm.
entries.literal: Secretariat gentlemen Zhang Ling, Gui Hao, Yuan Kang, Yang Qiao, Bian Shao, Dai Hui, and others are refined in both literary and substantive virtue and clearly understand the statutes of the state.

entries.zh: 內外之職，群才並列。
entries.en: Within the palace and without, talented men stand ready in every office.
entries.literal: Within and without, offices are filled with many talents arrayed together.

entries.zh: 而陛下委任近習，專樹饕餮，外典州郡，內幹心膂。
entries.en: Yet Your Majesty entrusts power to cronies and raises greedy parasites who rule the provinces abroad and meddle in the vital organs of government at court.
entries.literal: Yet Your Majesty entrusts power to close favorites, exclusively raising gluttonous beasts: abroad they govern provinces and commanderies, within they meddle in the heart and sinews of state.

entries.zh: 宜以次貶黜，案罪糾罰，抑奪宦官欺國之封，案其無狀誣罔之罪，信任忠良，平決臧否，使邪正毀譽，各得其所，寶愛天官，唯善是授。
entries.en: They should be demoted in turn, their crimes prosecuted, the eunuchs' illicit fiefs stripped away, and their false accusations punished; trust the loyal, judge merit and fault fairly, let the wicked and upright each receive their due, and honor the offices of state by granting them only to the worthy.
entries.literal: They ought to be demoted and dismissed in due order; crimes should be investigated and punished; the enfeoffments by which eunuchs deceive the state should be suppressed and seized; their baseless crimes of false accusation should be prosecuted; the loyal and good should be trusted; merit and fault should be judged fairly, so that the wicked and upright, whether praised or blamed, each receive what is due; treasure and honor the offices of Heaven, and grant them only to the worthy.

entries.zh: 如此，咎徵可消，天應可待。
entries.en: Then ominous signs may fade and Heaven's blessing may follow.
entries.literal: If this is done, ominous signs may be dispelled and Heaven's favorable response may be awaited.

entries.zh: 閒者有嘉禾、芝草、黃龍之見。
entries.en: Recently there have been reports of auspicious grain, lingzhi fungus, and yellow dragons.
entries.literal: Recently there have been sightings of auspicious grain, lingzhi fungus, and yellow dragons.

entries.zh: 夫瑞生必於嘉士，福至實由善人，在德為瑞，無德為災。
entries.en: Omens appear only where worthy men dwell; blessings truly come from the good—with virtue they are auspicious, without virtue they are calamity.
entries.literal: Auspicious omens arise only where there are worthy men; blessings in truth come from good men—with virtue they are omens, without virtue they are disasters.

entries.zh: 陛下所行，不合天意，不宜稱慶。」
entries.en: Your Majesty's conduct does not accord with Heaven's will; there is no cause for celebration."
entries.literal: What Your Majesty has done does not accord with Heaven's will; it is not fitting to proclaim celebration."

entries.zh: 竇武字游平，扶風平陵人，安豐戴侯融之玄孫也。
entries.en: Dou Wu, styled Youping, came from Pingling in Fufeng; he was a fourth-generation descendant of Dou Rong, Marquis Dai of Anfeng.
entries.literal: Dou Wu, courtesy name Youping, was a native of Pingling in Fufeng, and was the great-great-grandson of the Marquis Dai of Anfeng, Dou Rong.

entries.zh: 父奉，定襄太守。
entries.en: His father Dou Feng had served as governor of Dingxiang.
entries.literal: His father was Dou Feng, governor of Dingxiang.

entries.zh: 武少以經行著稱，常教授於大澤中，不交時事，名顯關西。
entries.en: From his youth Dou Wu was known for scholarship and upright conduct; he taught students amid the wetlands, kept clear of politics, and his reputation spread through the Guanxi region.
entries.literal: In youth Wu was renowned for his classical learning and conduct; he often taught in great marshlands, did not involve himself in current affairs, and his name was illustrious west of the passes.

entries.zh: 時，靈帝政化衰缺，四方兵寇，焉以為刺史威輕，既不能禁，且用非其人，輒增暴亂，乃建議改置牧伯，鎮安方夏，清選重臣，以居其任。
entries.en: Under Emperor Ling government faltered and rebellion spread. Liu Yan argued that provincial inspectors lacked real authority—unable to keep order, and that wrong appointments only bred more chaos—so he urged installing chief administrators over the regions to stabilize the empire and staffing those offices with senior, carefully chosen ministers.
entries.literal: At that time Emperor Ling's governance was decaying and flawed; armed bandits arose on every side. Yan held that the inspectors' authority was light: they could neither restrain trouble, and when the wrong men were appointed, violence only increased. He therefore proposed replacing them with regional shepherds, to pacify the realm, and selecting eminent ministers of proven weight to fill those posts.

entries.zh: 焉乃陰求為交阯，以避時難。
entries.en: He quietly angled for a posting to Jiaozhi, hoping to ride out the turmoil at a distance.
entries.literal: Yan then secretly sought appointment to Jiaozhi, to escape the troubles of the age.

entries.zh: 議未即行，會益州刺史郗儉在政煩擾，謠言遠聞，而并州刺史張懿、涼州刺史耿鄙並為寇賊所害，故焉議得用。
entries.en: Before the reform could take effect, Yi Province's Inspector Xi Jian had drawn widespread complaint for his harsh rule, while the inspectors of Bing and Liang, Zhang Yi and Geng Bi, had both fallen to rebels—circumstances that finally won acceptance for Liu Yan's proposal.
entries.literal: The proposal had not yet been carried out when Inspector Xi Jian of Yi Province proved vexatious in administration and rumors of it spread far; moreover Inspectors Zhang Yi of Bing and Geng Bi of Liang were both killed by bandits, so Yan's plan was adopted.

entries.zh: 出焉為監軍使者，領益州牧，太僕黃琬為豫州牧，宗正劉虞為幽州牧，皆以本秩居職。
entries.en: Liu Yan was named military overseer and shepherd of Yi Province, Huang Wan grand coachman and shepherd of Yu, and Liu Yu minister of the imperial clan and shepherd of You, each continuing at his former nominal grade.
entries.literal: Yan was sent out as Military Overseer and Envoy and appointed shepherd of Yi Province; Grand Coachman Huang Wan became shepherd of Yu Province; Minister of the Imperial Clan Liu Yu became shepherd of You Province; each held office at his existing salary rank.

entries.zh: 州任之重，自此而始。
entries.en: From that moment the office of provincial shepherd carried real power.
entries.literal: The weight of responsibility for a province began from this.

entries.zh: 劉焉字君郎，江夏竟陵人也，魯恭王後也。
entries.en: Liu Yan, styled Junlang, came from Jingling in Jiangxia and traced his line to Prince Gong of Lu.
entries.literal: Liu Yan, courtesy name Junlang, was a man of Jingling in Jiangxia, and a descendant of Prince Gong of Lu.

entries.zh: 肅宗時，徙竟陵。
entries.en: Under Emperor Suzong his clan was moved to Jingling.
entries.literal: In the time of Emperor Suzong, the family was relocated to Jingling.

entries.zh: 焉少任州郡，以宗室拜郎中。
entries.en: As a young man he served in provincial posts and, by virtue of his imperial lineage, received appointment as a Gentleman of the Palace.
entries.literal: In youth Yan held office in the provinces and commanderies, and as a member of the imperial clan was appointed Gentleman of the Palace.

entries.zh: 去官居陽城山，精學教授。
entries.en: He resigned, withdrew to Mount Yangcheng, pursued scholarship in earnest, and lectured to students.
entries.literal: Leaving office, he dwelt on Mount Yangcheng, devoted himself to study, and taught.

entries.zh: 舉賢良方正，稍遷南陽太守、宗正、太常。
entries.en: Recommended as an outstanding candidate for honest and upright conduct, he rose step by step to governor of Nanyang, minister for the imperial clan, and minister of ceremonies.
entries.literal: Recommended as Worthy and Good, Honest and Upright, he was gradually promoted to Governor of Nanyang, Minister of the Imperial Clan, and Minister of Ceremonies.

entries.zh: 和帝時，稍遷桂陽太守。
entries.en: Under Emperor He he rose to Guiyang governor.
entries.literal: Under Emperor He he was gradually promoted governor of Guiyang.

entries.zh: 郡濱南州，風俗脆薄，不識學義。
entries.en: Southern Guiyang was shallow in learning.
entries.literal: The commandery bordered the southern provinces—custom flimsy and thin—not knowing study and righteousness.

entries.zh: 荆爲設丧纪婚姻制度，使知禮禁。
entries.en: He codified funerals and weddings.
entries.literal: Jing established mourning and marriage regulations—letting them know ritual prohibitions.

entries.zh: 嘗行春到耒陽縣，人有蒋均者，兄弟爭財，互相言訟。
entries.en: At Leiyang the Jiang brothers sued over inheritance.
entries.literal: Once on spring circuit he reached Leiyang county—a man Jiang Jun—brothers quarreling over property—mutually sued.

entries.zh: 荆對之嘆曰：“吾荷國重任，而教化不行，咎在太守。”
entries.en: He blamed his own teaching for their quarrel.
entries.literal: Jing sighed at them: "I bear the state's heavy charge—yet transformation does not proceed—the fault lies with the governor."

entries.zh: 乃顾使吏上書陳狀，乞詣廷尉。
entries.en: He ordered a report draft requesting his own impeachment.
entries.literal: Thereupon turned ordering clerks memorialize status—begging to go to the minister of justice.

entries.zh: 均兄弟感悔，各求受罪。
entries.en: The brothers begged punishment instead.
entries.literal: Jun brothers felt shame—each sought punishment.

entries.zh: 在事十二年，父老稱歌。
entries.en: Twelve years brought folk songs.
entries.literal: Twelve years in office—elders sang praise.

entries.zh: 以病自上，征拜諫議大夫，卒于官。
entries.en: He retired reporting illness, became remonstrance counselor, died there.
entries.literal: Illness submitted upward—summoned remonstrance counselor—died in office.

entries.zh: 桂陽人爲立廟树碑。
entries.en: Guiyang built him temple and stone.
entries.literal: Guiyang people raised temple and stele.

entries.zh: 悼惠王子孝王將閭，將閭少子封牟平侯，子孫家焉。
entries.en: Filial Prince Jianglü, son of Prince Dao Hui, enfeoffed a youngest son as marquis of Muping, and the line settled there.
entries.literal: Prince Dao Hui's son Filial Prince Jianglü—Jianglü's youngest son was enfeoffed as marquis of Muping, and descendants settled there.

entries.zh: 父㔻，博學，號爲通儒。
entries.en: His father Liu Shi was famed as a polymath and called a thorough Confucian.
entries.literal: His father Shi was broadly learned and called a thorough Confucian.

entries.zh: 初，光武長于民間，頗達情僞，見稼穡艱難，百姓病害，至天下已定，務用安靜，解王莽之繁密，還漢世之輕法。
entries.en: Emperor Guangwu had been raised among ordinary folk, so he grasped what was real and what was not, and he had watched tillers suffer and the people sicken. Once the empire was his, he pursued calm government: he loosened Wang Mang’s suffocating code and brought back the Han tradition of relatively mild punishments.
entries.literal: Earlier, Guangwu had grown up among the common people and was fairly versed in true and false; he had seen the hardship of farming and the ills of the people. When the realm was finally settled, he strove for quiet rule, undid Wang Mang’s tangled severity, and restored the Han era’s lighter laws.

entries.zh: 身衣大練，色無重綵，耳不聽鄭、衛之音，手不持珠玉之玩，宫房無私爱，左右無偏恩。
entries.en: He dressed in single layers of homespun, shunned gaudy dyes, shut out the licentious airs of Zheng and Wei, and kept his hands from jeweled playthings. He showed no private infatuation in the harem and no uneven favor to attendants.
entries.literal: He personally wore thick plain silk; his garb held no doubled colors. His ears did not listen to the music of Zheng and Wei; his hands did not hold jade and pearl trinkets. The inner palace had no private favorites; those at his side received no lopsided grace.

entries.zh: 建武十三年，異國有獻名馬者，日行千里，又進寶劒，賈兼百金，詔以馬駕鼓車，劒賜騎士。
entries.en: In 37 a tributary state sent a thousand-li stallion and a blade worth a hundred catties of gold; the court hitched the horse to the ritual drum cart and gave the sword to a cavalryman instead of hoarding both.
entries.literal: In the thirteenth Jianwu year, a foreign land presented a famous horse that could travel a thousand in a day; it also offered a precious sword worth a hundredweight of gold. An edict used the horse to pull the drum cart and bestowed the sword on a horseman.

entries.zh: 損上林池籞之官，廢騁望弋獵之事。
entries.en: He cut keepers of the imperial parks and put an end to pleasure hunts and hawking.
entries.literal: He reduced the posts for Shanglin’s pools and preserves and abolished the business of coursing, gazing, and fowling for sport.

entries.zh: 其以手迹賜方國者，皆一札十行，細書成文。
entries.en: Letters to regional rulers were compact—one slip, ten lines, in his own tight hand.
entries.literal: Those to whom he granted his own hand to vassal states all received a single tablet of ten lines, fine script forming the text.

entries.zh: 勤約之風，行于上下。
entries.en: Thrift and restraint ran from the throne to the clerks.
entries.literal: Diligent frugality’s wind ran through high and low.

entries.zh: 數引公卿郎將，列于禁坐。
entries.en: He regularly called nobles, ministers, and generals to sit in the privy audience.
entries.literal: He often summoned ministers, counselors, and generals, arraying them in the inner seat.

entries.zh: 廣求民瘼，觀納風謠。
entries.en: He asked after popular hardship and listened to local ballads and complaints.
entries.literal: He broadly sought the people’s ailments and looked to take in the songs and laments of custom.

entries.zh: 故能内外匪懈，百姓寬息。
entries.en: So court and countryside stayed alert in duty, while commoners could breathe again.
entries.literal: Therefore inside and outside none slacked; the common people were relaxed and at rest.

entries.zh: 自臨宰邦邑者，競能其官。
entries.en: Local magistrates, for their part, rivaled one another in competence.
entries.literal: As for those who personally governed districts and cities, vied in fulfilling their office.

entries.zh: 若杜詩守南陽，號爲“杜母”，任延、錫光移變邊俗，斯其績用之最章章者也。
entries.en: Du Shi in Nanyang was nicknamed the “Nourishing Mother”; Ren Yan and Xi Guang transformed borderlands—their records stand out clearest among model officials.
entries.literal: Such as Du Shi guarding Nanyang, called “Mother Du”; Ren Yan and Xi Guang remade frontier custom—these are the most shining examples of their achievement and ability.

entries.zh: 又第五倫、宋均之徒，亦足有可稱談。
entries.en: The likes of Di Lun and Song Jun likewise deserve a word.
entries.literal: Also men like Di Lun and Song Jun are enough to merit mention in discussion.

entries.zh: 然建武、永平之間，吏事刻深，亟以謠言單辭，轉易守長。
entries.en: Still, in the Jianwu–Yongping years governance turned harsh: one whisper or isolated accusation could cost a magistrate his post.
entries.literal: Yet between Jianwu and Yongping, official business was severe and cutting; on slight rumor or single testimony, magistrates were often replaced.

entries.zh: 故朱浮數上諫書，箴切峻政，鍾離意等亦規諷殷勤，以長者爲言，而不能得也。
entries.en: Zhu Fu repeatedly protested the severity; Zhongli Yi and others pressed the same in careful language—useless against the trend.
entries.literal: Therefore Zhu Fu several times presented remonstrance, needling the harsh government; Zhongli Yi and others also earnestly counseled in oblique remonstrance, pleading the example of the elder sort—yet they could not prevail.

entries.zh: 所以中興之美，蓋未盡焉。
entries.en: The “restored golden age” therefore remains imperfect.
entries.literal: So the beauty of the restoration is probably not complete.

entries.zh: 自章、和以後，其有善績者，徃徃不絕。
entries.en: After the Zhangde and Yonghe reigns, capable magistrates kept appearing.
entries.literal: From Zhang and He onward, those with good records have never ceased to appear.

entries.zh: 如魯恭、吳祐、劉寬及潁川四長，並以仁信篤誠，使人不欺；
entries.en: Lu Gong, Wu You, Liu Kuan, and the Yingchuan quartet ruled so honestly that people stopped lying to one another.
entries.literal: Such as Lu Gong, Wu You, Liu Kuan, and the “four elders” of Yingchuan—all by benevolence, trust, and earnest good faith made men cease to deceive one another.

entries.zh: 王堂、陳寵委任賢良，而職事自理：斯皆可以感物而行化也。
entries.en: Wang Tang and Chen Chong delegated to talent and let affairs run themselves—they too transformed their jurisdictions.
entries.literal: Wang Tang and Chen Chong entrusted office to worthy men, and business ordered itself—these too could move things and carry transformation.

entries.zh: 邊鳳、延篤先後爲京兆尹，時人以辈前世趙、張。
entries.en: Bian Feng and Yan Du, one after the other as governors of the capital, were likened to the legendary Zhao and Zhang of old.
entries.literal: Bian Feng and Yan Du successively served as metropolitan governor; men of the age bracketed them with the Zhao and Zhang of earlier generations.

entries.zh: 又王渙、任峻之爲洛陽令，明發姦伏，吏端禁止，然導德劉禮，有所未充，亦一時之良能也。
entries.en: Wang Huan and Ren Jun as Luoyang magistrates exposed crime and kept clerks honest; moral instruction through ritual still fell short of the ideal, yet they ranked among the best of their time.
entries.literal: Further Wang Huan and Ren Jun as magistrates of Luoyang laid bare hidden villainy; clerks stood straight and prohibitions held—yet in guiding virtue through ritual propriety something still fell short; still they were capable officers of their day.

entries.zh: 今綴集殊聞顯迹，以爲《循吏篇》云。
entries.en: What follows gathers notable deeds into the chapter "Chapter on Upright Officials" (the Xunli pian).
entries.literal: Now I string together unusual hearings and shining deeds to form this chapter titled "Chapter on Upright Officials" (Xunli pian).

entries.zh: 董宣字少平，陈留圉人也。
entries.en: Dong Xuan, whose courtesy name was Shaoping, came from Yu in Chenliu commandery.
entries.literal: Dong Xuan, courtesy name Shaoping, was a native of Yu in Chenliu.

entries.zh: 初为司徒侯霸所辟，举高第，累迁北海相。
entries.en: He was first recommended by Minister of Education Hou Ba, placed first in the high-ranking group, and eventually promoted step by step to Prefect of Beihai.
entries.literal: At first he was summoned by Minister of Education Hou Ba, ranked at the top of his class, and rose in stages to Prefect of Beihai.

entries.zh: 到官，以大姓公孙丹为五官掾。
entries.en: On arriving he named the powerful local magnate Gongsun Dan as his aide for the five offices.
entries.literal: When he took office, he appointed the great clan head Gongsun Dan as his aide for the five offices.

entries.zh: 丹新造居宅，而卜工以为当有死者，丹乃令其子杀道行人，置尸舍内，以塞其咎。
entries.en: Gongsun Dan had just finished a new house when the geomancer declared that a death was fated to occur there; Dan then told his son to murder a traveler, leave the body in the building, and so “answer” the omen.
entries.literal: Dan had newly built a residence, and the diviner said someone must die there; Dan then ordered his son to kill a passerby on the road, place the corpse inside the house, and thereby ward off the ill omen.

entries.zh: 宣知，即收丹父子杀之。
entries.en: When Dong Xuan found out, he immediately seized Gongsun Dan and his sons and executed them.
entries.literal: When Xuan learned of it, he at once arrested Dan and his sons and put them to death.

entries.zh: 丹宗族亲党三十余人，操兵诣府，称冤叫号。
entries.en: Over thirty members of Gongsun Dan’s lineage and their allies armed themselves, marched to the yamen, and loudly protested their innocence.
entries.literal: More than thirty kinsmen and partisans of Dan’s clan took up arms, went to the prefectural headquarters, and cried out that they had been wronged.

entries.zh: 宣以丹前附王莽、虑交通海贼，乃悉收系剧狱，使门下书佐水丘岑尽杀之。
entries.en: Dong Xuan, recalling that Gongsun Dan had once served Wang Mang and fearing he might be in league with pirates, jailed the lot in the prison for capital cases and ordered his clerk Shuiqiu Cen to slaughter them all.
entries.literal: Xuan, because Dan had formerly adhered to Wang Mang and he feared collusion with coastal bandits, then arrested them all and held them in the jail for serious criminals, ordering his clerk Shuiqiu Cen to kill every one of them.

entries.zh: 青州以其多滥，奏宣考岑，宣坐征诣廷尉。
entries.en: The provincial authorities of Qingzhou, judging the bloodshed excessive, reported Dong Xuan and had him and Shuiqiu Cen tortured for confession; Dong Xuan was consequently cited to the capital commandant of justice.
entries.literal: Qing Province, deeming the killings excessive, memorialized to have Xuan and Cen interrogated under torture; Xuan was therefore summoned to the Commandant of Justice.

entries.zh: 在狱，晨夜讽诵，无忧色。
entries.en: In his cell he chanted the classics day and night and never lost his composure.
entries.literal: In prison he recited texts morning and night and showed no sign of worry.

entries.zh: 及当出刑，官属具馔送之，宣乃厉色曰：“董宣生平未曾食人之食，况死乎！”
entries.en: When his execution drew near, his staff set out a parting feast; Dong Xuan said sharply, “Dong Xuan has never eaten at another’s expense in his life—least of all on the way to his death!"
entries.literal: When the time came for him to go out to execution, his subordinates prepared a farewell meal; Xuan then said sternly, “In all my life Dong Xuan has never eaten another man’s food—how much less at the hour of death!”

entries.zh: 升车而去。
entries.en: With that he climbed into the cart and rode away.
entries.literal: He mounted the cart and departed.

entries.zh: 时，同刑九人，次应及宣，光武驰使驺骑特原宣刑，且令还狱。
entries.en: Nine others were condemned with him, and when the roll call would next have fallen on Dong Xuan, Emperor Guangwu sent relay riders at a gallop to commute his sentence and had him sent back to jail.
entries.literal: At that time nine men were to suffer the same sentence, and when his turn should have reached Xuan, Guangwu sent mounted couriers at full gallop especially to spare Xuan from execution and ordered him returned to prison.

entries.zh: 遣使者诘宣多杀无辜，宣具以状对，言水丘岑受臣旨意，罪不由之，愿杀臣活岑。
entries.en: An imperial messenger was sent to upbraid him for slaughtering the guiltless; Dong Xuan laid out the whole affair, declared that Shuiqiu Cen had merely obeyed his commands, that the blame lay with himself, not with Cen, and begged to die so that Cen might live.
entries.literal: He dispatched an envoy to rebuke Xuan for having killed many innocents; Xuan set forth the facts in reply, saying that Shuiqiu Cen had acted on his orders, that the fault was not Cen’s, and that he wished to die in Cen’s place and let Cen live.

entries.zh: 使者以闻，有诏左转宣怀令，令青州勿案岑罪。
entries.en: The messenger relayed his words; an edict followed, demoting Dong Xuan to magistrate of Huai county and forbidding Qingzhou to pursue charges against Shuiqiu Cen.
entries.literal: When the envoy reported this, an edict came demoting Xuan to Magistrate of Huai and ordering Qingzhou not to prosecute Cen.

entries.zh: 岑官至司隶校尉。
entries.en: Shuiqiu Cen eventually rose to become colonel director of retainers.
entries.literal: Cen rose in office to Colonel Director of Retainers.

entries.zh: 后特征为洛阳令。
entries.en: He was later specially called to office as magistrate of Luoyang.
entries.literal: Later he was specially summoned to serve as Magistrate of Luoyang.

entries.zh: 时湖阳公主苍头白日杀人，因匿主家，吏不能得。
entries.en: At that time a household slave of the Princess of Huyang had murdered someone in daylight and then taken refuge in her mansion, beyond the clerks’ reach.
entries.literal: At that time a slave of the Princess of Huyang had killed a man in broad daylight and then hidden in the princess’s household, so the clerks could not seize him.

entries.zh: 及主出行，而以奴骖乘，宣于夏门亭候之，乃驻车叩马，以刀画地，大言数主之失，叱奴下车，因格杀之。
entries.en: When she rode out with the killer as her side attendant, Dong Xuan ambushed her at the Summer Gate watchpost, halted her team, seized the bridle, traced lines on the earth with his blade while shouting her misdeeds aloud, forced the slave from the cart, and beat him to death on the spot.
entries.literal: When the princess went out, she had the slave ride as her outrider; Xuan waited for her at the Summer Gate pavilion, stopped the carriage, seized the horse’s bridle, scored the ground with his knife while loudly enumerating the princess’s faults, ordered the slave to get down, and then struck him dead.

entries.zh: 主即还宫诉帝，帝大怒，召宣，欲箠杀之。
entries.en: She hurried to the palace to denounce him; the emperor flew into a rage, summoned Dong Xuan, and meant to club him to death.
entries.literal: The princess at once returned to the palace to complain to the emperor, who was furious and summoned Xuan, intending to beat him to death with clubs.

entries.zh: 宣叩头曰：“愿乞一言而死。”
entries.en: Dong Xuan kowtowed and said, “Grant me one word before I die.”
entries.literal: Xuan kowtowed and said, “I beg leave to speak one sentence before I die.”

entries.zh: 帝曰：“欲何言？”
entries.en: The emperor asked, “What is it?”
entries.literal: The emperor said, “What would you say?”

entries.zh: 宣曰：“陛下圣德中兴，而从奴杀良人，将何以理天下乎？
entries.en: Dong Xuan replied, “Your Majesty’s sagely power brought the house back from ruin; if a slave may slaughter the guiltless, how are you to govern all under Heaven?
entries.literal: Xuan said, “Your Majesty’s sacred virtue restored the dynasty; if you let a slave kill an innocent commoner, how will you order the realm?”

entries.zh: 臣不须箠，请得自杀。”
entries.en: I need no beating from you; let me kill myself.”
entries.literal: “I have no need of clubs; allow me to take my own life.”

entries.zh: 即以头击楹，流血被面。
entries.en: He then dashed his head against a column until his face ran with blood.
entries.literal: He thereupon struck his head against a pillar until blood covered his face.

entries.zh: 帝令小黄门持之，使宣叩头谢主，宣不从，强使顿之，宣两手据地，终不肯俯。
entries.en: The emperor told a young eunuch to hold him back and ordered Dong Xuan to bow in apology to the princess; he would not. They tried to press his head down, but he planted both hands on the floor and never lowered his brow.
entries.literal: The emperor ordered a minor eunuch to restrain him and told Xuan to kowtow and apologize to the princess; Xuan refused, and when they forced him to bow his head, he braced both hands on the ground and would not bend.

entries.zh: 主曰：“文叔为白衣时，臧主匿死，吏不敢至门。
entries.en: The princess cried, “When Wenshu was still a commoner, he concealed fugitives for me, and no bailiff dared knock at my door.
entries.literal: The princess said, “When Wenshu was a commoner, he hid condemned men for me, and clerks dared not come to my gate.

entries.zh: 今为天子，威不能行一令乎？”
entries.en: Now that he is Son of Heaven, can his power not reach a single county magistrate?”
entries.literal: Now that he is Son of Heaven, can his authority not reach even one magistrate?”

entries.zh: 帝笑曰：“天子不与白衣同。”」
entries.en: The emperor smiled and said, “The Son of Heaven is not a commoner.”
entries.literal: The emperor laughed and said, “The Son of Heaven is not the same as a commoner.”

entries.zh: 因敕强项令出。
entries.en: He then told the “stubborn-necked magistrate” to withdraw.
entries.literal: He then ordered the “stiff-necked magistrate” dismissed.

entries.zh: 赐钱三十万，宣悉以班诸吏。
entries.en: He awarded three hundred thousand cash; Dong Xuan handed every coin to his subordinates.
entries.literal: He granted three hundred thousand cash, which Xuan distributed entirely among his clerks.

entries.zh: 由是搏击豪强，莫不震栗。
entries.en: After that, whenever he moved against the powerful, they quaked with fear.
entries.literal: From then on, whenever he struck at the mighty, none failed to tremble.

entries.zh: 京师号为“卧虎”。
entries.en: The capital dubbed him the “crouching tiger.”
entries.literal: The capital nicknamed him the “Crouching Tiger.”

entries.zh: 歌之曰：“枹鼓不鸣董少平。”
entries.en: A ditty ran: “You never hear the drum while Dong Shaoping is in charge.”
entries.literal: They sang of him, “The drum is never sounded for Dong Shaoping.”

entries.zh: 在县五年。
entries.en: He served five years in that county.
entries.literal: He remained in the county for five years.

entries.zh: 年七十四，卒于官。
entries.en: He died in harness at the age of seventy-four.
entries.literal: At age seventy-four he died in office.

entries.zh: 诏遣使者临视，唯见布被覆尸，妻子对哭，有大麦数斛、敝车一乘。
entries.en: The court sent an inspector to his home; all they saw was a hemp sheet over the body, his wife and children weeping beside it, a few measures of barley, and a single rickety cart.
entries.literal: An edict ordered an envoy to attend his funeral; they found only a cloth quilt covering the corpse, his wife and children weeping opposite him, several hu of barley, and one broken-down cart.

entries.zh: 帝伤之，曰：“董宣廉洁，死乃知之！”
entries.en: The emperor was stricken and said, “Dong Xuan was honest—I learned it only when he was gone!"
entries.literal: The emperor was moved and said, “Dong Xuan was incorrupt; only after his death did I know it!”

entries.zh: 以宣尝为二千石，赐艾绶，葬以大夫礼。
entries.en: Because Dong Xuan had once borne rank at two thousand piculs, he was given the mottled ribbon and buried with ceremonies fit for a high minister.
entries.literal: Because Xuan had once held a two-thousand-dan post, he was granted the ai ribbon and buried with the rites due a grandee.

entries.zh: 拜子并为郎中，后官至齐相。
entries.en: His son Dong Bing was made a gentleman of the palace and eventually became prefect of Qi.
entries.literal: His son Bing was appointed gentleman of the palace and later rose to Prefect of Qi.

entries.zh: 樊晔字仲华，南阳新野人也。
entries.en: Fan Ye, courtesy name Zhonghua, hailed from Xinye in Nanyang commandery.
entries.literal: Fan Ye, courtesy name Zhonghua, was a native of Xinye in Nanyang.

entries.zh: 与光武少游旧。
entries.en: In his younger days he had been Guangwu’s companion on the road.
entries.literal: In youth he roamed about with Guangwu.

entries.zh: 建武初，徵為侍御史，遷河東都尉，引見雲臺。
entries.en: Early in the Jianwu reign he was called up as attendant censor, advanced to commandant of Hedong, and received an audience in the Cloud Terrace.
entries.literal: At the beginning of the Jianwu era he was summoned as attendant censor, promoted to commandant of Hedong, and granted audience in the Cloud Terrace.

entries.zh: 初，光武微时，尝以事拘于新野，晔为市吏，餽饵一笥，帝德之不忘，仍赐晔御食，及乘舆服物。
entries.en: Long before, when Guangwu was still unknown, he had been held at Xinye over some matter; Fan Ye, then a market inspector, sent a hamper of food, and the emperor cherished the deed ever after, later presenting him with dishes from the palace kitchen and clothing from the imperial wardrobe.
entries.literal: Earlier, when Guangwu was still obscure, he had once been detained at Xinye for an affair; Ye, then a market clerk, sent him a basket of cakes, and the emperor remembered the kindness and never forgot it, later bestowing on Ye imperial viands and garments from the imperial wardrobe.

entries.zh: 因戏之曰：“一笥饵得都尉，何如？”
entries.en: He joked, “One hamper of snacks bought you a commandant’s commission—fair trade?”
entries.literal: He then teased him, saying, “A basket of cakes for a commandant—how does that bargain strike you?”

entries.zh: 晔顿首辞谢。
entries.en: Fan Ye kowtowed and demurred.
entries.literal: Ye kowtowed and declined with thanks.

entries.zh: 及至郡，诛讨大姓马適匡等。
entries.en: On reaching his post he wiped out powerful houses such as that of Ma Shi Kuang.
entries.literal: When he reached the commandery, he executed and extirpated the great clan heads Ma Shi Kuang and the like.

entries.zh: 盗贼清，吏人畏之。
entries.en: Robbery ceased, and both officials and townsfolk stood in awe of him.
entries.literal: Banditry was cleared away, and clerks and commoners feared him.

entries.zh: 数年，迁杨州牧，教民耕田种树理家之术。
entries.en: After some years he became governor of Yang province and instructed the populace in farming, arboriculture, and household economy.
entries.literal: Several years later he was transferred to Governor of Yang Province, where he taught the people methods of plowing fields, planting trees, and managing their households.

entries.zh: 视事十余年，坐法左转积长。
entries.en: He governed for over a decade, then ran afoul of the statutes and was reduced to chief of Ji canton.
entries.literal: After more than ten years in office he broke the law and was demoted to chief of Ji.

entries.zh: 光武即位，拜阳平令。
entries.en: After Guangwu mounted the throne, Li Zhang became magistrate of Yangping.
entries.literal: When Guangwu took the throne, Zhang was appointed Magistrate of Yangping.

entries.zh: 时赵、魏豪右往往屯聚，清河大姓赵纲遂于县界起坞壁，缮甲兵，为在所害。
entries.en: In those days magnates of Zhao and Wei commonly mustered private forces, and Zhao Gang, a powerful clan of Qinghe, threw up a fortified stockade on the county line, outfitted troops, and terrorized the countryside.
entries.literal: At that time the powerful families of Zhao and Wei often gathered in armed bands, and the great Zhao surname of Qinghe, Zhao Gang, then raised fortifications on the county border, repaired armor and weapons, and became a scourge to the region.

entries.zh: 章到，乃设飨会，而延谒纲。
entries.en: Li Zhang’s first move was to host a feast and politely summon Zhao Gang.
entries.literal: When Zhang arrived, he set a banquet and courteously invited Gang.

entries.zh: 纲带文剑，被羽衣，从士百余人来到。
entries.en: Zhao Gang came with a patterned sword, a feathered robe, and over a hundred armed retainers.
entries.literal: Gang wore an inscribed sword, draped a feathered cloak, and arrived with more than a hundred followers.

entries.zh: 章与对宴饮，有顷，手剑斩纲，伏兵亦悉杀其从者，因驰诣坞壁，掩击破之，吏人遂安。
entries.en: Li Zhang drank with him awhile, then suddenly drew his blade and struck off Zhao Gang’s head while hidden troops cut down every follower; he raced to the fort, stormed it flat, and peace returned to the district.
entries.literal: Zhang feasted and drank with him; after a while he drew his sword and beheaded Gang, while concealed soldiers slew all his attendants; he then galloped to the stockade, stormed and broke it, and thereafter clerks and people were secure.

entries.zh: 李章，字第公，河內懷人也。
entries.en: Li Zhang, courtesy name Digong, came from Huai in Henei commandery.
entries.literal: Li Zhang, courtesy name Digong, was a native of Huai in Henei.

entries.zh: 五世二千石。
entries.en: For five generations his forebears had borne rank at two thousand piculs.
entries.literal: For five generations his family had held two-thousand-dan posts.

entries.zh: 章习《严氏春秋》，经明教授，历州郡吏。
entries.en: Li Zhang studied the Yan school’s Gongyang commentary, excelled in the canon, instructed disciples, and worked his way through posts in various provinces and commanderies.
entries.literal: Zhang studied the Gongyang commentary in Yan’s tradition, mastered the classics, taught students, and served successively as a clerk in provinces and commanderies.

entries.zh: 光武为大司马，平定河北，召章置江曹属，数从征伐。
entries.en: While Guangwu served as grand marshal and was bringing Hebei to heel, he called Li Zhang to his staff in charge of river works, and Zhang rode with him on many expeditions.
entries.literal: When Guangwu was grand marshal and was pacifying Hebei, he summoned Zhang and placed him on the staff of the river office, and Zhang repeatedly accompanied the campaigns.

entries.zh: 迁千乘太守，坐诛斩盗贼过滥，征下狱免。
entries.en: He was raised to prefect of Qiansheng, then cited for excessive slaughter in suppressing bandits, jailed, and stripped of office.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Prefect of Qiansheng but, because he had executed bandits beyond proper measure, was summoned, imprisoned, and dismissed.

entries.zh: 岁中拜侍御史，出为琅邪太守。
entries.en: The same year he became attendant censor and was posted as prefect of Langye.
entries.literal: Within the year he was appointed attendant censor and sent out as Prefect of Langye.

entries.zh: 时北海安丘大姓夏长思等反，遂囚太守处兴，而据营陵城。
entries.en: Then the magnates of Anqiu in Beihai—Xia Changsi and his confederates—rose in revolt, jailed Prefect Chu Xing, and occupied Yingling.
entries.literal: At that time the great families of Anqiu in Beihai, Xia Changsi and others, rebelled, imprisoned Prefect Chu Xing, and seized the city of Yingling.

entries.zh: 章闻，即发兵千人，驰往击之。
entries.en: Li Zhang heard the news, immediately mobilized a thousand men, and rode to strike them.
entries.literal: When Zhang heard the news, he at once raised a thousand troops and galloped to attack them.

entries.zh: 掾史止章曰：“二千石行不得出界，兵不得擅发。”
entries.en: His aides warned him, “A prefect may not cross his border, and you have no orders to call out soldiers.”
entries.literal: His clerks remonstrated, “A two-thousand-dan official may not leave his jurisdiction, nor may troops be raised without authorization.”

entries.zh: 章按剑怒曰：“逆虏无状，囚劫郡守，此何可忍！
entries.en: Li Zhang clutched his sword and roared, “Rebels have kidnapped the governor—how can I stand by?
entries.literal: Zhang gripped his sword in wrath and said, “These traitors have seized our prefect—how can I endure it!

entries.zh: 若坐讨贼而死，吾不恨也。”
entries.en: If I die putting down outlaws, I will not regret it.”
entries.literal: If I die punishing rebels, I will have no regret.”

entries.zh: 遂引兵安丘城下，募勇敢烧城门，与长思战，斩之，获三百余级，得牛马五百余头而还。
entries.en: He led his force to Anqiu, enlisted daredevils to torch the gates, fought Xia Changsi, cut off his head, claimed over three hundred enemy heads, and drove home five hundred-odd cattle and horses.
entries.literal: He therefore led his troops beneath the walls of Anqiu, recruited the bold to burn the gates, fought Changsi, beheaded him, took more than three hundred heads, and captured five hundred-odd head of cattle and horses before returning.

entries.zh: 兴归郡，以状上帝，悉以所得班劳吏士。
entries.en: When Chu Xing was back in his yamen, he memorialized the whole affair; the emperor had every prize shared out to reward the officers and men.
entries.literal: When Xing returned to the commandery, he reported the affair to the emperor, who ordered all the booty distributed to reward clerks and soldiers.

entries.zh: 后坐度人田不实征，以章有功，但司冠论。
entries.en: Li Zhang was later found guilty of misreporting land surveys used for taxation, but on account of his past service the court merely handed him over to the Minister of Justice for judgment instead of harsher punishment.
entries.literal: Later he was convicted for having surveyed others’ fields untruthfully in connection with tax levies; because Li Zhang had merit, he was only remanded to the Minister of Justice for sentencing.

entries.zh: 月余免刑，归。
entries.en: A little over a month later he was released from torture and sent home.
entries.literal: After more than a month he was spared corporal punishment and returned home.

entries.zh: 复征，会病卒。
entries.en: The court called him back to office, yet he sickened and died before he could take up the post.
entries.literal: He was summoned again, but fell ill and died before reporting.

entries.zh: 迁平原相。
entries.en: He was next promoted to chancellor of Pingyuan.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Chancellor of Pingyuan.

entries.zh: 出教曰：“相前莅高唐，志埽奸鄙，遂为贵郡所见枉举。
entries.en: He published an order: “When last I governed Gaotang I meant to scour out wickedness, and your honorable commandery repaid me with a trumped-up impeachment.
entries.literal: He issued an instruction saying: “Your chancellor formerly governed Gaotang, intent on sweeping away the vile, and was thereupon slandered and impeached by your honorable commandery.”

entries.zh: 昔桓公释管仲射钩之仇，高祖赦季布逃亡之罪。
entries.en: Duke Huan of Qi forgave Guan Zhong’s arrow at his belt hook; Gaozu spared Ji Bu the fugitive’s guilt.
entries.literal: “In old times Duke Huan released Duke Guan’s guilt for shooting his hook-buckle, and the Supreme Ancestor pardoned Ji Bu’s crime of flight.”

entries.zh: 虽以不德，敢忘前义。
entries.en: Though I am a lesser man, I would not forget such magnanimity.
entries.literal: “Though I lack virtue, how dare I forget such prior righteousness.”

entries.zh: 况君臣分定，而可怀宿者哉！
entries.en: Besides, lord and minister each have a part—who should nurse ancient grudges?
entries.literal: “Moreover, when ruler and minister have fixed roles, who may cling to old resentments!”

entries.zh: 今一蠲往愆，期诸来效。
entries.en: Henceforth I cancel old scores and expect new loyalty from you.
entries.literal: “Now I once for all wipe away past faults and look to you for future service.”

entries.zh: 若受教之后而不改奸状者，不得复有所容矣。”
entries.en: Anyone who keeps his criminal habits after this warning will find no mercy left.”
entries.literal: “If after receiving this instruction you do not reform your villainous conduct, you will find no further tolerance.”

entries.zh: 郡中咸畏服焉。
entries.en: The whole commandery stood in awe and obeyed.
entries.literal: Throughout the commandery all feared and submitted.

entries.zh: 时，天下大旱，司空张颢条奏长吏苛酷贪污者，皆罢免之。
entries.en: An empire-wide drought struck; Minister of Works Zhang Hao filed charges against magistrates who were brutal or venal, and every one named was removed.
entries.literal: At that time a great drought afflicted the realm; Minister of Works Zhang Hao submitted a memorial listing senior officials who were harsh, cruel, or corrupt, and all were dismissed.

entries.zh: 球坐严苦，征诣廷尉，当免官。
entries.en: Yang Qiu’s harshness brought him before the commandant of justice, where the verdict should have stripped him of rank.
entries.literal: Qiu, because of his severity, was summoned to the Commandant of Justice and ought to have been dismissed from office.

entries.zh: 灵帝以球九江时有功，拜议郎。
entries.en: Emperor Ling remembered his service in Jiujiang and instead named him gentleman consultant.
entries.literal: Emperor Ling, recalling Qiu’s merit at Jiujiang, appointed him gentleman consultant.

entries.zh: 汉承战国余烈，多豪猾之民。
entries.en: The Han took over a world still marked by the Warring States, and among its people were many who were bold, ruthless, and cunning.
entries.literal: The Han inherited the lingering fierceness of the Warring States era, and its people included many bold and crafty sorts.

entries.zh: 其并兼者则陵横邦邑，桀健者则雄张闾里。
entries.en: The powerful swallowed weaker neighbors and rode roughshod over whole districts; the violent and the able made themselves masters of every lane and ward.
entries.literal: Those who annexed others then overawed and trampled the towns and districts; those who were fierce and strong lorded it over their neighborhoods.

entries.zh: 且宰守旷远，户口殷大。
entries.en: Moreover, the officials set over the people held sway across vast distances, and the population within their registers was immense.
entries.literal: Moreover, the magistrates who governed were stationed far away, while registered households were exceedingly numerous.

entries.zh: 故临民之职，专事威断，族灭奸轨，先行后闻。
entries.en: So those who held authority over common folk leaned on terror and arbitrary judgment: they wiped out entire families for alleged villainy, struck first, and asked permission only later.
entries.literal: Therefore those charged with overseeing the people devoted themselves to awe-inspiring decisions, exterminating whole clans for treacherous wrongdoing, acting first and reporting afterward.

entries.zh: 肆情刚烈，成其不桡之威。
entries.en: They indulged their own harshness and forged a reputation for inflexible terror.
entries.literal: They gave rein to harsh, unbending temperaments and thereby forged an awe that would not bend.

entries.zh: 违众用己，表其难测之智。
entries.en: They brushed aside consensus, trusted only themselves, and cultivated an air of inscrutable cunning.
entries.literal: They defied the multitude and followed their own judgment, displaying a cleverness none could fathom.

entries.zh: 至于重文横入，为穷怒之所迁及者，亦何可胜言。
entries.en: When the law was stretched to trap the innocent and men were swept up by fury run past all bounds, the toll became literally beyond words.
entries.literal: When, moreover, legal formulas were twisted to ensnare people, and men became the objects of rage pushed to its limit—how can such cases even be fully told?

entries.zh: 故乃积骸满穽，漂血十里。
entries.en: Corpses were heaped until the burial pits overflowed, and blood ran in streams for miles.
entries.literal: Thus bones piled until they filled the pits, and blood floated for ten li.

entries.zh: 致温舒有虎冠之吏，延年受屠伯之名，岂虚也哉！
entries.en: So it was that Wang Wenshu produced underlings called “tiger-hatted” enforcers, and Yan Nian won the nickname “the butcher’s broker”—and those reputations were no idle tales.
entries.literal: Hence Wang Wenshu gained clerks likened to tiger-capped officers, and Yan Nian earned the name “butcher-broker”—could that have been empty rumor?

entries.zh: 若其揣挫强伤，摧勒公卿，碎裂头脑而不顾，亦为壮也。
entries.en: There were also men who humbled the powerful, humiliated grandees, and split skulls without flinching—acts the age could only call bold.
entries.literal: As for those who humbled the mighty and wounded the strong, who broke and drove the high ministers and shattered skulls without a second thought—that too could be called heroic.

entries.zh: 太傅陳蕃辟之，與參政事。
entries.en: Grand Tutor Chen Fan brought him into government.
entries.literal: Grand Tutor Chen Fan summoned him to join in governance.

entries.zh: 蕃敗，休坐廢錮，乃作《春秋公羊解詁》，覃思不窺門，十有七年。
entries.en: When Chen Fan fell, He Xiu was banned from office and spent seventeen years indoors writing his Gongyang gloss.
entries.literal: When Fan was defeated, Xiu sat in dismissal and prohibition from office; thereupon he composed Glosses on the Gongyang Spring and Autumn, pondering so deeply that he did not peer out his gate for seventeen years.

entries.zh: 又注訓《孝經》、《論語》、風角七分，皆經緯典謨，不與守文同說。
entries.en: He also glossed the Classic of Filial Piety, the Analects, and wind-omen lore, aiming at classical models rather than narrow literalism.
entries.literal: Further he annotated and glossed the Classic of Filial Piety, the Analects, and wind-horn seven parts, all patterned on canonical models and not the same as pedants who cling to the letter.

entries.zh: 又以《春秋》駁漢事六百餘條，妙得《公羊》本意。
entries.en: He used Gongyang to critique over six hundred Han precedents, capturing the school's core intent.
entries.literal: Further by the Spring and Autumn he refuted more than six hundred items in Han affairs, subtly obtaining the original intent of Gongyang.

entries.zh: 休善曆算，與其師博士羊弼，追述李育意以難二傳，作《公羊墨守》、《左氏膏肓》、《穀梁廢疾》。
entries.en: With his teacher Erudite Yang Bi he developed Li Yu's attacks on the Zuo and Guliang schools in three famous polemics.
entries.literal: Xiu was good at calendrical calculation; together with his teacher the Erudite Yang Bi he pursued and stated Li Yu's ideas to object to the two traditions, composing Gongyang Ink-Bound, Zuo Ailing, and Guliang Morbid.

entries.zh: 《前書》魯人申公受《詩》於浮丘伯，為作詁訓，是為《魯詩》；
entries.en: The Han shu records that Shen Gong of Lu studied the Odes under Fuqiu Bo and compiled glosses—what became the Lu school of the classic.
entries.literal: The Former Documents: Shen Gong of Lu received the Odes from Fuqiu Bo, for them made gloss and exegesis, and this is the 'Odes in the Lu tradition';

entries.zh: 齊人轅固生亦傳《詩》，是為《齊詩》；
entries.en: Yuan Gu of Qi handed down another line—the Qi Odes.
entries.literal: Yuan Gu of Qi likewise transmitted the Odes, and this is the 'Odes in the Qi tradition';

entries.zh: 燕人韓嬰亦傳《詩》，是為《韓詩》；
entries.en: Han Ying of Yan founded the Han school of the Odes.
entries.literal: Han Ying of Yan likewise transmitted the Odes, and this is the 'Odes in the Han tradition';

entries.zh: 三家皆立博士。
entries.en: All three received chairs at the imperial academy.
entries.literal: All three houses had Erudites established.

entries.zh: 趙人毛萇傳《詩》，是為《毛詩》，未得立。
entries.en: Mao Chang of Zhao taught what became the Mao commentary, which had no doctoral chair in Western Han.
entries.literal: Mao Chang of Zhao transmitted the Odes, and this is the 'Mao Odes'; it did not obtain establishment.

entries.zh: 杜笃字季雅，京兆杜陵人也。
entries.en: Du Du, whose courtesy name was Jiya, came from Duling in the metropolitan region of Jingzhao.
entries.literal: Du Du, courtesy name Jiya, was a native of Duling in Jingzhao.

entries.zh: 高祖延年，宣帝时为御史大夫。
entries.en: An ancestor, Du Yannian, had served as Imperial Counselor during the reign of Emperor Xuan.
entries.literal: His ancestor Yannian served as Imperial Counselor under Emperor Xuan of Han.

entries.zh: 笃少博学，不修小节，不为乡人所礼。
entries.en: As a young man Du Du read widely, scorned petty propriety, and won no respect from the people of his district.
entries.literal: In youth Du was broadly learned, kept no meticulous minor deportment, and was not treated with courtesy by his fellow villagers.

entries.zh: 居美阳，与美阳令游，数从请托，不谐，颇相恨。
entries.en: While living in Meiyang he associated with the county magistrate and often tried to secure favors through him; when those efforts failed, the two grew mutually resentful.
entries.literal: He lived in Meiyang and kept company with the magistrate of Meiyang; repeatedly he asked favors through him; they did not succeed and came greatly to resent each other.

entries.zh: 令怒，收笃送京师。
entries.en: The magistrate, infuriated, had Du Du seized and escorted to the capital under arrest.
entries.literal: The magistrate grew angry, arrested Du Du, and sent him to the capital.

entries.zh: 会大司马吴汉薨，光武诏诸儒诔之，笃于狱中为诔，辞最高，美帝之，赐帛免刑。
entries.en: Just then Grand Marshal Wu Han died, and Emperor Guangwu summoned the literati to mourn him in verse. From his cell Du Du submitted a dirge that surpassed the rest; the emperor admired it, rewarded him with silk, and released him without sentence.
entries.literal: It happened that Grand Marshal Wu Han died; Guangwu ordered the scholars to compose dirges for him. Du Du, in prison, wrote a dirge; among them his text ranked highest; the emperor praised it and granted him silk, remitting punishment.

entries.zh: 是时，孝武因其余财府帑之蓄，始有钩深图远之意，探冒顿之罪，校平城之仇。
entries.en: Then Emperor Wu, drawing on overflowing treasuries, first dreamed of distant schemes—to reckon Modun's offenses and settle scores for the humiliation at Pingcheng.
entries.literal: At that time Emperor Wu, relying on surplus wealth stored in the treasury, first conceived intentions to probe deep and plan far, investigating Modun's crimes and measuring revenge for the Pingcheng defeat.

entries.zh: 遂命票骑，勤任卫青，勇惟鹰扬，军如流星，深之匈奴，割裂王庭，席卷漠北，叩勒祁连，横分单于，屠裂百蛮。
entries.en: He charged the Swift Cavalry command and leaned hard on Wei Qing; armies swept like meteors and valor rose like hawks—deep into the steppe they shattered the royal court, rolled up the northern sands, stormed Qilian, split the Chanyu, and carved apart countless tribes.
entries.literal: He therefore commissioned the Swift Cavalry general, heavily tasked Wei Qing; bravery soared like hawks, armies moved like meteors; he thrust deep into the Xiongnu, tore apart the royal court, swept the northern desert, stormed Qilian, split the Chanyu asunder, butchered the hundred barbarians.

entries.zh: 烧罽帐，系阏氏，燔康居，灰珍奇，椎鸣镝，钉鹿蠡，驰坑岸，获昆弥，虏亻数侲，驱骡驴，御宛马，鞭駃騠。
entries.en: They torched yurts, seized the Chanyu consort, burned Kangju to ash, shattered whistling arrows, pinned enemy princes, raced gorges and ridges, took the Wusun ruler and boy captives, drove pack animals and rode Ferghana steeds, laying the lash to every swift mount.
entries.literal: He burned felt tents, bound the Chanyu consort, set Kangju ablaze, reduced rare treasures to ash, smashed whistling arrows, pinned the Luoli prince, galloped ravines and cliffs, seized the Kunmi king, captured youthful hostages, drove mules and donkeys, mastered Ferghana horses, and whipped swift steeds.

entries.zh: 拓地万里，威震八荒。
entries.en: Borders stretched ten thousand li and terror rang through every quarter.
entries.literal: He expanded territory ten thousand li and awe shook the eight directions.

entries.zh: 肇置四郡，据守敦煌。
entries.en: They planted four western commanderies and anchored Dunhuang.
entries.literal: He first established four frontier commanderies and held Dunhuang fast.

entries.zh: 并域属国，一郡领方。
entries.en: Dependent states along the frontier were folded in so that one commandery could oversee whole regions.
entries.literal: Border chiefdoms were folded in; one commandery governed an entire quarter.

entries.zh: 立侯隅北，建护西羌。
entries.en: Marquises anchored the northern marches; inspectors watched the western Qiang.
entries.literal: Marquises stood guard on the northern rim; Protectors of the Western Qiang were installed.

entries.zh: 捶驱氐、僰，寥狼卭、莋。
entries.en: They drove Di and Bo tribes and cleared wolf-like threats from Qiong and Zuo.
entries.literal: He drove the Di and Bo peoples and scattered wolves among Qiong and Zuo.

entries.zh: 东摩乌桓，蹂辚濊貊。
entries.en: To the east they brushed the Wuhuan and trampled the Huimo.
entries.literal: Eastward he rubbed against the Wuhuan and trampled the Huimo.

entries.zh: 南羁钩町，水剑强越。
entries.en: To the south they leashed Gouding and crossed blades with powerful Yue along the rivers.
entries.literal: Southward he tethered Gouding and crossed swords with mighty Yue by water.

entries.zh: 残夷文身，海波沫血。
entries.en: They broke the tattooed southern peoples until the seas foamed crimson.
entries.literal: He mutilated the tattooed tribesmen; seas foamed with blood.

entries.zh: 郡县日南，漂概硃崖。
entries.en: Counties stretched to Rinan and standards fluttered toward Zhuya.
entries.literal: Commanderies reached Rinan; banners streamed toward Zhuya.

entries.zh: 部尉东南，兼有黄支。
entries.en: A southern colonel held the southeast until even Huangzhi fell within reach.
entries.literal: A colonel watched the southeast and Huangzhi was swept in as well.

entries.zh: 连缓耳，琐雕题，摧天督，牵象犀，椎蚌蛤，碎琉璃，甲玳瑁，戕觜觿。
entries.en: Long-ear tribes and tattooed foreheads were yanked into submission—armies shattered Tian-du, hauled back elephants and rhinos, crushed shells and glass, smashed tortoise and horn ornaments.
entries.literal: Linked ear-loops and carved foreheads; Tian-du destroyed; elephants and rhinos dragged home; shells smashed; glass shattered; tortoise shell and hawksbill crushed; pipes and jades broken.

entries.zh: 于是同穴裘褐之域，共川鼻饮之国，莫不袒跣稽颡，失气虏伏。
entries.en: Even peoples who dwelt in caves and furs and drank river-water through their noses came barefoot to knock their heads in the dust, breathless and prostrate.
entries.literal: Thus in lands where cave-dwellers wore furs and peoples drank from the same rivers with their noses, none failed to bare feet, knock foreheads to earth, lose their breath, and crouch like captured beasts.

entries.zh: 非夫大汉之世盛，世借雍土之饶，得御外理内之术，孰能致功若斯！
entries.en: Without Han's golden age, Yongzhou's abundance, and skill at ruling interior and frontier alike, who could have piled up such deeds!
entries.literal: Were it not for the Han's glorious age, borrowing Yongzhou's bounty and wielding arts to manage within and without, who could have wrought merit like this!

entries.zh: 故创业于高祖，嗣传于孝惠，德隆于太宗，财衍于孝景，威盛于圣武，政行于宣、元，侈极于成、哀、祚缺于孝平。
entries.en: The line began with Gaozu, flowed through Emperor Hui, rose in virtue with Emperor Wen, spread wealth with Emperor Jing, blazed in might with Emperor Wu, ran smoothly under Emperors Xuan and Yuan, burned brightest in excess under Cheng and Ai, and shattered under young Emperor Ping.
entries.literal: Thus the enterprise began with the Supreme Founder, passed to Emperor Xiaohui, virtue peaked with Emperor Wen, wealth accumulated under Emperor Jing, might crested with Emperor Wu, policy flourished under Emperors Xuan and Yuan, extravagance peaked under Emperors Cheng and Ai, and the mandate cracked under Emperor Xiaoping.

entries.zh: 传世十一，历载三百，德衰而复盈，道微而复章，皆莫能迁于雍州，而背于咸阳。
entries.en: Eleven reigns spanned three centuries—power ebbed and flowed, the Way dimmed and returned—yet no ruler could drag the capital from Yongzhou or turn away from Xianyang.
entries.literal: Eleven generations passed across three hundred years; virtue waned then waxed again, the Way dimmed then brightened—yet none could shift the seat from Yongzhou or turn their back on Xianyang.

entries.zh: 宫室寝庙，山陵相望，高显弘丽，可思可荣，羲、农已来，无兹著明。
entries.en: Palaces and tombs crowd the horizon, vast and splendid, stirring pride—nothing since Fu Xi and Shen Nong has gleamed so visibly.
entries.literal: Palace halls and ancestral shrines, imperial tumuli facing one another—lofty, splendid, stirring and glorious—since Fu Xi and Shen Nong none has shone so bright.

entries.zh: 夏恭字敬公，梁国蒙人也。
entries.en: Xia Gong, known as Jinggong, came from Meng in Liang.
entries.literal: Xia Gong, courtesy name Jinggong, was a native of Meng in the Liang kingdom.

entries.zh: 习《韩诗》、《孟氏易》，讲授门徒常千余人。
entries.en: He mastered the 《Han Shi Poetry》 tradition and the 《Meng Lineage Changes》 school and routinely taught over a thousand students.
entries.literal: He studied 《Han Shi Poetry》 and 《Meng Lineage Changes》; his lecture hall often held more than a thousand disciples.

entries.zh: 王莽末，盗贼从横，攻没郡县。
entries.en: When Wang Mang collapsed, bandits swarmed and seized county seats.
entries.literal: At the end of Wang Mang's reign bandits ran rampant and overran counties.

entries.zh: 恭以恩信为众所附，拥兵固守，独安全。
entries.en: Xia Gong earned loyalty through humane dealing; he kept his men steady and alone preserved his district.
entries.literal: Gong won the people's attachment through kindness and good faith; he held his troops fast and alone remained secure.

entries.zh: 光武即位，嘉其忠果，召拜郎中，再迁太山都尉。
entries.en: Emperor Guangwu admired his steadfast courage, called him to court as a gentleman, and twice raised him to Taishan commandant.
entries.literal: When Guangwu took the throne he praised Gong's loyalty and resolve, summoned him as gentleman, and twice promoted him to commandant of Taishan.

entries.zh: 和集百姓，甚得其欢心。
entries.en: He soothed the populace and truly earned their hearts.
entries.literal: He reconciled and gathered the common people and deeply won their affection.

entries.zh: 皇帝以建武十八年二月甲辰，升舆洛邑，巡于西岳。
entries.en: In Jianwu 18, on the day jiachen of the second month, the Son of Heaven rode out from Luoyang to inspect the Western Marchmount.
entries.literal: On the jiachen day of the second month in the eighteenth Jianwu year, the emperor mounted his carriage at Luoyang and toured the western marchmount.

entries.zh: 推天时，顺斗极，排阊阖，入函谷，观厄于崤、黾，图险于陇、蜀。
entries.en: He aligned the journey with Heaven's seasons, tracked the pole star through Changhe Gate into Hangu, studied the defiles of Xiao and Min, and traced the perilous terrain of Long and Shu.
entries.literal: He reckoned celestial timing, followed the Pole Star, pushed open Changhe Gate, entered Hangu Pass, surveyed the narrows at Xiao and Min, and mapped hazards in Long and Shu.

entries.zh: 其三月丁酉，行至长安。
entries.en: That third month, on dingyou, he reached Chang'an.
entries.literal: In the third month on the day dingyou he arrived at Chang'an.

entries.zh: 经营宫室，伤愍旧京，即诏京兆，乃命扶风，斋肃致敬，告觐园陵。
entries.en: He toured the palace grounds, mourned the fallen glory of the former capital, ordered Jingzhao and Fufeng to prepare rites, and with solemn fasting announced his presence at the ancestral tombs.
entries.literal: He surveyed palace foundations, grieved for the old capital, issued edicts to Jingzhao and commanded Fufeng; fasting in purity he announced his visit to the imperial tombs.

entries.zh: 凄然有怀祖之思，喟乎以思诸夏之隆。
entries.en: He was stirred by thoughts of his forebears and sighed over the grandeur the Central States once knew.
entries.literal: Sadly he harbored thoughts of his ancestors; sighing, he recalled the splendor of the Hua domains.

entries.zh: 遂天旋云游，造舟于渭，北<方亢>泾流。
entries.en: Then, as if heaven wheeled overhead, he launched vessels on the Wei and bent his course north along the Jing River.
entries.literal: Thereupon Heaven seemed to wheel and clouds to drift; he built boats on the Wei and proceeded north along the current of the Jing.

entries.zh: 千乘方毂，万骑骈罗，衍陈于岐、梁，东横乎大河。
entries.en: Thousands of chariots squared their tracks and myriad horsemen filled the roads; the columns swept Qi and Liang and stretched east across the Yellow River.
entries.literal: A thousand chariots squared their hubs, ten thousand riders ranged in rows; formations stretched across Qi and Liang and bridged eastward over the great Yellow River.

entries.zh: 瘗后土，礼圜郊。
entries.en: He buried offerings to the Earth Spirit and performed the rites at the round suburban altar.
entries.literal: He buried offerings to Hou Tu and performed the rite at the round suburban altar.

entries.zh: 其岁四月，反于洛都。
entries.en: In the fourth month of that year he turned back toward Luoyang, the eastern capital.
entries.literal: That same fourth month he returned to Luoyang, the eastern capital.

entries.zh: 明年，有诏复函谷关，作大驾宫、六王邸、高车厩于长安。
entries.en: The following year an order reopened Hangu Pass and raised the Grand Procession Hall, guest residences for the royal princes, and tall-chariot stables at Chang'an.
entries.literal: The next year an edict restored Hangu Pass and built the Grand Procession palace, the lodges for the six kings, and the tall-chariot stables at Chang'an.

entries.zh: 修理东都城门，桥泾、渭，往往缮离观。
entries.en: Workers repaired the eastern capital's gates, spanned the Jing and Wei with bridges, and patched lookout towers along the way.
entries.literal: They repaired the gates of the eastern capital, bridged the Jing and Wei, and here and there restored detached watchtowers.

entries.zh: 东临霸、浐，西望昆明，北登长平，规龙首，抚未央，覛平乐，仪建章。
entries.en: To the east lay Ba and Chan; to the west, Kunming Pool; climbing Changping in the north they traced Longshou Hill, walked Weiyang and Pingle, and measured Jianzhang Palace against the sky.
entries.literal: Eastward they overlooked Ba and Chan; westward Kunming Pool; northward they climbed Changping, surveyed Longshou, paced Weiyang, viewed Pingle, and took the measure of Jianzhang.

entries.zh: 逮及亡新，时汉之衰，偷忍渊囿，篡器慢违，徒以势便，莫能卒危。
entries.en: When Xin fell and Han tottered, Wang Mang lurked in that same fertile basin, stole the regalia and mocked Heaven's charge, trusting only convenience—yet even he could not finish the ruin he began.
entries.literal: When it came to doomed Xin, at the hour of Han's decline, sneaking patience in the imperial preserve, usurping the vessels and slighting the mandate, relying merely on convenience—they could not in the end bring down the peril.

entries.zh: 假之十八，诛自京师。
entries.en: Eighteen years into his reign, retribution arrived out of the capital.
entries.literal: After eighteen years of usurpation, punishment came from the capital.

entries.zh: 天畀更始，不能引维。
entries.en: Heaven raised up Emperor Gengshi, yet no hand could steady the traces.
entries.literal: Heaven invested Gengshi but could not hold the reins.

entries.zh: 慢藏招寇，复致赤眉。
entries.en: Slipshod guarding drew marauders and summoned the Red Eyebrows anew.
entries.literal: Careless hoarding invited bandits and once again brought the Red Eyebrows.

entries.zh: 海内雲擾，諸夏滅微。
entries.en: The empire seethed like storm clouds; the Central States verged on collapse.
entries.literal: Within the seas storm-clouds boiled; the Hua heartland flickered toward extinction.

entries.zh: 群龙并战，未知是非。
entries.en: Contenders rose like rival dragons; no one knew which cause was just.
entries.literal: Many dragons battled together; none could tell right from wrong.

entries.zh: 于时圣帝，赫然申威，荷天人之符，兼不世之姿。
entries.en: Then our sage lord revealed awe-inspiring might, shouldered the mandate of Heaven and humanity, and embodied a presence beyond common kings.
entries.literal: Then the sage emperor blazed forth his majesty, bore the tally uniting Heaven and man, and united an aura not seen in ordinary ages.

entries.zh: 受命于皇上，获助于灵祇。
entries.en: He took his mandate from on high and won help from the spirits.
entries.literal: He received the charge from High Heaven and aid from the numinous spirits.

entries.zh: 立号高邑，搴旗四麾。
entries.en: He proclaimed his reign from Gaoyi and planted standards on every front.
entries.literal: He raised his title at Gaoyi and seized banners on every quarter.

entries.zh: 首策之臣，运筹出奇；
entries.en: The counselors who framed the opening moves devised stratagems no one foresaw;
entries.literal: Ministers who first devised strategy plotted surprises beyond reckoning;

entries.zh: 虓怒之旅；
entries.en: Behind them came armies that howled with rage;
entries.literal: troops roaring with rage;

entries.zh: 如虎如螭。
entries.en: fierce as tigers and hornless dragons.
entries.literal: like tigers and hornless dragons.

entries.zh: 师之攸向，无不靡披。
entries.en: Wherever those hosts marched, nothing stood uncut.
entries.literal: Wherever the army turned, nothing escaped being swept flat.

entries.zh: 盖夫燔鱼剸蛇，莫之方斯。
entries.en: Not even the oldest tales of burning fish and slicing serpents equal such speed.
entries.literal: Surely even burning fish and slicing snakes cannot match this.

entries.zh: 大呼山东，响动流沙。
entries.en: Their war cry east of the mountains rattled the sands beyond the frontier.
entries.literal: A great shout east of the mountains shook the drifting sands.

entries.zh: 要龙渊，首镆铘，命腾太白，亲发狼、弧。
entries.en: He belted Longyuan, raised Moyé, called on the White Planet to rise, and shot on foot toward Bow and Wolf.
entries.literal: He girded the sword of Longyuan, brandished Moyé, commanded the star Tai-bai to sweep aloft, and himself drew the Bow and Wolf constellations.

entries.zh: 南禽公孙，北背强胡，西平陇、冀，东据洛都。
entries.en: To the south he trapped Gongsun Shu; to the north he threw back the steppe riders; to the west he quieted Long and Ji; to the east he anchored the seat at Luoyang.
entries.literal: Southward he caged Gongsun Shu; northward he turned back the fierce Hu; westward he pacified Long and Ji; eastward he seized the Luoyang capital.

entries.zh: 乃廓平帝宇，济蒸人于涂炭，成兆庶之□，遂兴复乎大汉。
entries.en: He swept the world clear, snatched the common folk from ruin, secured the multitude's well-being—one graph missing here—and thus restored the Han house.
entries.literal: Thus he cleared the imperial realm, lifted the people from fire and flood, secured the teeming millions' welfare where one graph is missing in the received text, and revived great Han.

entries.zh: 今天下新定，矢石之勤始瘳，而主上方以边垂为忧，忿葭萌之不柔，未遑于论都而遗思雍州也。
entries.en: The empire is only just stable; the scars of siege are still fresh, yet the throne worries about the marches, bristles at stubborn Jiameng, and cannot spare breath for capital polemics while Yongzhou slips from mind.
entries.literal: Now the realm is newly settled; the wounds of arrow and stone have barely scarred, yet our ruler already frets the frontiers, burns over Jiameng's defiance, and has no leisure to debate capitals while forgetting Yongzhou.

entries.zh: 方躬劳圣思，以率海内，厉抚名将，略地疆外，信威于征伐，展武乎荒裔。
entries.en: He pours his own counsel into governing the heartland, steadies renowned commanders, pushes the frontier outward, lets punitive awe speak for itself, and flaunts force even in the outer wastes.
entries.literal: Just now he bends his own sagely thought to lead the interior, heartens famous generals, extends control beyond the borders, spreads awe through campaigns, and displays arms in the farthest wilds.

entries.zh: 若夫文身鼻饮缓耳之主，椎结左衽□鍝之君，东南殊俗不羁之国，西北绝域难制之邻，靡不重译纳贡，请为籓臣。
entries.en: From tattooed chiefs with bored ears to skirted lords in far provinces—one character is damaged here—southeastern peoples outside the norm and northwestern neighbors beyond easy rule: every one sent interpreters, delivered tribute, and asked to serve as outer subjects.
entries.literal: As for lords who tattoo their bodies, drink through the nose, or lengthen their ears, chiefs with topknots and left-lapped robes with belt ornaments damaged in the text, exotic realms of the southeast that defy control, remote neighbors of the northwest hard to bind—none failed to send relay interpreters with tribute and beg to become vassals.

entries.zh: 上犹谦让，而不伐勤。
entries.en: The Son of Heaven stays modest and refuses to trumpet battlefield glory.
entries.literal: The sovereign still demurs and will not boast of military toil.

entries.zh: 意以为获无用之虏，不如安有益之民；
entries.en: He judges worthless prisoners a bad bargain beside citizens who can feed the realm;
entries.literal: His meaning is that useless captives are a poor exchange for settled, productive people;

entries.zh: 略荒裔之地，不如保殖五谷之渊；
entries.en: grabbing sterile frontier acres matters less than tending the breadbasket heartland;
entries.literal: seizing barren border wastes is a poor exchange for guarding the granaries of the five grains;

entries.zh: 远救于已亡，不若近而存存也。
entries.en: rescuing the ruined far away cannot match protecting what still breathes close at hand.
entries.literal: distant succor for what is already lost cannot compare with cherishing what still lives nearby.

entries.zh: 今国家躬修道德，吐惠含仁，湛恩沾洽，时风显宣。
entries.en: The state walks the moral path openly, seasons policy with mercy, lets generous edicts soak every district, and lets honest winds blow everywhere.
entries.literal: Today the court cultivates virtue in person, exhales kindness and breathes benevolence; deep grace saturates the land and timely instruction shines abroad.

entries.zh: 徒垂意于持平守实，务在爱育元元，苟有便于王政者，圣主纳焉。
entries.en: Its aim is steady fairness and tangible good for the black-haired masses; any measure that truly helps the throne, the sage accepts.
entries.literal: It aims only at balance and substance, cherishing the common people; whatever serves royal government, the sage ruler adopts.

entries.zh: 何则？
entries.en: Why so?
entries.literal: Why?

entries.zh: 物罔挹而不损，道无隆而不移，阳盛则运，阴满则亏，故存不忘亡，安不讳危，虽有仁义，犹设城池也。
entries.en: Pour from any vessel and it empties; lift any doctrine and it shifts; thriving yang rolls onward, filling yin withdraws—so remember doom in days of peace and name danger in times of calm; even under humane rule, ramparts remain necessary.
entries.literal: Nothing can be poured out without diminishing; no Way waxes without shifting; when yang peaks it moves on; when yin fills it ebbs—therefore even while preserving life remember ruin, and even in safety speak of peril; though benevolence and right prevail, still build walls and moats.

entries.zh: 昔在强秦，爰初开畔，霸自岐、雍，国富人衍，卒以并兼，桀虐作乱。
